en: Preface to the Continued Commentary on the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* Although the Great Hero (the Buddha) manifested in the human realm and taught immeasurable Dharma-gates, if one summarizes their ultimate destination, they converge solely upon the One Mind.
If one traces the branching streams of these teachings, there are three schools: namely, the Faxiang (Dharma-characteristics), the Poxiang (Destruction of characteristics), and the...

It is merely the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). As for what is called "characteristics of phenomena" (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), it refers to establishing the five positions, opening up the hundred dharmas, positing the three natures, and distinguishing the two selves based upon the eight consciousnesses of arising and ceasing.
In this system, practice must rely on gradual fulfillment, and the afflictions must be expected to be gradually severed.
The fruit must necessarily be established over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. Therefore, there are the six *pāramitās* to be cultivated, ignorance to be overcome, and *bodhi* to be realized;
in terms of the teaching, this constitutes the gradual approach. This is the great purport of the Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

As for those who speak of "shattering characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-bhaṅga*), it means relying on the single mind of quiescent extinction to directly manifest true nature, without speaking of the characteristics of phenomena; regarding all that exists—
These are merely false imaginings. The entire dharma-realm is beyond words; the five dharmas and the three natures are both empty.

The eight consciousnesses and the two kinds of selflessness are all discarded. The teachings are censured to encourage detachment; appearances are destroyed and the mind is extinguished. To give rise to a thought is itself delusion.
Non-arising is itself Buddhahood. There are no six perfections to be cultivated, no ignorance to be overcome, and no enlightenment to be realized.
Within the teachings, there is no suddenness; this is the great purport of the "Destruction of Characteristics" (Poxiang).

As for the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), it is unified within the quiescent single mind, yet manifests as the six coarse and three subtle levels of consciousness. Therefore, the gate of True Suchness (tathatā) is opened to reveal emptiness.
Regarding all that exists: by establishing the gate of arising and ceasing, one clarifies that all things are ultimately non-existent.
Although True Suchness is vast and expansive, karmic retribution is not lost; although delusions and karma are in chaotic profusion, the Dharma-nature remains unmoving.

It is essence and appearance simultaneously; it is emptiness and existence simultaneously; it is delusion and truth simultaneously. Within the teachings, this constitutes sudden enlightenment and gradual cultivation—this is the Dharma-nature.
This is the general tenor [of their doctrine]. Therefore, those who follow the Dharma-characteristics (Faxiang) maintain that True Suchness is unchanging and do not admit that it follows conditions;

they assert merely that all phenomena arise from the transformations of consciousness and that every particular thing exists as a substantial reality. The flaw in this view is that it leads to a form of eternalism.

Regarding those who hold to a dogmatic position and destroy appearances: they claim that phenomena arising through conditions do not enter into the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), and therefore assert that the three realms are merely the one mind, while all phenomena are empty.
The corruption of this view flows into nihilism; it constitutes a reckless and chaotic doctrine. Regarding the *dharmatā*:
it refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is unchanging yet, by following conditions, is able to give rise to all phenomena. Therefore...
There is no fault of the mutual emptiness of phenomena and their nature, for True Suchness remains unchanging while following conditions, thereby being able to dissolve all phenomena;

thus, there is no partiality toward the mutual existence of things and events. In this way, emptiness and existence manifest alternately, and the extremes of attachment and nihilism are both discarded.
Therefore, we know that to manifest existence by means of the myriad dharmas is "wondrous existence" (miaoyou), and to manifest emptiness apart from the myriad dharmas is "true emptiness" (zhenkong).
To manifest the Middle Way through neither identity nor separation is to manifest wondrous existence by means of true emptiness;
thus, although it is empty, it is not empty. It is to manifest true emptiness by means of wondrous existence; thus, although it exists, it does not exist. However,
Although the two preceding schools differ in their respective establishments, each possesses its own profound intent.

However, Aśvaghoṣa unifies them all under the single mind and nine consciousnesses, much like the three legs of a tripod or the three dots of the character "伊" (yi). They are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither separate nor identical.

This truly accords with the principle of the single mind and three contemplations (*ekacitta-trivipaśyanā*) in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, proceeding side by side without contradiction. This [is the teaching of] Aśvaghoṣa...
The *Awakening of Faith* (Mingyi lun) is particularly profound, all-encompassing, and unimpeded; it stands alone, surpassing all others without rival.
Regarding the composition of this treatise, there is a commentary by Bodhisattva Fazang and a sub-commentary by Xianshou.

Since Yongming Yanshou took this treatise as his basis to compose the *Zongjing*, I have compiled those passages from within the *Zongjing* that mutually elucidate one another to create this "Continued Sub-commentary" (*Xusbu*). As for the term "Continued Sub-commentary," it continues the work of Xianshou.
This commentary clarifies that [the teachings] do not lie outside of Xianshou (Fazang), yet it does not exhaustively cover Xianshou’s thought either.
Within it, the establishment of the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—the general and the specific—is set forth as the structural framework for the entire treatise.

If one understands the treatise through these measures of valid cognition, one will not only comprehend the single school of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), but will simultaneously understand both the schools of Dharma-characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) and the refutation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vibhāga*).
A Brief Biography of the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, the Master of the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
The Great Being Aśvaghoṣa was a native of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. In former times, he was the King of the Vaiśālī kingdom.
Because there was a class of people in that country who were naked, like horses stripped bare, the king then exercised his supernormal powers and divided his body into many forms.
He was clothed in silk produced by silkworms. Later, he was born in Central India; because his horse neighed mournfully out of longing for him, he was named Aśvaghoṣa (Horse-Neigh).
He is also called Guṇabhadra, so named because his various merits, both active and unconditioned, were most preeminent.
At that time, the eleventh patriarch, the Venerable Punanayasa, arrived in that country.
A certain elder came to the Dharma assembly, and the Patriarch said to the multitude, "Do you recognize this person who has come?
The Buddha prophesied that the noble Mātr̥ceṭa shall succeed to my Dharma. Thereupon, Mātr̥ceṭa paid his respects and asked, "I wish to know the Buddha; which one is he?"
"This is it. The Patriarch said, "If you wish to recognize the Buddha, that which you do not recognize is he. He asked, "Since I do not recognize the Buddha, how can I know that it is he?
The Patriarch said, "Since you do not recognize the Buddha, how can you know that it is not he? He said, "This is the meaning of the saw. The Patriarch said, "That is the meaning of the wood.
The Patriarch asked, "What is the meaning of the saw? He replied, "It emerges level with the Master. [The Patriarch] struck him and then questioned him further.
"What is the meaning of 'wood'? The Patriarch said, "You have been liberated by me. Asvaghosa attained sudden and thorough enlightenment; he then requested ordination.

The Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying, "The Tathāgata made a prophecy that six hundred years after his parinirvāṇa, Asvaghosa would appear in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī to subdue the heretics and deliver immeasurable people, thereby receiving the transmission of the Dharma. Later, at Huā... [text ends]
The Master turned the wondrous Wheel of Dharma in the kingdom, manifesting various supernormal powers and subduing the works of Māra.
At that time, a non-Buddhist sought to debate the Master. The king’s ministers and the fourfold assembly were assembled together at the site of the debate.
The Master asked, "What is the fundamental tenet of your doctrine? He replied, "Whatever is spoken, I am able to refute it all. The Master then pointed to the king and said, "When [the king]..."
Now that the king is in good health and long-lived, I entreat you to shatter [this work]; thus the heretics will be subdued.
Later, he composed the *Ikṣu-śāstra* in one hundred thousand verses, further compiling the essential meanings of a hundred Mahāyāna sūtras to create this treatise.
It may be said that among all medicines, he has taken only the excellence of *ādarśa*; from among all jewels, he has sought only the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*).
A single pearl can cover all others; by means of the root, the branches are subsumed.
This concludes the Brief Biography of the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa, the Master of the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (details are found in the Master’s full biography).
*Continued Commentary on the Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, Volume One.
Composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa;
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Liang Dynasty,
the Śramaṇa Jñānagupta, who served as the interpreter for Prince Puṣyavarman of the Yuezhi Kingdom.
An Explanation of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* by Tongrun.

In elucidating the two characters "Mahāyāna" (Great Vehicle), it refers to the essence of the mind which is nameless and formless, neither ceasing nor arising, a luminous clarity beyond all dependence.
Because this mind universally pervades and contains all things, it is called "Great" (*mahā*); because it carries and conveys all beings, it is called "Vehicle" (*yāna*).
It is called "Vehicle" (yāna). If one discusses its meaning based on the literal text, it is "Great" because this Dharma possesses the three greatnesses of essence, characteristics, and function.
It is a "Vehicle" when spoken of in terms of persons, because this Dharma is that which all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas ride upon.
If one discusses the meaning based on the treatises, then the two characters "Mahāyāna" apply to both person and Dharma; for example, there may be a person who gives rise to the Great Mind.
Cultivating the great cause and realizing the great fruit—such a person is one of the Mahāyāna, and this teaching is called the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Because the vehicle upon which they ride is great, the person who rides it is likewise called great. Thus begins the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
This Mahāyāna Dharma is equally and fully possessed by all sentient beings; yet, due to a lack of the power of faith, they are unwilling to mount it, and the Way likewise does not carry them.
Consequently, they remain long submerged in the ocean of suffering and drowned in the river of heterodoxy.
Now, this treatise elucidates this meaning, desiring that people give rise to right faith and mount upon this Great Dharma. The aforementioned four characters are [the title].

That which is explained is the subject matter, while the treatise (*śāstra*) is that which explains it. This means that by carefully clarifying the two fundamental texts and precisely determining their ultimate intent, it enables those of initial resolve to easily believe and easily enter [the path];
therefore, it is called a "treatise. Question: For a practitioner of initial resolve who believes in this Mahāyāna, what superior power does this entail?
Answer: If one possesses correct understanding that is perfectly clear and enters with decisive faith, there is the merit of transcending kalpas, and one attains—

By the power of attaining sainthood, though dwelling within birth and death, they constantly enter nirvana; though perpetually abiding amidst the dust and toil of the world, they never depart from the pure realm.
They manifest with the physical eye while opening the radiance of the wisdom-eye; without altering their ordinary mind, they immediately share the knowledge and vision of the Buddha’s mind.
It is like a prince possessing the true marks of a sovereign, or like the kalaviṅka bird surpassing the song of all other birds.
Using a lion’s sinew as a lute string, its lingering resonance cuts off all other sounds; using the *sudarśana* medicine to treat illness, all ailments vanish without a trace.
It possesses the efficacy of Nara’s arrows, piercing through iron drums, and the power of a vajra hammer.
If one intends to shatter the mountain of gold, then the dust and toil of afflictions will extinguish themselves without waiting for their severance;

the wondrous fruit of Bodhi will be spontaneously realized without depending on cultivation. Thus, one comes to regard enemies and kin as equal, harmonizes disputes and arguments, aligns the ordinary and the sage, dissolves self and other, transcends coming and going, seals identity and difference, merges the long and the short, and blends the center and the periphery. The worldly and world-transcending dharmas are thus [inseparable].
He speaks with the power of the unspeakable, such that none can surpass him. The *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* states:

"For example, suppose there were a person who could chew Mount Sumeru, fly through the void, cross the ocean on a raft of stone, and carry the four continents along with Mount Sumeru upon their back."
Using the legs of mosquitoes as a ladder, one ascends to the Brahma palace. When the kalpa ends in flames, a single spurt of saliva instantly extinguishes the kalpa-fire;

a single breath instantly restores the world. To suspend Mount Sumeru with a lotus fiber or to catch the rain from the four continents with one's hand—though such feats may be performed, they are not yet considered difficult.
What the Tathāgata has taught—that which is signless, unconditioned, unborn, and undying—is truly difficult.
To cause people to believe and understand the single-flavor Mahāyāna dharma-characteristic of equality is indeed difficult.
This is because those who give rise to this mind can overturn all gates of worldly affliction (*kleśa*) and accomplish the eighty-four thousand gates of samādhi. It continues:
"This mind is the greatest among the great, the highest among the high, the most perfect among the perfect, the most complete among the complete, and the truest among the true."
It is true; it is the reality within reality, the inconceivable within the inconceivable.
As soon as one is willing to believe and enter, it is like the lion’s majestic leap—most fierce and heroic—or the elephant king’s trampling stride—its power peerless.
Therefore, those who wish to enter this gate cannot do so without the power of faith. For this reason, this treatise is titled *The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna*.

I take refuge in those who have reached the end of the ten directions, the most excellent ones with all-encompassing knowledge, who possess mastery over form without obstruction, the Great Compassionate Saviors of the world;
and in their physical forms and marks, the ocean of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-tathatā*), the treasury of immeasurable merit, and those who practice according to reality.

In order to cause sentient beings to eliminate doubt, abandon false attachments, and give rise to right faith in the Mahāyāna, so that the lineage of the Buddhas shall not be severed, I intend to compose this treatise;

therefore, I first pay homage to the Triple Gem and state the reasons for composing this treatise. In the opening four lines, I take refuge in the Buddha-gem, which refers to both the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body).

Because no other holy ones can equal him, he is called "supreme" (*agrya*). He is able to transcend the... [one... *(Note: The source text appears to be a fragment from Vasubandhu’s commentary on the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, specifically the section concerning the homage verse. The translation reflects the provided fragment while maintaining the technical terminology and flow of the original.)*
Because he transcends all [conditioned] phenomena, he is called "Victorious" (Jina). His "activity" refers to the functional operation of the three wheels, which is the inconceivable activity.
"Universal Knowledge" is the supremacy of his mental activity (*manas-karman*); "unimpeded mastery over form" is the supremacy of his physical activity (*kāya-karman*);

and "Savior of the World" is the supremacy of his verbal activity (*vāk-karman*). The Tathāgata has no mind of his own; he takes the minds of sentient beings as his own mind, and thus is able to possess universal knowledge. As it is said:
The Tathāgata has no body; he takes the bodies of sentient beings as his own body, and thus attains unimpeded mastery over form. The Tathāgata has no speech;
yet, he preaches the Dharma according to the faculties and capacities of sentient beings, and thus is able to save the world.
These most excellent three karmas are all accomplished through the Tathāgata’s great compassion of identical essence, which entirely accords with the minds of sentient beings.

Because [the Buddha] manifests [thus], it is collectively termed "Great Compassion. The character "zhě" (者) concludes the description of virtues and attributes them to the person. As for the two subsequent lines, they constitute the taking of refuge in the Dharma Jewel.

Regarding the phrase "and that 'zhě'": this refers back to and points toward the two Buddhas of recompense and transformation. As for the phrase "the body and its marks": this indicates that the essential form of the two bodies—recompense and transformation—is taken as the Dharma-body;
thus, the Dharma-body itself constitutes the Dharma Jewel. This is what is meant by: [The text continues: ...the so-called...
The *dharmatā-kāya* (Dharma-nature body) is the essence of *tathatā* (suchness). Regarding "Dharma-nature," it is the self-nature of all phenomena (*dharma*).
Regarding "suchness," it is a designation for that which is non-delusive and unchanging. Because it is profound, vast, and boundless, it is metaphorically compared to the ocean.
That a Buddha is a Buddha and that a Saṃgha is a Saṃgha both rely upon this Dharma; therefore, the subsequent passage states: "All Buddhas..."
Because it is that which all Bodhisattvas ride upon to reach the stage of the Tathāgata.
The two phrases concerning "the immeasurable" constitute the taking of refuge in the Saṅgha Jewel. This means that within the ocean of *dharmatā*, immeasurable merits are fully present;

when one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*), one realizes this nature. From this nature, one gives rise to cultivation and practices the practice of reality itself, which is called "cultivation like a jewel."

Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*): it refers to the various stages (*bhūmi*). Because those in the stage of the three levels of worthiness (*tri-śukla-bhūmi*) practice according to the perfuming of the Dharma (*dharma-vāsanā*), they have not yet realized the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and thus are not called "as-it-is" (*yathābhūta*).
Some take the single phrase "repository of immeasurable merit" (*apramāṇa-guṇa-garbha*) as belonging to the preceding section;
however, according to the later translation which reads "the Saṃgha, a repository of boundless virtues, who diligently seeks perfect enlightenment," it belongs to the following sentence.
Next, in order to provide the basis for composing this treatise, [the author] proceeds as follows:
Because sentient beings do not believe that True Suchness is the essence of the single Dharma-realm, the great universal characteristic Dharma-gate, they give rise to false conceptualizations.

Furthermore, because they do not know that the Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome, they recklessly give rise to erroneous thoughts. Therefore, the treatise first demonstrates the correct meaning so that they may...
This is to eliminate doubt. As for the counteractive treatment of false attachments, it is to cause them to relinquish those attachments.

As for the detailed analysis of the characteristics of setting out upon the path, it is to cause them to give rise to the faculty of faith and thereby mount the Great Dharma. Only when one possesses correct faith and mounts the Great Dharma can one ensure that the life-force of wisdom of the Triple Gem is perpetuated without interruption.
The Commentary states: There is a dharma (the mind) that possesses the functional capacity to give rise to the faculty of faith in Mahāyāna;

therefore, this should be explained. This is the fundamental thesis of this treatise. "There is a dharma" refers to the primordially existing dharma. According to the subsequent text, it contains two meanings:
first, it is the dharma of the original essence, which is the single essence of Mahāyāna dharma, eternally constant and unchanging.

The first is the provisional cultivation and accomplishment, which belongs to the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*). The second is the fundamental dharma of its own nature; that is, the Mahāyāna dharma of self-essence, self-characteristic, and self-function.
That delusion awakens to awakening and awakening awakens from delusion is entirely due to perfuming (*vāsanā*), which belongs to the *ālayavijñāna*.
Because sentient beings neither know that True Suchness is pure awakening nor know that the *ālaya* is the gateway between delusion and awakening.
Because they give rise to false attachments and produce divergent heterodoxies, the Master of the Treatise first sets forth the two characters "dharmin" (the subject) as the foundation of the thesis.
Next, taking this dharmin within the section on establishing the meaning, he formulates the formal inference (*pramāṇa*) in general terms: The mind of sentient beings is the dharmin;
To manifest the meaning of Mahāyāna is the thesis (*pakṣa*); The reason (*hetu*) is: because true thusness (*tathatā*) and arising-and-ceasing mutually encompass one another.

The concordant example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is like a golden ornament. Furthermore, regarding the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā-mukha*), a separate formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established as follows:
"True Suchness" is the subject (*dharmin*); "it is the essence of the Dharma-gate of the Great Universal Characteristic of the Single Dharma-realm" is the thesis (*pakṣa*).

The reason (*hetu*) is: "because it is neither born nor extinguished. The concordant example is like space. Furthermore, regarding the gate of Arising and Ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*), a separate formal argument is established as follows: "The Ālaya..."
The *ālaya-vijñāna* is an existent phenomenon (*dharmin*). That it is a synthesis of the unborn and undying with the birth-and-death [process] is the thesis (*pakṣa*).

The reason (*hetu*) is: "because it is neither identical nor different. The concordant example (*sapakṣa*) is like atoms and earthenware vessels. These three syllogisms—general and specific—are established as the framework of this treatise.
It requires that one first suddenly awaken to True Suchness (*tathatā*) within one's own person, and subsequently [awaken] to the birth-and-death [process].
Because one gradually cultivates and gradually realizes within the gates [of practice], it is called Mahāyāna;
this is translated as "Great Vehicle" (*Mahāyāna*), for these two gates are both the dharmas practiced by those of great capacity. "Faith" (*śraddhā*) is one of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
There are three kinds of faith: first, faith in actual existence, which means having deep faith and acceptance regarding the true facts and principles of all phenomena. Second...
Faith in virtue means that one has deep faith and delight in the true and pure virtues of the Triple Gem.
Faith in capability means that one has deep faith in the power of all mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas to be attained and accomplished, thereby giving rise to aspiration.
Only by possessing this faculty of faith can one enter [the path]. Long ago, Venerable Yan-yang asked Zhaozhou:
"When not a single thing is brought forth, what then? Yangzhou said, "Put it down. Yang said, "If not a single thing is brought forth, what is there to put down?
Yangzhou said, "Then take it up and go. At this, Yang attained great enlightenment.
This is one who develops the root of faith from the Dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Luoshan asked Yantou, "Arising and ceasing never cease."
"How is it at that time? Tou replied, "Tsk! Who is it that arises and ceases? At this, Luoshan attained great enlightenment.

This is because one who possesses the faculty of faith arising from the *ālayavijñāna* (the storehouse consciousness) can be a teacher of others. Thus, the *Zongjing* says: "The true orthodox lineage of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is True Consciousness-Only (*tathatā-vijñaptimātra*).
As soon as there is a point of faith, one is capable of being a person for others. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states, faith is the hand; like a person who has hands, [one can grasp the Dharma].
Upon reaching the place of jewels, one may gather them at will; yet if one lacks hands, one will obtain nothing at all.
Likewise, those who enter the Buddha-dharma possess the hand of faith, by which they may gather the jewels of the path and dharma at will; if they lack faith, they shall obtain nothing.
Emptiness has nothing to be attained; yet there is this benefit, and for that reason I have composed this treatise.

It consists of five divisions. What are these five? First, the Division on Causes and Conditions (the causes being identical). Second, the Division on Establishing the Thesis (briefly indicating the great meaning).

Third, the Division on Exegesis (extensively explaining so as to produce understanding in others). Fourth, the Division on Cultivating Faith (arousing practice based upon understanding). Fifth, the Division on the Benefits of Encouraging Practice (arguing that failing to practice the Dharma is like a poor man counting another’s treasures, and thus encouraging practice).

The Section on Causes and Conditions (*nidāna*) sets forth the origins for composing this treatise. The Section on Establishing the Meaning (*arthavyavasthāpana*) establishes the great principles of this treatise.

The Section on Exegesis (*vyākhyāna*) analyzes the subtle and hidden points of the established meaning. The Section on Cultivating Faith (*śraddhābhāvanā*) is for those whose faith is not yet perfected, so that they may cultivate it.
The Section on Encouraging Practice and Benefits (*anuśaṃsā-praśaṃsā*) encourages people to advance in practice so that they will certainly obtain benefit. If...

This should be understood according to the three divisions of a typical sūtra: the first is the introduction (nidāna), the next three constitute the main body (śarīra), and the last is the dissemination (pariṇāmanā).
The first part explains the causal conditions (hetu-pratyaya). Question: What are the causes and conditions for composing this treatise? Answer: These are the causes and conditions.
There are eight kinds. What are these eight? First is the general characteristic of the causal conditions for the great matter:
namely, to cause sentient beings to leave all suffering behind and attain ultimate bliss, rather than seeking worldly fame, profit, or honor.

The causes and conditions for composing this treatise are both general and specific. Regarding the general, it refers to the overall reasons for composing the treatise. Regarding the specific, it clarifies the particular purpose of this treatise.

Suffering consists of the three types of suffering, the eight types of suffering, and the suffering of the two kinds of death. Happiness consists of the happiness of humans and devas, that of the two vehicles, and the bliss of cessation (*nirvāṇa*).
What is now called "being free from all suffering" refers to being free from the suffering of birth and death within the realms of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*).
The two types of death refer to the suffering of transformation and change. What is now called "attaining ultimate bliss" refers to attaining the bliss of unsurpassed bodhi and great nirvāṇa.
Second, it is intended to explain the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata, so that all sentient beings may attain correct understanding without error.

Therefore, there are two fundamental roots: first, True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is the root of Bodhi and Nirvana; second, Ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the root of the three subtle and six coarse states.
Now, when it is said that the Tathāgata is the fundamental root, it is intended to lead people toward the root of ignorance.

Because this very limit enters into the fundamental state of the Tathāgata. As the subsequent text states: "Its essential purport is none other than to transcend conceptual thought and return to suchness.
Correct understanding (*samyag-adhimokṣa*) is precisely *adhimokṣa* (resolute conviction); it has the nature of confirming and maintaining a determined object.
It is an action that cannot be diverted; it is one of the five object-specific mental factors (*pañca-viṣaya-niyata*).

Because there is right faith (*samyak-śraddhā*), correct understanding (*samyag-adhimukti*) can arise. Thus, while "right faith" was mentioned previously, "correct understanding" is stated here again.

When this correct understanding exists, one perceives reality without error and is also able to rectify the errors of others. Therefore, this corresponds to the subsequent section which reveals the correct meaning as an antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
It is a false attachment.
Third, it is for the sake of causing those sentient beings whose roots of goodness have matured to become capable of non-retrogressive faith in the Mahāyāna Dharma.
"Ripened" means that the locus of ripening has already arisen and the locus of birth has already matured. "Capable" means being able to shoulder this task without ever falling back or losing it.

Therefore, the subsequent text says: "That is to say, based on sentient beings of the indeterminate group, because they possess the power of the roots of goodness cultivated through perfuming, they believe in the retribution of karma and its fruits, are able to give rise to the ten wholesome actions, and feel weary of the suffering of birth and death, desiring to seek [liberation]."
Regarding supreme bodhi, one practices with faith for ten thousand kalpas. When this faith is perfected, one enters the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and never again regresses;

thus one abides within the lineage of the Tathāgata. This is called the "accomplishment of faith," and it corresponds to the characteristics of the stage of setting out on the path (*pratipatti-mārga*).
Fourth, it is for the sake of causing sentient beings with meager roots of goodness to cultivate faith.

Although faith has been aroused, their manifest delusions have not yet been eliminated; their resolve is unstable, and in their daily routines they are constantly turned by delusions, unable to remain single-minded.
Therefore, they are said to have "meager roots of goodness" and their faith is not yet fulfilled, such that they are unable to bear [the burden].
Entrusting them with the Great Dharma, [the Buddha] causes them to cultivate faith. As the subsequent text states:

"If there are sentient beings whose roots of goodness are meager and whose afflictions have been deep and thick for a long time, even if they encounter a Buddha, they may give rise to the seeds of humans, devas, or the two vehicles.
Even if they seek the Mahāyāna, their faculties are not fixed; encountering adverse conditions, they immediately fall away and regress."
Because [the preceding] pertains to the stages of the two vehicles, the "Section on Cultivating Faith" is taught. Fifth,
it is to demonstrate the skillful means for eliminating the obstacles of evil karma, properly guarding the mind, remaining far removed from delusion and pride, and escaping the net of heterodoxy.
Although one has generated the mind of faith, it may be obstructed by evil karma and invaded by demons and spirits.
If one cannot protect it, one will succumb to various heterodox influences; failing to attain what has not been attained, one gives rise to ignorance and arrogance.

Therefore, expedient means are shown so that one may guard and maintain this faith without falling back or losing it. Thus, the subsequent text says: "If a person, though practicing with faith, because they..."
If you are afflicted by heavy obstacles, or distressed by demons, spirits, illness, or suffering, or entangled in worldly affairs, you should practice with courageous diligence:
pay homage to the Buddhas, repent, request [the turning of the wheel of Dharma], rejoice [in the merit of others], and dedicate [your roots of virtue] toward Bodhi, never ceasing.
One shall escape all obstacles and one's roots of goodness will increase; therefore, it is said that this is to demonstrate skillful means for the purpose of well-guarding the mind.
Or, while practicing samādhi, if various māras manifest forms to confuse and disturb one, one should cause them to observe so that they do not fall into the net of heterodoxy.
Therefore it is said: "To distance oneself from delusion and arrogance is to emerge from the net of the heterodox. This refers to the practice of the lower grade.
Sixth, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as an antidote to the mental faults of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles.
Although faith may have been generated, if there is no counteractive practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one will fall to the level of ordinary beings or the two vehicles;
therefore, one is directed to cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. As the subsequent text states:

"If one cultivates *śamatha*, it counteracts the ordinary being’s attachment to the world and enables the relinquishing of the timid views of the two vehicles. If one cultivates *vipaśyanā*, it counteracts the non-arising [of wisdom] in the two vehicles."
It is because of the fault of a narrow and inferior mind regarding great compassion, which distances one from ordinary beings and prevents the cultivation of roots of goodness;

therefore, one should practice this in a medium degree. Seventh, it is to demonstrate the skillful means (of the Pure Land) for single-minded recollection and contemplation of the Buddha, so that one may be born before the Buddha and certainly never retreat from the faith.
This means that by focusing the mind on the recitation of the Buddha's name, one protects and sustains their faith, ensuring it does not regress or fall away. As the subsequent text states:
"When sentient beings first study this Dharma and seek to attain right faith, their minds are timid and weak; they say to themselves that they cannot encounter a Buddha."
Having personally received offerings, one may fear that the mind of faith is difficult to accomplish and thus intend to retreat.

It is said that by means of the causal conditions of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation), one will be born accordingly in the Buddha-lands of other directions; because the mind of faith is constantly sustained and protected, there shall ultimately be no retreat.
This constitutes the superior grade of cultivation. The three types mentioned above are all expedient means for cultivating the mind of faith.
Eighth, it is for the purpose of demonstrating benefits and exhorting [the practitioner] to engage in cultivation. It is due to such causes and conditions that this treatise was composed.

Because one is exhorted to cultivate and spurred on, the various practices mentioned previously are accomplished; thus, this constitutes the section on the benefits of exhortation to practice, as follows.
This concludes the eightfold set of reasons for composing the treatise.
The Gate asks: "This Dharma is already fully contained within the Sūtras; why is it necessary to state it again? The Answer says:

"Although this Dharma exists within the Sūtras, because the faculties and practices of sentient beings are unequal, their conditions for receiving and understanding [it] differ—'receiving' means taking it into the mind, while 'understanding' refers to the arising of wisdom.

That is to say, when the Tathāgata was in the world, sentient beings possessed sharp faculties (referring to the Bodhisattvas), the speaker (referring to the Tathāgata) had excellence in both form and mental karma, and his single utterance of the perfect voice (referring to vocal karma) was heard equally by all diverse classes [of beings]."

If [the meaning] is already understood, then there is no need for further discussion. However, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there may be sentient beings who are able to attain understanding through extensive hearing by means of their own power;
there may be sentient beings who are also able to attain much understanding through little hearing by means of their own power;
there may be sentient beings who lack the power of their own minds and attain understanding by relying on extensive treatises; and furthermore, there may be sentient beings who...
Since an extensive treatise would be too cumbersome, for those whose minds delight in *dhāraṇī*— who can grasp the meaning through concise wording that encompasses vast significance—
this treatise (*the Awakening of Faith*) should be expounded, as it seeks to comprehensively condense the boundless meanings of the Tathāgata’s vast and profound Dharma.
The section on causes and conditions has already been explained.

This is the resolution of objections and difficulties. The objection states: As for the eight kinds of causes and conditions described above, the Tathāgata has already expounded them all in his sūtras. For what reason, then, was this treatise composed? The answer is:

Because the faculties, mental dispositions, and conduct of sentient beings vary in being sharp or dull, their reception and comprehension of either the sūtras or the treatises differ according to those specific conditions. If...
While the Tathāgata was in the world, the teacher was supreme and the disciples were strong in their capacities;

thus, when his perfect voice was uttered but once, beings of diverse natures would, upon the mere contact of their faculty of hearing, attain realization according to their respective dispositions. At that time, since there already existed the sūtras, what further need was there for śāstras?

Now, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, since there is no longer the Perfect Sound (maṇḍala-svara) of the speaker and listeners cannot understand equally, if this sūtra were not established with its great meaning and provided with detailed exegesis, I fear that those of middling and inferior capacities would never attain understanding or entry.
Therefore, following the sūtra, there are further treatises (śāstra). Thus, the sūtra possesses the merit of the sūtra, while the treatise possesses [the merit of the treatise].
Regarding the benefit of this treatise: teachings are established according to the times, each being appropriate for its particular occasion; it is not without purpose.

As for those who claim to attain understanding through their own efforts and extensive study, they possess their own discernment and further delight in widely seeking the meanings of the scriptures to gather great learning.
Regarding those whose innate disposition and intelligence are such that they possess little self-reliance yet achieve much understanding through hearing:
these individuals likewise possess their own mental power, whereby they can grasp the essentials upon briefly investigating the meaning of the scriptures.

As for those who lack this mental power and attain understanding only through extensive treatises, they are like the *siphonophora* (water mother) which has no eyes of its own and must rely on shrimp to seek food. Furthermore, for them, the extensive treatises are considered too prolix.
Regarding those who delight in *dhāraṇī*, they fear complexity and prefer simplicity;

desiring to obtain the one and thereby obtain all—this passage below clearly demonstrates that this treatise is specifically designed for this final class of practitioners. As for the phrase "vast dharma":
"True Suchness" (tathatā) is an implicit reference [to the former]. "Profound Dharma" is an implicit reference to the *ālayavijñāna*.
"Boundless Meaning" is an implicit reference to the meaning of the two gates; as the subsequent text states: "The first is the Dharma, and the second is the meaning.
This concludes the section on the causal conditions (*nidāna*).
Next, the section on establishing the doctrine (the fundamental tenet of the Mahāyāna) is explained. Regarding the Mahāyāna, there are generally two kinds. What are these two?
First, the Dharma (the essence of the treatise); second, the Meaning (its essence, characteristics, and function).
This is precisely using the aforementioned phenomena (*dharma*) to establish the meaning of Mahāyāna. "Phenomena" refers to the guiding principles;
it points to the "one mind," because the one mind serves as the guiding principle for all forms. "Meaning" refers to the fundamental tenets;

it points to the "three great aspects," because the phenomenon of the one mind possesses these three great aspects as its fundamental tenets. This is what is called the "gate of the establishing proof. Formerly, in the South...
National Teacher Yangzhong was debating on the meaning of the Dharma with Palace Attendant Zilin. The Attendant said, "I ask the Master to establish a thesis;
I shall refute it. The Master said, "The thesis has been established. The Attendant asked, "What is this thesis? The Master replied, "As expected, you do not see it. It is not within your realm.
Therefore, know that before a word is even uttered, the thesis is already established. As soon as one speaks of 'dharmas,' it is already [lost]."
Entanglements cover the ground; how much more so when every stroke of the blade is applied? It is simply because my compassionate heart could not help but speak too much.

As for that which is called "Dharma," it does not issue forth from elsewhere—it is the mind of sentient beings. This mind encompasses all mundane phenomena (the three subtleties and six gross states) and all supramundane phenomena (original suchness and the two types of awakening).
The Dharma-body transmigrates through the six realms of existence; this is what is called "sentient beings.
Therefore, the mind of sentient beings is taken as a "dharma" (an existing entity). This mind is that which encompasses all mundane and supramundane dharmas;
this explains why the mind is termed a "dharma. The single character "mind" (citta) refers to both the true and the delusive; it means that this mind is able to universally encompass them all.
The Dharma of the gate of true suchness (*tathatā*) is pure; furthermore, it universally encompasses all defiled dharmas within the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*).
Because it embraces both the real and the delusive, it universally subsumes these two gates. As the Great Sūtra says: "The mind is like a skilled painter."
All forms and images are painted forth; the five aggregates arise entirely from this. There is no phenomenon that is not created [therein]. An ancient worthy said:
"The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates all return to the single square inch of the mind. The ocean-sand-like virtues of nature are all contained within the source of the mind.
Therefore, the one mind can encompass all phenomena. The *Zongjing* asks: "The skillful means and teaching gates of all Buddhas are all based upon sentient beings..."
Roots arise; since these roots are not equal, the phenomena (dharmas) are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Why, then, is only the single mind established as the fundamental tenet? Answer:

This single mind-dharma is the perfect integration of principle and phenomena. It is the Great Compassionate Father, the Mother Prajñā, the Treasury of the Dharma Jewel, and the Source of the myriad practices.
It encompasses all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas within the entire realm of phenomena, as well as...
All sentient beings possess this same mind. The Buddhas have already awakened to it, yet sentient beings do not know it.

Now, for the sake of those who do not yet know, I shall provide a direct pointing through skillful means. Because it is inherently possessed and because it is that which should be attained, if one realizes one's own mind, [one attains Buddhahood].

One suddenly attains the wisdom of Buddhahood; this may be likened to merging a hundred rivers into a single body of water, kneading various incenses into a single pill, melting bracelets and rings into a single piece of gold, or transforming cream and curd into a single flavor. Thus, the Sūtra says: "If one does not understand one's own mind..."

How can one know the Buddha’s wisdom? Those who seek it elsewhere outside themselves and learn falsely from others are like those who drill ice to find fire or press sand to extract oil; though they desire its practical utility, their efforts are in vain.
If one can clearly realize one's own mind and not falsely seek elsewhere, it is like fire emerging from wood or oil from sesame seeds—this does not destroy the truth.
Because it can be swiftly accomplished, a single mind is established as the primary tenet.

Relying upon this mind, the meaning of the Mahāyāna is revealed. Why is this? Because the aspect of the suchness (*tathatā*) of this mind demonstrates the essence of the Mahāyāna (the seed of the Mahāyāna within its own substance);
and because the aspect of the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of this mind can demonstrate the self-nature and characteristics of the Mahāyāna.
For this reason, it is clarified here that based on the single dharma of the one mind, two types of Mahāyāna gates are established. An objection is raised:
since the mental dharma of sentient beings encompasses both the real and the false, and pervades both the defiled and the pure, the Mahāyāna is the truth mounted by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Regarding pure dharmas: could that which is mounted by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas also be permeated by defiled delusion? Answer:

Although the Mahāyāna is truly pure, it must manifest within the deluded defilement of sentient beings. This is because the mental phenomena of sentient beings possess both a defiled and a pure portion.
Now, that which is established as a single portion within the minds of sentient beings—eternal, constant, and unchanging—is called "True" (the True Mind).
Suchness. This true suchness (*tathatā*) is the pure dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, that which is established as a portion within the minds of sentient beings—the perfuming of causes and conditions for both defilement and purity—is termed the "characteristic of arising and ceasing.

Because this arising and ceasing can further manifest its own essence, its own characteristics, and its own functions, one knows that the fundamental source of the Mahāyāna Dharma is not false defilement.
Now, because we follow the perfuming of deluded defilement, it is through that very deluded defilement that [the teaching] is manifested. Question:

Why is it said in the Gate of True Suchness (tathatā) that it "manifests," whereas in the Gate of Arising and Ceasing it is said that it "is able to manifest"? Answer: Regarding the term "manifests": because the entirety of the characteristic of True Suchness is itself the Mahāyāna;
if one were to depart from True Suchness, there would be no separate essence of the Mahāyāna. Therefore, it is said to "manifest."
It is said: "This is precisely what is shown. To say "capable of showing" means that within the essence of this *tathatā* (suchness), infinite marks and functions are fully present.
These marks and functions do not depart from the arising and ceasing of the daily activities of sentient beings; therefore, they are right here at the very edge of cessation.
Furthermore, it is able to manifest the essence, characteristics, and function of True Suchness (tathatā); therefore, it is said that "it can demonstrate.
As the ancient masters have said: "If you wish to recognize the Teacher of all Buddhas, seek him within the mind of ignorance.

If you wish to recognize the nature of all things that does not wither, seek it in the midst of the shifting and changing of all things. Question: For what reason is one to enter by way of the gate of True Suchness?

Regarding the Mahāyāna Dharma that establishes only the name of its essence (*tattva*): it is the Mahāyāna Dharma entered through the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-dvāra*), wherein its own specific name is established.
Answer: Suchness (*tathatā*) is the gate of submerging characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) to reveal the nature (*dharmatā*).

It does not consort with the myriad dharmas, nor does it confront the various sense objects (*viṣaya*). Because it lacks other-characteristics (*para-lakṣaṇa*), it likewise lacks self-characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*). Since there is neither self nor other...
Therefore, its essence alone is revealed. "The other" refers to all unwholesome dharmas; "the self" refers to all pure dharmas.
Arising and ceasing is the gate of the formation of phenomena based upon principle; their essence relies entirely upon *tathatā* (suchness).
As for their characteristics and functions, they are in fact fully possessed by the very substance of *tathatā*, yet they are merely obscured by other defiled dharmas.

It cannot be manifested [in isolation]. However, it is only by refuting others that one can manifest oneself; therefore, it is said that "one can demonstrate its own essence, its own characteristics, and its own function.
This may be understood through the formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*). Thus, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says: "Mind alone is Buddha, and Buddha is likewise mind alone;

mind alone is sentient beings, and sentient beings are likewise Buddha. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. An ancient master said: "[The ordinary person] is fully endowed with..."
As for the Dharma, ordinary beings do not know it; though they possess the Dharma of the sages, the sages do not recognize it.
If ordinary beings were to know it, they would be sages; if sages were to recognize it, they would be ordinary beings. This is precisely the meaning [of this teaching]. Question:
What is the reason that the One Mind opens into two gates—True Suchness and Arising-and-Ceasing? Answer: It is because the One Mind gives rise to Mahayana faith.
The two gates refute the attachments of false views. By means of the Gate of True Suchness (*tathatā-mukha*), one gains certainty in the wondrous principle;

by means of the Gate of Arising and Ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*), one believes that karmic activity does not perish. This may be called the perfect fusion of principle and phenomenon, and the non-obstruction between the ultimate and the conventional.
The *Śīlamahāyāna-śāstra* states: "The Gate of the Mind as True Suchness has ten names. The first is called the Gate of the Tathāgatagarbha."
First is the gate of non-confusion, because there is no disorder. Second is called the gate of non-dual equality, because there is no differentiation.
Third is called the gate of the purity of the single path, because there are no divergent branches. Fourth is called the gate of non-arising and non-movement, because it is free from karmic activity.
Fifth is called the gate of no severance and no bondage, because there is no need for remedial treatment of hindrances. Sixth—
This is called the gate of neither going nor coming, because it is without ascent or descent. Seventh is called the supramundane gate, because it is without the four marks.
Eighth is called the gate of quiescent extinction, because it is without the tendency toward rebirth.
Ninth is called the gate of the great universal characteristic, because it is without particular characteristics. Tenth is called the gate of *tathatā* (suchness), because it is without falsehood.
Therefore, these ten names collectively encompass all the names of the Dharma-gates and the principles of equality within the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas.
Within the gate of arising and ceasing, there are ten kinds of names: first, it is called the Gate of the *ālayavijñāna*, because it stores and maintains all defiled and pure dharmas;
second, it is called the Gate of the *Tathāgatagarbha*, because it conceals the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata.
Therefore: Third, it is called the gate of many characteristics and many divergent aspects, because the dharmas of defilement and purity exceed the sands of the Ganges in number.

Fourth, it is called the gate of activation and movement, because of the continuous performance of karma. Fifth, it is called the gate of having severance and having bondage, because there are remedies for hindrances.
Sixth, it is called the gate of having going and having coming, because there are ascending and descending [stages]. Seventh...
The first is called the "Gate of the World," because the four characteristics (birth, abiding, change, and extinction) operate simultaneously.

The eighth is called the "Gate of Flowing On and Returning Extinction," because it fully encompasses both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. The ninth is called the "Gate of Mutual Reliance and Co-arising," because there is no phenomenon that exists through self-origination.
The tenth is called the "Gate of Arising and Ceasing," because it manifests the characteristic of impermanence. These are the ten names.
This [text] comprehensively subsumes the names of all the various differentiated dharma-gates within the treasury of all dharmas.

Therefore, one should know that while "One Mind" is established as a general designation, it contains manifold meanings. Within the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*), there is neither self nor other; within the gate of arising and ceasing, there is both good and evil.

Although they differ in their opening and closing according to conditions, when considered from the perspective of nature, the single principle is without distinction. Such are the meanings of the ten gates mentioned above.
The flavor is sufficient. Furthermore, when opened, the principle of the immeasurable and boundless is taken as the central tenet;

when closed, the dharma of the two gates within one mind is taken as the essential. As for the meaning of the two gates, they encompass ten thousand meanings without confusion; as for the meaning of the boundless, it...
They are blended and unified within a single mind; thus, opening and closing are sovereign, establishing and refuting are unimpeded.
One may open without prolixity, close without narrowness, establish without attainment, and refute without loss.
This is the marvelous technique of Aśvaghoṣa and the essential substance of the *Awakening of Faith*.

As for what is called "meaning," there are three kinds. What are these three? First is the Greatness of Essence (*tathatā*), which refers to the fact that the *tathatā* of all phenomena (whether belonging to ordinary beings or sages) is entirely pervasive and equal, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Second is the Greatness of Characteristics (*tathatā-manifested as characteristics*), which refers to the *tathāgatagarbha*, because it is fully endowed with immeasurable innate virtues.

Third is the Greatness of Function (*the inconceivable wondrous function of the sense faculties and transformation bodies, which constitutes the greatness of function*), because it can produce all wholesome causes, both mundane (such as the five precepts leading to the realms of humans and devas) and supramundane (such as the six perfections and pure conduct leading to Buddhahood).

Because it is the fruit (the above summarizes the general meaning of the word "function"). Because it is that which all Buddhas have fundamentally mounted; because all Bodhisattvas mount this Dharma and thereby reach the stage of the Tathāgata.
The section on the establishment of the doctrine has already been explained (the text must not fail to establish the doctrine, and once established, the doctrine must also be explained).
This explains the meaning of Mahāyāna. Regarding the "Greatness of Essence" (*tathatā-mahattva*):
it refers to the essence of the sentient beings' mind, which is equal and non-dual with the four types of noble ones and the six classes of ordinary beings; this is termed *tathatā*.

This nature of *tathatā* pervades all places, yet it is specifically situated within the *ālayavijñāna* cave of sentient beings; its essence has never been anything but great. Regarding the "Greatness of Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-mahattva*), it refers to...
The minds of sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and characteristics of the Tathāgata; this is called the Tathāgatagarbha.

This garbha is not empty, for it fully encompasses immeasurable innate virtues without deficiency or excess. Although it is shrouded by the karmic marks of ignorance, its nature has never ceased to be vast.
As for its "great function," it means that the minds of sentient beings possess great functional efficacy, which follows [their conditions].
Its functions are all capable of producing mundane and supramundane wholesome causes and fruits;

therefore, although it exists within the karmic activities of birth and death, its functioning has never been anything but great. Thus, even the practitioners of the Two Vehicles and ordinary beings possess this great essence.
To turn one's back on it and remain unaware of it—this is its great characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). To neglect it and disregard it—this is its great function (*vṛtti*).
To abandon it and fail to employ it—this is its great utility. Only the Buddhas ride upon this to sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*);
only the Bodhisattvas ride upon this to ascend to the shore of awakening. Because this single mind possesses these three meanings, the principle of the "one mind" is established and named "Great."

This concludes the section on the vehicle. Next is the explanation of the analytical section (*vyākhyāna-bhāga*). There are three kinds of explanation. What are the three? First, the manifestation of the correct meaning (referring to the aforementioned "meaning," namely the meaning of the Mahāyāna Dharma).
Second is the counteracting of false attachments; third is the discernment of the characteristics of setting out upon the path.
The preceding section briefly indicated its source; this section extensively expounds its branches; hence it is called "Exegesis.

That which displays the correct meaning is the door of establishment; that which counteracts false attachments is the door of refutation; and the discernment of setting out upon the path [is the door of practice].
The characteristics of the Way are the gateway for progressive cultivation. Having clarified what is deviant and what is correct, one proceeds without entering byways or detours;
it is only then that one advances in cultivation. To reveal the correct principle: based on the dharma of the one mind, there are two gates.
What are these two? First is the gate of the true suchness of the mind; second is the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind. These two gates each, in their entirety, encompass all dharmas.

What is the meaning of this? Because these two gates are not mutually exclusive, this provides a general explanation of the two meanings—true thusness (*tathatā*) and arising-and-ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*)—within the single mind as established in the "Section on the Establishment of the Meaning.
Regarding the gate of the true thusness of mind: it refers to the primordially abiding nature; it is neither defiled nor pure, neither arising nor ceasing, unmoving and non-transforming.
It is of equal and single flavor; its nature is without differentiation. This takes the ground of pure awakening as its root.

As for the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind, it refers to the nature of perfuming; it undergoes transformation according to perfuming, resulting in the defiled and the pure. Although the defiled and the pure are thus established, [the fundamental nature remains unchanged].
The nature is eternally unchanging; it is solely through immobility that it can bring about both defilement and purity. Therefore, immobility also exists within movement.

This takes the ignorance that initiates karma as its root. Question: Regarding these two minds—the true and the deluded—what constitutes their mind, what constitutes their substance, and what constitutes their characteristic?
Answer: True Suchness (Tathatā) takes spiritual awareness and quiescent illumination as its mind.
Non-emptiness and non-abiding constitute its essence; the true mark constitutes its characteristic. The deluded mind takes the reflected images conditioned by the six sense objects as its mind;
it takes the absence of intrinsic nature as its essence and discursive thought as its characteristic. These two gates each comprehensively encompass all phenomena:
that is to say, the gate of True Suchness encompasses all mundane and supramundane phenomena, and the gate of Arising and Ceasing likewise encompasses them.
Regarding all mundane and supramundane dharmas, it may be asked: True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the gate of immutability; why does it encompass mundane dharmas?
Arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*) is the gate of following conditions (*pratyaya-anuvidhāna*); why does it also encompass supramundane dharmas? The answer is:

because these two gates are not mutually exclusive. This is because True Suchness possesses the meaning of being immutable while following conditions, and the delusory [phenomena] possess the nature of emptiness.
Regarding the meaning of the accomplishment of phenomena: because the True (the Real) does not change, the essence of the delusory is empty;

this constitutes the Gate of Suchness (*tathatā-mukha*). Because the True follows conditions, the delusory accomplishes phenomena; this constitutes the Gate of Arising and Ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*).

Since arising and ceasing are themselves Suchness, the Sūtra says that sentient beings are originally in *nirvāṇa* and possess the characteristic of eternal quiescence. Since Suchness is itself arising and ceasing, the Sūtra speaks of the *dharmakāya*.
Those who transmigrate through the six realms are called "sentient beings. Since one knows that the single mind possesses these two gates, both aspects are fully manifested herein.
Question: True Suchness (*tathatā*) and the gate of arising-and-ceasing each encompass all phenomena. I do not yet know whether the meaning of this "encompassment" is the same or different. Answer:
Within the gate of arising-and-ceasing, it is termed "comprehensive inclusion" (*gaishō*). Within the gate of True Suchness, it is termed...
Through integration and inclusion, both defilement and purity exist; through integration and inclusion, both defilement and purity are simultaneously transcended.
Because they are simultaneously transcended, there is a single flavor without differentiation; because they coexist, their distinctions are clearly manifest.
The suchness of the mind is the very essence of the Dharma-gate of the Great Universal Characteristic of the One Dharma-realm.
That is to say, the nature of the mind (the dharma-body of suchness) is neither born nor extinguished. All phenomena exist only through the distinctions created by deluded thought;

if one is free from mental conceptualization, then there are no signs of any objective realms whatsoever. Therefore, all dharmas have, from the very beginning, been free from the characteristics of verbal expression.
It is free from the characteristics of names and free from the characteristics of mental objects; it is ultimately equal, without change or variation, and indestructible.
It is solely the one mind, and is therefore called *tathatā* (established as a name based on its meaning). This is because all verbal expressions are merely provisional designations without reality;
they follow deluded thoughts and cannot be apprehended.
This is a detailed explanation of the gate of the permanence, constancy, and immutability of *tathatā*. The formal logical argument (*pramāṇa*) may be understood accordingly.
It is said that this *tathatā* is the essence of the *dharmadhātu*—the Great Universal Gate of Dependent Origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)—in the *Avataṃsaka*. This single Dharma-gate...
The entire body is entirely non-arising and non-ceasing; yet the entire body also entirely manifests arising and ceasing. Thus, the *Canyuan ji* states:
"The fundamental basis of all sages and ordinary beings is entirely this single Dharma-realm mind, the precious light of intrinsic awakening, which is perfectly complete in each and every instance.
Originally, it is not named 'Buddhas,' nor is it named 'sentient beings. It is simply because this mind is subtle and wondrous by itself..."

It abides without maintaining its own nature; following the conditions of delusion and enlightenment, it manifests as the affairs of the holy and the ordinary. Therefore, it is called *tathatā* (True Suchness).
In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it is named "the nature of all minds," and in the *Awakening of Faith*, it is named "the Great *Dhāraṇī*.

This is it. An objection is raised: "We currently perceive that all phenomena are each distinct and differentiated; how can you instead claim they are a single Dharma-realm? The answer is: [The essence of] our school...
Jing said: "All dharmas are originally a single dharma; in reality, there are no two characteristics. It is because of the arising of deluded thoughts that distinctions are perceived.
For instance, when one presently perceives objects such as blue or white, the objects themselves are fundamentally empty and do not say, 'I am blue' or 'I am white.

All such [perceptions] are the spontaneous conceptualization of the nature of the visual consciousness itself, together with the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) performing its calculations."
One discriminates between blue and white; one uses the mind to conceptualize them as form and uses speech to designate them as "blue.

All of these are merely false constructions established by the mind and its expressions. Furthermore, the nature of the six sense objects is dull; their substance does not establish itself, nor do their names call themselves forth.
All things lack intrinsic nature; they are all merely mental constructs. Therefore it is said: "The myriad phenomena are fundamentally tranquil, yet people themselves create clamor.

Thus, where the mind with conceptualization arises, the myriad objects are all present; where the empty mind arises, the myriad objects are all empty. Emptiness does not become empty of itself; it is empty because of the mind.
Existence does not become existent of itself; it is existent because of the mind. Since they are neither existent nor empty, [they transcend both].
Thus, there is only consciousness and only mind. If there were no mind, upon what could the myriad phenomena rely? A former master also said:
"All dharmas fundamentally do not speak of form, nor do they speak of emptiness; nor do they speak of right or wrong, defilement or purity.
It is only that people themselves falsely conceptualize and cling to them, forming various interpretations, giving rise to numerous cognitions and views, and producing [various afflictions]."

Regarding love and fear: if one realizes that all phenomena do not arise from themselves, but exist solely due to one's own single moment of inverted thought, and understands that mind and objects fundamentally do not reach one another—then there is liberation in this very place, quiescence in this very place, and the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) in this very place.
Thus, one knows that all phenomena, from the very beginning, cannot be grasped by the mouth; therefore, they are beyond the characteristics of verbal expression.
Because it cannot be named, it is free from the mark of names. Because it cannot be grasped by the mind, it is free from the mark of mental objects.
Because its nature is each fully complete, it is ultimately equal. Because each abides in its own fundamental position, there is no change or alteration.
Because it is fundamentally without fabrication, it cannot be destroyed. Because there is no second dharma, it is solely this one mind. This very one—

The mind is a single dharma-realm; therefore, it is called *tathatā* (suchness). Because all phenomena are merely mental verbalizations and exist only as provisional names, they lack any real meaning and are ultimately unattainable. Thus, Master Dazhu said:
"Among all the phenomena of arising and ceasing in the world, there is not a single dharma that does not return to suchness. The *Zongjing* asks: What is meant by the true mind? What is meant by...
Question: What is deluded thought? Answer: Deluded thought arises from the subject and object; it originates through discrimination.

It manifests as the temporary function of the floating faculties, forming a false cognition of the perceived object. If separated from external objects, this mind has no substance; it arises as an illumination dependent upon those objects.
When objects cease, illumination vanishes; as thoughts arise, dust accumulates; when thoughts are empty, the dust subsides.

If one takes these shadowy phenomena to be the work of the Buddha, they constitute a cause of delusion and will only result in the fruit of annihilation. As for the True Mind, it is profoundly still yet luminously aware; it does not arise from external objects.
It embraces emptiness and accommodates conditions without ever forming intentional thought. It is brilliantly clear and never obscured—this is what constitutes complete understanding.
It is known through constant awareness. When extended, it leaves no trace; when withdrawn, it leaves no mark. It is like a clear pool reflecting the wilds or a bright mirror suspended in space:
the myriad phenomena are arrayed within it, yet it is a vast, empty mirror—neither emerging nor entering, neither existent nor non-existent.
This is where the thousand sages silently return and where the ten thousand spirits converge. Those who believe in it penetrate the source of the Great Way; those who embody it...

It accomplishes the virtue of eternal abiding. All Buddhas equally realize this mind; this is called attaining perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and it is also called the Buddha of True Nature, the Buddha of Dharma-nature, the Buddha of Dharmakāya, and the Buddha of Suchness (*tathatā*). Although these names are manifold, they are all merely distinct appellations for this very mind.
That which is called *tathatā* (suchness) is likewise without characteristics; it is the ultimate limit of verbal expression. By means of words, words are dispelled.
This essence of *tathatā* cannot be dispelled—what is dispelled is merely its characteristic mark. Since all phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely *tathatā*, there is nothing that can be established;
since all phenomena are identical to *tathatā*, one should know that all phenomena are inexpressible (beyond speech), inconceivable (transcending thought), and therefore named "True."

An objection is raised: "The true mind is devoid of traces, and its principle transcends both existence and non-existence. Since it is called 'True Suchness' (Tathatā), does this not fall into the conceptual mark of names and verbal expressions?
The reply is: "The gateway of the One Mind is subtle and profound, difficult to fathom; few can exhaustively understand it through intellectual comprehension or discursive discrimination."
It is "inadequate," which is what is meant by *tathatā* (suchness). This is merely using words to eliminate words;
it does not mean that *tathatā* actually falls within the realm of verbal expression or the characteristics of names. Question:

Since all verbal expressions are to be eliminated, why is the name "*tathatā*" alone not subject to elimination? Answer: Indeed, the name "*tathatā*" can be eliminated, yet the essence of *tathatā* is truly...
It cannot be discarded, because all phenomena are the single reality (*eka-tattva*) and there is nothing remaining [to be removed]. Question:
If it cannot be discarded, then can the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) be established? Answer:

It also cannot be established, because all phenomena are identical to the one suchness (*eka-tathatā*) and there is nothing lacking [to be added]. One should know that all phenomena cannot be grasped and cannot be relinquished.
It cannot be deliberated upon; it cannot be approached from nearby; it cannot be named or designated, yet it is forcibly called "True Suchness" (*tathatā*).
Thus Xuan Sha said: "Beyond the state of Suchness-as-such, there is nothing to be arranged; it is just like a blazing furnace that harbors not even a mosquito.

This principle is fundamentally level and plain—what need is there for carving or removing? The Way is not to be forced; to establish it through effort deviates from the Truth. If you reach this point...
Within this, there is not even the slightest bit of reception. To apply a deliberate thought is to err; even if a thousand sages were to appear, they could not place a single word therein.
He asked: "If this is the meaning, how can all sentient beings accord with it and thereby gain entry? He replied:
It is said: If one knows all phenomena such that, although there is speaking, there is neither a speaker nor anything spoken;
and although there is mindfulness, there is neither a mindful subject nor anything to be minded—this is called "conformity. If one is free from such mindfulness, it is called "attaining entry."

Question: Since the Dharma of True Suchness does not fall within the reach of verbal expression nor descend into the realm of conceptual thought, how can sentient beings apply effort so as to accord with it?

How can they direct their minds so as to enter into it? Answer: If one knows that all phenomena are fundamentally ineffable and inconceivable, then there is no place to apply effort, nor is there any place to direct the mind.

If, while engaged in daily life at the moment of opening the mouth and moving the tongue to speak all dharmas, one turns back to observe the speaker, there is fundamentally not a single word that can be spoken.

Furthermore, while engaged in daily life at the moment of reaching out toward the east and following after the west to contemplate all dharmas, if one turns back to observe the one who contemplates the dharmas, there is fundamentally not a single thought to which one can become attached. To apply effort in this manner is as follows:
This application of the mind does not accord with phenomena, but is able to accord with True Suchness (*tathatā*). Nevertheless, although it is thus, a habitual mold still remains;
one has not yet forgotten conditions and has not yet attained entry, because a slight residue of objects still persists before one.
If, through diligent effort and inquiry, one reaches the point where there is no place for the mind to apply itself, then in a single thought-moment, conditioned arising is non-arising.
At that moment, one is able to enter and abide with one's entire being within the gate of *tathatā* (suchness). Thus, the *Zongjing* says:
"If one enters this gate, then all Buddha-dharma appears equally; there is no need to record a single word, yet one has contemplated the entirety of all sutras.
There is no need to understand a single dharma, yet one has realized the infinite meanings. There is no need to speak a single word, yet one constantly turns [the wheel of Dharma]."
The True Wheel of Dharma does not require taking a single step. To universally encounter the friends of the Dharma-dhātu—why?
If you "remember" it, this is the limit of conceptualization; if you "understand" it, you fall into the realm of the mental faculty; if you "explain" it, this is the gate of eloquence;
if you "investigate" it, you fall into the ground of external paths. None of these accord with one's own ground; they are not subsumed herein, like trying to grasp empty space with the hand.
Empty. It is merely a waste of mental effort. Thus it is said: "If you welcome it, you do not see its head; if you follow it, you do not see its tail.
When it is present, everything is empty; when it is absent, it exists everywhere.

First, one must not cling to the literal meaning or form intellectual interpretations based on a single mechanism or a single object. Truly, there is no fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can speak. This is the Dharma-gate.
In this context, one does not deliberate on such matters; one simply knows that one's own mind is it and rests there, no longer pondering what came before or what lies ahead.
In the past, when Changqing first visited Lingyun, he asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? Lingyun replied, "The donkey’s business is not yet finished."
The matter of the horse arrived. For twenty years the Master investigated in this manner, wearing out seven meditation cushions, yet he did not understand this matter.
One day, as he rolled up the curtain, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. He then composed a verse, saying: "How very strange! How very strange!
Rolling up the curtain, one sees the whole world. If someone asks me what school I understand, I raise my whisk."
The Master struck him with his fist. "When Changqing broke through the meditation cushion seven times, that was 'following along.
When he rolled up the curtain, that was 'entering. He asked, "Upon entering this gate, what merit is there?

He replied, "At the moment of realizing entry into the self-substance of the true mind, it cannot be expressed by words; it is as profound as boundless empty space, and as clear as a perfect [mirror]."
It is a bright, pure mirror that neither praise nor blame can reach; its principles are difficult to fathom, for the two gates of merit and fault are absolutely beyond all duality.
Thus the Sūtra says: "The mind dwells nowhere; this mind that dwells nowhere is solely the One Mind."

The essence of the single mind is originally quiescent and extinguished; its traces cannot be exhausted by means of existence or non-existence, nor can its substance be pointed out through the measurement of consciousness and wisdom. Only those who have entered it know it within their own minds.
