Relying on this coarse, discriminative consciousness, one perceives only the coarse marks of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and does not perceive the subtle marks of the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body).
It is like an ordinary person seeing the Buddha as the appearance of an old bhikṣu, or those of the Two Vehicles seeing the Buddha as an arhat and so forth;

yet they do not know that this is the *nirmāṇakāya*. This is entirely because their perception of marks has not been forgotten, [for these appearances] originally arise from one's own eighth consciousness.
Manifested by the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), they fail to realize that there is only consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*) and instead conceive of external objects as existing.

Now, seeing the Buddha’s body as if it were outside the mind, they consequently cling to the notion that such forms truly exist externally to the mind. Furthermore, failing to realize that form is itself mind and that, fundamentally, there is no division or limitation, they grasp at the characteristics of limited portions.
They do not know that the Buddha’s transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) respond according to the conditions of those who perceive them; in reality, they have no [independent] existence.

This is also limited. Second, "the lower" explains that what the bodhisattvas perceive is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body). From the stage of the ten faiths and below, all are in accordance with *karmic consciousness*;
therefore, they remain within the stage of the provisions (*sambhārāvasthā*). It is only upon reaching the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*) that one perceives the Buddha-body [as it truly is].

All are called the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*). Regarding the term "reward": because the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*) is the sovereign lord of total retribution, those who transform this consciousness all attain the vision of the Reward Body.
"The body has [no limit]" below [this] reveals that the primary retribution (*vipākaphala*) is without boundaries. "That which is dwelt upon" below...

This demonstrates that even the basis of grasping has no limits. Regarding the phrase "according to what is appropriate," it means that because the mind of that bodhisattva is without limits, that which is perceived is likewise without limits. "Always able to maintain, without destroying or losing" means:
It is not like the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which possesses coming and going, birth and extinction. "Thus" and below conclude by returning to the fundamental cause.
"The perfuming of untainted practice" refers to the untainted karma perfumed by the ten *pāramitās*.
"Inconceivable perfuming" refers to the perfuming of ignorance by True Suchness (*tathatā*). By the power of these two kinds of perfuming, one is thus able to...
The retributive suffering of birth and death, produced by outflowing ignorance, is transformed into the mark of the tranquil bliss of the outflow-free;
therefore, it is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body). Thus one knows that the Buddha has no fixed locus of dependence, but manifests universally in accordance with the capacities of beings.

His color is not a fixed color, like a *maṇi* gem reflecting blue or yellow; his form is not a fixed form, like a shadow or light assuming length or shortness according to its conditions; his marks are not fixed...
Its appearance is like a bright mirror reflecting beauty and ugliness; thus, it manifests according to one's inclinations.

Furthermore, what is seen by ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles is its coarse form, which appears differently to each according to their respective realms within the six paths of existence.
Because these various diverse forms do not possess the characteristics of being objects of enjoyment, they are said to be "corresponding.

Furthermore, that which is perceived by Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds upon enlightenment is seen only partially, because they have deep faith in the Dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

They know that such matters as the adornment of physical forms neither come nor go; they are free from spatial limitations and manifest solely in dependence upon the mind, never departing from True Suchness. However, this...
Bodhisattvas still engage in conceptual discrimination because they have not yet entered the stage of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

If they attain the pure mind, that which they perceive becomes subtle and wondrous, and its function becomes increasingly superior until it reaches the final stage of the Bodhisattva grounds. Ultimately, if one is free from the karmic consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), there is no aspect of seeing;
for within the Dharma-bodies of all Buddhas, there are no mutual perceptions of color-forms or characteristics belonging to self or other.
This identifies what is seen by ordinary beings within the six realms as the *nirmāṇakāya*.

Because ordinary beings carry the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the evil karma of the six realms from the past, they may see the Buddha’s body receiving golden spears and parched grain, or his body being beaten until it bleeds.
Some may see the Buddha as a tree spirit, a celestial deity, a black-footed elephant, or even a sheep three feet tall;

they may see a sheep among sheep or a deer among deer—none of which are signs of bliss. A bodhisattva of the sudden teaching (donjiao), from the beginning to the end of the Mahāyāna, having realized that all is consciousness-only (weishi), understands that this Buddha-body is merely a manifestation of the evolving consciousnesses (zhuan shi) within the ālayavijñāna; therefore, they see the Buddha.
The body is solely a manifestation of the mind; it does not depart from *tathatā* (suchness), has no boundaries, and pervades all places.

It manifests spontaneously according to the faculties of sentient beings; this is the characteristic of experiencing bliss. Furthermore, the passage below clarifies that what is perceived by those of the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) and the ten stages of sagehood (*daśa-ārya-bhūmi*) is the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (enjoyment body).
"Those of deep faith" refers to the bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness who understand the dharma of *tathatā*. As for "different":

The preceding ten stages are called "faith" (*śraddhā*). Because one has not yet realized the *dharmakāya*, they are termed "faith. Because one has attained a semblance of awakening, they are termed "seeing a small portion.
One knows that the two aspects of that body and land are fundamentally without coming or going, and are likewise without limit;

they are all merely the measure manifested by one's own mind. However, because one has not yet severed the conceptual clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), one has not yet attained direct realization of the state of equality.

Because it is the equal *dharmakāya*, it is simply said that "one knows. If one realizes the first stage (*bhūmi*), one attains non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and realizes a portion of the equal *dharmakāya*, thereby attaining partial awakening.

The *saṃbhogakāya* perceived is far more subtle than before the stages, and its functional activity is far superior to that prior to the stages. The second stage is superior to the first, the third is superior to the second, and so on.
That which is seen on the ten stages is the most extremely subtle; beyond this, there is no further superior characteristic, and thus it is called ultimate.

Upon reaching the stage of wondrous enlightenment, ignorance has been exhausted and the karma-consciousness has become empty. The seeing and the seen are both extinguished, leaving only True Suchness (Tathatā), with no further seeing or seen.
This is because each Buddha personally realizes the Dharma-body, wherein no characteristics of self or other can be found.
Because he sees [thus], it is said: "The Buddha does not see a body to know that he is the Buddha; if there were truly a knowing, there would be no Buddha apart from it. Question:

Since it is said that all sentient beings are identical to the Buddha-nature, they ought to attain Buddhahood simultaneously. Why is it that the three vehicles perceive the Buddha with various differences?
Answer: The Dharma-body is without marks; true nature is without form. Since even form and marks do not exist, how much less could there be distinctions?

What is the distinction? It is that this mirror of one's own consciousness reflects images differently. For example, five hundred Brahmins conceived faith upon seeing their own bodies reduced to ashes;
the householder Kuśīla generated the aspiration for enlightenment upon seeing [the Buddha] at three feet tall;

the Bodhisattva Anantagātra found that even the highest realms were not exhaustive [of his vision]; while those dwelling as Lesser Sages or ordinary beings perceived the sixteen-foot form as inexhaustible. All of these...
These appear according to what is induced by the mind; the images differ because of the variations in one's own karma, not because there is any difference in the Buddha.

It is like observing a single body of water that suddenly divides into four; these differences are all seen through one's own perception. Or it is like sharing a single precious vessel where the color of the rice differs; this is not due to the karma of another being experienced.
Question: If the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is free from the marks of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), how can it manifest forms?
Answer: Because this very Dharma-body is the substance of form, it is able to manifest form. That is to say, from the very beginning, form and mind are non-dual;

because the nature of form is itself wisdom (*jñāna*), the substance of form is formless (lacking form-marks). It is [only] by way of conventional designation (*prajñapti*) that it is called the "Wisdom-body" (*jñāna-kāya*). This is because the nature of wisdom is itself form.

Therefore, [the mind in which] the dharmatā of true emptiness and form are non-dual is called the *dharmakāya* (having the Dharma as its body). It pervades all places. The forms manifested therein have no boundaries;

according to the mind, they can manifest throughout the worlds of the ten directions (wherein a single hair-pore, a single mark, or a single ray of light universally illumines the entire *dharmadhātu*).

The infinite *saṃbhogakāyas*, their infinite rewards, and their infinite adornments are each distinct, yet all are without boundaries and do not obstruct one another. This cannot be known through the discrimination of the mental consciousness, for it is *tathatā*.

Because it possesses the meaning of sovereign function, the Dharma-body is entirely the substance of form; therefore, it can manifest form. It is like a bright mirror, which is entirely the substance of images;

therefore, it can manifest images. Linji said: "The four great elements do not understand how to preach or listen to the Dharma; empty space does not understand how to preach or listen to the Dharma."

Regarding listening to the Dharma: when that which is vividly manifest before your very eyes is solitary clarity without form or segment, only then do you understand how to preach and listen to the Dharma.
What is called "without form or segment" is the Dharmakāya of all Buddhas; it is also your own fundamental mind.
What follows below clearly demonstrates the non-duality of form and mind: because form is itself mind, the characteristics of form are thereby completely exhausted. Therefore—
Regarding its essence, it is simply called the "Wisdom Body" (*jñānakāya*). "Wisdom" refers to the wisdom of original enlightenment (*mūlapratyavekṣājñāna*).

Because the mind is itself form, the mind is consequently identical to form; thus, it is said that the Dharma-body pervades all places, yet the forms it manifests are in reality without limitation—they are merely manifestations of limitations according to the mind.
If there are immeasurable bodhisattvas, each of whom is distinct, [the manifestations likewise differ].
The Tathāgata, in accordance with the minds of bodhisattvas, manifests immeasurable reward bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*) and reward lands (*saṃbhogakṣetra*), each of which is distinct.
Nevertheless, none of them have fixed boundaries, and they do not obstruct one another. All of these are the inconceivable realm of the Tathāgata;
they are not objects known through discursive thought or discrimination. This is because they are the functioning of True Suchness (*tathatā*), pervading everywhere.
It is universally pervasive, perfectly interfused, sovereign, and unimpeded. The *Zongjing* asks:

"Since it is said that the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is fundamentally devoid of form and characteristics, how can it manifest various forms and characteristics? The answer is: The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says, "For example, suppose there is one person..."
It possesses many capacities. When it runs, it is called a "runner"; when about to reap, it is called a "reaper";
when preparing food, it is called a "cook"; when working with timber, it is called a "craftsman";
and when forging gold and silver, it is called a "goldsmith. The Dharma is also like this: its reality is one, yet it has many names. Therefore...
In terms of function, it is manifold; in its essence, it is eternally one and darkly unified. When extended, it becomes the myriad phenomena; when rolled up, it is simply the one mind.

Within the one, there are the infinite; within the infinite, there is the one. Therefore, know that the principle of the one mind is the gate of the Perfect and Sudden, the path of complete sufficiency.
The above concludes the explanation of the essence, characteristics, and functions.
Next, it demonstrates how to enter the gate of True Suchness (tathatā) directly from the gate of Arising and Ceasing.

This refers to the investigation of the five aggregates (skandhas), matter and mind, and the objective realms of the six sense objects, which are ultimately devoid of thought (observing that the objective realms of the six senses lack intrinsic nature). Since the mind has no form or appearance, one seeks it throughout the ten directions.

Ultimately, it cannot be obtained that [arising and ceasing] are anything other than True Suchness (tathatā). It is like a person who, due to delusion, mistakes the east for the west; yet the directions themselves do not actually change. Sentient beings are likewise.

Due to the delusion of ignorance, one takes the mind to be thought; yet the mind is in reality unmoving. If one can observe and know that the mind is without thought, one will immediately attain compliance and enter the gate of True Suchness (Tathatā).
This summarizes the return from the gate of arising and ceasing to the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*). "Investigation" refers to the wisdom that is capable of contemplation.
"The objects of form and mind" refer to the realms that are the objects of contemplation. "Ultimately being without thought" refers to both the internal body and external objects.
Investigate each one thoroughly; ultimately, not even a single hair’s breadth of a mental thought can be found.
Since this mind has no form or substance, if the very mind that manifests cannot be apprehended, how could the objects manifested by it be apprehended?
Therefore, Nanquan said: "The Way of Dīpaṃkara Buddha is exhausted. If it were something produced by the thoughts of the mind...
All phenomena that arise are false and unreal. Why is this? Since even the mind does not exist, how could there be the arising of phenomena?
They are like a form and its shadow, or like discriminating within empty space, or like a person taking up a sound and placing it inside a casket.
It is also like blowing into a net, desiring to make it full; this is precisely that meaning. "As when a person... below provides the analogy to clarify this. "The various classes of beings...
below applies the teaching to the principle. "If one can... below concludes by returning to the initial gate.

To know that the mind is without thought is the secret instruction transmitted from Buddha to Patriarch for entering the Gate of True Suchness (Tathatā); therefore, it is concluded again at this point. The *Tongxin lun* says: "Now, as for bondage..."

Bondage arises from the mind; liberation arises from the mind. Both liberation and bondage depend on the mind and concern nothing else. The essential method for escaping bondage is solely the contemplation of the mind.
By contemplating the mind, one perceives its true nature (*dharmatā*), and everything is simultaneously understood. Therefore, the wise person should first turn back and contemplate their own mind:
it is deceptive and unreal, like an illusion or a magical transformation; it is restless and unstable, just like a monkey.
Leaping, galloping, and rushing about like a wild horse, it truly lacks intrinsic nature; it exists because of objects, and when there are no objects, it is non-existent.

Furthermore, observing all objects, one sees that objects lack intrinsic nature; they exist because of seeing, and when there is no seeing, they are non-existent. Furthermore, investigating the locus of seeing, one finds that seeing lacks intrinsic nature;
it exists because of the movement of the mind, and when there is no movement, it is non-existent. Furthermore, one investigates the moving mind. Movement...
There is no intrinsic nature. It arises solely from non-awakening; when awakened, there is no movement. Furthermore, if one investigates this non-awakening, it has no fundamental root.
It proceeds directly from beginningless, empty habituation, wherein thought after thought one is deluded of oneself. When free of thought, True Suchness is simply nothing at all.
This is the essential method for entering the Gate of True Suchness from the Gate of Arising and Ceasing. The above clarifies the gate that establishes [the principle].

[The section on] "counteracting false attachments" concludes. As for all false attachments, they all rely upon the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), which is the root of all false attachments. If one is free from the self, then there are no false attachments.

This view of self is of two kinds. What are these two? First is the view of a personal self (*pudgala-ātma-dṛṣṭi*) [spoken in reference to ordinary beings]. Second is the view of a phenomenal self (*dharma-ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
"View" (is explained in terms of the Two Vehicles).
From here below, the "gate of refutation" is revealed. To reason incorrectly is called "perversion" (*mithyā*); to cling tenaciously and refuse to relinquish is called "grasping" (*abhiniveśa*).
The "view of self" (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is so called because it arises from the notion of a self; thus, it is named the view of self. This is the root of two types of clinging:

first, the conception that the phenomena of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) possess a real, governing subject, which is called the view of a personal self (*pudgala-ātma-dṛṣṭi*); second, the conception that the phenomena of the five aggregates possess a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), which is called the view of a phenomenal self (*dharma-ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Within this context, erroneously grasping the body of the Tathāgata as a personal self is [an instance of] the view of a personal self. Furthermore, erroneously...

Grasping at the true nature of reality constitutes the view of a self in phenomena (*dharma-ātman-dṛṣṭi*). Because sentient beings with false views take what is medicine and turn it into a disease, the Master of the Treatise further administers medicine in response to that very illness.

Regarding the view of a self in persons (*pudgala-ātman-dṛṣṭi*), five types are taught based on the ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). What are these five? First, [the view arising from] hearing and cultivation...
Tāra said: "The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is ultimately quiescent, like empty space. Because [sentient beings] do not understand this, they fall into attachment;
thus, they mistakenly claim that empty space is the nature of the Tathāgata. How is this to be remedied? By clarifying the characteristics of empty space."

These are delusive phenomena (*mṛṣā-dharma*). The essence [of the Tathāgata] is not unreal; it exists only in contrast to form (*rūpa*), as a visible characteristic that causes the mind to arise and perish.

Since all phenomena of form are fundamentally the mind—truly there is no external form (apart from the mind, no form can be apprehended)—if there were no form, then the characteristic of space would not exist.
Thus, all objective realms exist solely because the mind falsely arises (the three subtle states). If the mind were separated from...
When false movement ceases, all objective realms vanish, and there remains only the single true mind, which is omnipresent (like the pure void).
This is called the ultimate meaning of the Tathāgata’s vast nature-wisdom; it is not like the characteristics of empty space.
This is the erroneous attachment to stubborn emptiness as the nature of awakening. Regarding the phrase "How so? and below, the correct meaning is set forth.

It says that empty space is a delusive phenomenon because it is produced by obscured darkness; that its substance is non-existent because it has a name but no reality; and that it is unreal because...
Because it cannot be grasped or rubbed. Regarding "it exists in contrast to form": emptiness is manifested by means of form;
this is because they are correlative phenomena. Regarding "this visible characteristic causes the mind to arise and perish":
the azure color is the object confronted by the eye, and because it can cause arising and perishing, all dharmas of form are one's own mind. Apart from the mind, there is truly nothing that exists.

Regarding form (*rūpa*): if there were no form, there would likewise be no emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Therefore, one knows that the two dharmas of emptiness and form both exist solely through the deluded movement of the mind.
If the mind does not move, form and emptiness naturally cease to exist; there is only the single true mind, which is omnipresent everywhere. Thus, a sutra says:
"Emptiness arises within the Great Enlightenment, like a single bubble surfacing upon the ocean. It further says: "Not knowing the void..."
From the void outward to the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—all are objects manifested within the wondrously luminous true mind.
Therefore, what is described in the treatise all refers to the ultimate meaning of the Tathāgata’s vast, intrinsic wisdom.
This is the emptiness of reality; this is ultimate emptiness. Thus, space is borrowed as a metaphor; it does not mean that space itself is [the true nature].
This is the nature of the Tathāgata. Therefore it is said: "Those who are free from the marks of thought are equal to the realm of empty space.

Second, when one hears the sūtras state that all worldly phenomena are ultimately empty in essence, and even the dharma of nirvāṇa and true suchness (tathatā) is also ultimately empty—being primordially and inherently empty and free from all marks—one fails to understand this and instead regards it as a refutation.
Because of such attachments, one claims that the nature of *tathatā* and *nirvāṇa* is exclusively empty. How is this countered?
It is clarified that the self-substance of the *dharmakāya* of *tathatā* is not empty, because it is fully endowed with immeasurable intrinsic merits (*guṇa*).
This is the erroneous attachment that takes the emptiness of annihilation to be true suchness (*tathatā*). "Worldly phenomena" refers to the phenomena of birth and death;
"nirvāṇa and true suchness phenomena" refers to supramundane phenomena. "Only this is empty" means that both birth and death and nirvāṇa are empty.

It is simply one emptiness; there is not another single thing. This is what is called "vast and open emptiness" (*hòudá kōng*). Regarding the phrase "How so? below, it sets forth the correct principle:
that which is here referred to as birth-and-death and nirvana belongs to the gate of arising and ceasing; because these are relative phenomena, they are described merely as empty.
The self-substance of True Suchness (*tathatā*), however, is fully endowed with sands-of-the-Ganges virtues that accord with its nature; therefore, it is said to be non-empty. Thus...
This refers to emptiness that is not empty; it is not an emptiness of annihilation. As it is said regarding "no-mind":
it is simply the absence of objects within the mind that is called "no-mind," not the non-existence of the essence of mind itself. It is analogous to an empty bottle:
it is called an "empty bottle" because there are no objects within the bottle, not because the substance of the bottle itself is also non-existent. Therefore, the Patriarch said: "You..."
It is simply that there is no concern with phenomena within the mind, and no mind directed toward phenomena. Thus, it is naturally empty yet spiritual, still yet wondrous.
Based on this, it means there is no deluded mind; it does not mean there is no true mind.

Third, when one hears it stated in the sūtras that the Tathāgata-garbha neither increases nor decreases and that its essence is fully endowed with all dharmas of merit, yet because of a lack of understanding, one claims that the Tathāgata-garbha possesses the distinct characteristics of material and mental dharmas. How is this countered?

It is because [the sūtras] speak solely from the perspective of the meaning of True Suchness (tathatā), while manifesting [the teaching] through the perspective of the defiled meaning of arising and ceasing.
This is because it explains the distinctions [between them].

This erroneous attachment holds that within the *tathāgatagarbha* there exist both material and mental phenomena (*rūpa-citta-dharma*). Regarding the passage beginning with "How so?"—it sets forth the correct meaning.
That "the essence is replete with all merits, without increase or decrease" is spoken according to the principle of the equality of *tathatā*. As for the distinctions between matter and mind...

As for the separate mention of increase and decrease, this is spoken in terms of the meaning of the arising and ceasing of defilement. Therefore it is said: "There are distinctions only based on deluded thought.
It is further stated: "This is shown by means of the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*)."

Fourth, one hears it stated in the sūtras that all worldly phenomena of birth, death, and defilement exist in dependence upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, and that all worldly dharmas do not depart from *tathatā*.
Because they do not understand this, they claim that the *tathāgatagarbha* itself inherently possesses all worldly phenomena such as birth and death.
How is this to be remedied? [It is shown that] the *tathāgatagarbha*, from the very beginning...
Since beginningless time, there have been only pure merits exceeding the sands of the Ganges, because they do not depart from, cease, or differ from the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness).
This is because the defiled dharmas of afflictions exceeding the sands of the Ganges exist only as false appearances;
their nature is fundamentally non-existent, and since beginningless time, they have never been associated with the *tathāgatagarbha*. If the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha* possessed falsity...
To claim that the Dharma can cause one to realize and permanently extinguish delusions while [the Tathāgatagarbha] still possesses defiled phenomena is impossible.
This is a mistaken adherence to the view that the Tathāgatagarbha contains defiled dharmas. Regarding the passage beginning with "How so?"—it sets forth the correct principle:
the Tathāgatagarbha is associated only with all pure merits and is not associated with defiled dharmas, because all...
The defiled dharmas are by nature originally non-existent; they have never been associated with the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Therefore, it is said that what is called "emptiness" is because it is not associated with any defiled dharmas. All sentient beings, possessing a deluded mind, engage in conceptual discrimination from moment to moment;
for this reason, [the *tathāgatagarbha*] is described as empty. If the *tathāgatagarbha* actually possessed defiled dharmas, yet one wished to...
It is impossible for everyone to realize entry and everyone to attain accord such that those defilements are forever severed and never arise again.
This is because the *tathāgatagarbha* is fundamentally free from defilement; therefore, it is able to effect their eternal severance. As the ancient masters said:
"Defilement is not to be found, yet cultivation and realization are not non-existent. This is precisely the meaning of this [passage]. Of the four attachments mentioned above, the first two...
The first is that which is adhered to by those who have lost the true meaning of the sudden teaching, the teaching on emptiness, and the Chan school of the Southern Lineage.
The next two are that which are adhered to by those who have lost the true meaning of the Mahāyāna Dharma-lakṣaṇa school and the Chan school of the Northern Lineage.

Fifth, when hearing the sūtras state that it is because of the *tathāgatagarbha* that there is saṃsāra, and because of the *tathāgatagarbha* that there is nirvāṇa, those who do not understand this claim that sentient beings have a beginning.

Because they perceive a beginning, they further claim that the nirvāṇa attained by the Tathāgata has an end, such that he returns to becoming a sentient being. How is this to be remedied? By means of the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Because there is no prior limit, the characteristic of ignorance likewise has no beginning. If one were to say that there are sentient beings who first arise outside the three realms, that would be the teaching of the non-Buddhist scriptures. Furthermore, the Tathāgatagarbha has no subsequent limit;
as it corresponds with the nirvāṇa attained by all Buddhas, it likewise has no subsequent limit.
This is a mistaken attachment to the notion that both defilement and purity possess a beginning and an end.

It is claimed that the initial arising of a single thought-moment of the ignorance of the "mark of birth" (*jāti-nimitta-avidyā*) constitutes the beginning of sentient beings. Now, when one awakens to this mark of birth through "initial awakening" (*ādi-bodhi*), the mark of birth is extinguished;
thus, sentient beings have an end. Yet, it is argued that awakening has a beginning, and since whatever has a beginning must necessarily have an end. [The text asks: "How is this so? and so forth.

This establishes the correct principle. Because phenomena have no prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), one knows that birth and death are beginningless. Because phenomena have no posterior limit (*aparākoṭi*), one knows that *nirvāṇa* is endless.
Therefore, it is said that the perfuming of defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) is uninterrupted until later, when it is severed; this is "having no beginning but having an end.
The perfuming of pure phenomena (*viśuddha-dharma*), however, is never interrupted and extends to the end of the future; this is [having no beginning and] no end.
There is a beginning but no end. The first part breaks the attachment to a self (*ātman-grāha*); the second part breaks the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

Regarding those with the view of a self in phenomena (*dharmātman-dṛṣṭi*), because they possess the dull faculties of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), the Tathāgata taught them only the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).

Because that teaching was not ultimate, they perceive the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as phenomena subject to arising and ceasing; thus, they fear birth and death and falsely grasp at nirvāṇa. Why?
What is the antidote? Since the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) do not arise by way of their own nature (*svabhāva*), they do not cease; they are originally *nirvāṇa*.
This [teaching] is intended to counteract the erroneous attachment that takes the five aggregates to be real dharmas.

Because the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma varies according to the occasion—seeing that those of the two vehicles have dull faculties and fear birth and death—he spoke of *nirvāṇa* but did not teach that all dharmas [are empty].

It is primordially and eternally abiding, truly without arising or ceasing; therefore, although one may sever the grasping at a self and realize the emptiness of persons, one still falls into the grasping at phenomena.
In the passage beginning with "How so? the correct meaning is set forth: the dharmas of the five aggregates are dependently originated and fundamentally lack intrinsic nature.
Since there is not even birth, what is there to be extinguished? Based on this principle, it is said that all sentient beings are primordially and eternally abiding in nirvāṇa.
Therefore, one should know that if one clings to the mind and its objects as being real, then persons and phenomena are not empty.

If one merely undergoes cultivation for ten thousand kalpas, one will ultimately not realize the fruit. If, however, one suddenly comprehends non-self and deeply penetrates the emptiness of all things, then subject and object are dissolved;
what dharma would not be realized? It is like a light boat following a swift current, or like fine dust rising with a favorable wind.
One only fears that by failing to believe in the single mind, one creates difficulties and perils for oneself. If one enters this gate, there is no dharma that cannot be attained.

Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: The Buddha declared, "Because I have no attachment to any phenomena (*dharma*), I have attained a constant radiance of one fathom and a body of true golden color.
Therefore, when both attachments to persons and phenomena are simultaneously extinguished, the divine light of the singular path manifests spontaneously.
As the former masters said: "If you wish to realize it now, realize it directly; simply do not grasp at any marks (*nimitta*)."
It is attained; there are no further words. If one knows that all phenomena arise from the mind, one should not cling to them; to cling is to remain ignorant.

Furthermore, for one who has ultimately abandoned false attachments, it should be known that defiled and pure phenomena are entirely mutually dependent and possess no self-characteristic that can be described.
Therefore, all phenomena, from the very beginning, are neither form (the five aggregates) nor mind, neither wisdom (the essence of True Suchness) nor...

Consciousness is neither existent nor non-existent; its ultimate characteristic is ineffable. That there are nevertheless verbal expressions should be understood as the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), employing provisional speech to guide sentient beings.
Their underlying intent is entirely for the purpose of transcending conceptual thought and returning to True Suchness (*tathatā*).
This is because conceiving of all phenomena through conceptual thought causes the mind to arise and perish, thereby preventing entry into true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
The above refutations of the self and the refutations of dharmas, as well as the distinctions between the defiled and the pure, are all provisional expedients for a single lifetime.
These are relative phenomena that collectively belong to the realm of common characteristics; they pertain entirely to the shores of birth and death and are not yet called ultimate.

This is because the nature of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not fall into the realm of verbal expression. Only when both the defiled and the pure are equally empty, such that not even a single thread clings to one, does one truly [attain it].
The fundamental face is silently accorded; like a fish drinking water, its coldness or warmth is known by itself. This is precisely why it is not related to verbal expression.

Therefore, when one investigates the intrinsic characteristics of all phenomena, fundamentally there are no characteristics such as form, mind, wisdom, consciousness, existence, or non-existence that can be described.
Nevertheless, one speaks of form, speaks of mind, speaks of wisdom, speaks of consciousness, and speaks of existence.
There is nothing [ultimately real]; all these are the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), using provisional names to guide sentient beings.

In truth, the intent of the Tathāgata requires that one neither think nor understand by means of the hundred [dualistic categories], remaining unstained by existence or non-existence, purity or defilement.
To personally behold the original source and return to the fundamental ground—this is his intent. For whether thinking of good or thinking of evil, both are but the arousal of [the mind].
Karma and ignorance act as the masters, causing the mind to arise and perish; thus, one cannot enter the true wisdom of *tathatā*.
As the ancient masters said: "The phrase 'is' is also erased; the phrase 'is not' is also erased. This is the mind-dharma transmitted from Buddha to Buddha and Patriarch to Patriarch;
therefore, I have been insistent in reaching this point. The section on the gate of "able to destroy" is hereby concluded.

Regarding the characteristics of the various ways of setting out upon the path: this refers to the path realized by all Buddhas, in the sense that all Bodhisattvas set their minds on awakening, practice, and proceed toward it.
Briefly stated, there are three kinds of setting the mind [on awakening]. What are the three? First, the setting of the mind through the fulfillment of faith;

second, the setting of the mind through the stage of practice based on understanding; and third, the setting of the mind through realization (which involves the destruction of a portion of ignorance).

Having established these two gates, the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox is now complete. Below this, the characteristics of a bodhisattva’s arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) and their progression toward the Buddha-way will be revealed.
This is because it was previously stated that "all bodhisattvas ride upon this Dharma to reach the stage of the Tathāgata.

Nevertheless, there are differences in the stages of the three levels of worthies (*tri-śaikṣa*) and ten stages of sages (*daśārya*); likewise, there are differences in the arousal of the mind, the practice, and the realization attained.
Therefore, it must be distinguished. Regarding the "arousing of the mind through the perfection of faith": "faith" here refers to the sense of taking responsibility.
It requires a full ten thousand kalpas before it can be perfected, because this matter is a gate that is difficult to understand and enter, and a teaching that is difficult to contemplate and know.
Thus, at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Śāriputra made three requests, and the fourfold assembly was struck with wonder.
I have doubts. Consider, for instance, those who withdrew from their seats when the assembly numbered five thousand; they were all individuals who had already attained the fruits of sainthood.

Yet, upon hearing the teaching that directly points to one's own mind, they still harbored doubts and rose from their seats in protest. How much more so for those of the initial capacity in this age of Dharma-decline?

Their obscurations are already deep, their views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are especially heavy, the dust of the sensory passions still blocks them, and the fire of desire still burns within them. How could such people be capable of shouldering this great [teaching]?
This is the essential matter. Therefore, by wondrously attaining the gateway, one achieves Buddhahood without departing from the present thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*).
If one loses this fundamental intent, practice will merely lead to exhaustion over many lifetimes. It depends solely upon faith; there is no other expedient means.

For faith is the source for entering the Way and the mother of all merit and virtue. By simply believing in this school, principle and phenomena are perfectly fulfilled; thus, understanding and practice—

Regarding the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*): from the ten stages (*bhūmi*) up to the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), because one is able to comprehend the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and practices the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) accordingly, and because the ten perfections reach maturity and the mind of dedication is aroused, the *Zongjing* says: "Vivid and perfect insight is the eye."

The union of practice and realization constitutes the feet; when these feet are further supported by the eye, and when principle and practice mutually assist one another, one may proceed toward the realm of Nirvana and reach the land of cool serenity.

If concentration and wisdom have not yet permeated one’s being, it is like a mani jewel hidden within its ore; its essential nature and characteristics cannot be distinguished, much like an ancient mirror that has not yet been polished.
To desire to behold one's reflection in such a vessel or to expect it to rain down jewels is impossible. If the mind...
Once purified, as soon as the mirror of the mind becomes clear, it is further refined and made increasingly radiant through cultivation by means of the myriad practices.
As the former masters have said: "All Buddha-activities and boundless gates of transformation proceed by relying on the harmonious transformation of one's own dharma.

Because within one's own mind there is the Greatness of the Essence of True Suchness (tathatā), one realizes this essence today and brings forth the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). From within one's own mind..."
There is the Greatness of the Aspect of True Suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa-mahattva*); today one attains thorough realization of it, thereby drawing forth the Reward Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*).

Because within one's own mind there is the Greatness of the Function of True Suchness (*tathatā-vṛtti-mahattva*), today one practices it, thereby drawing forth the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*).

Even the ten *pāramitās* and all the myriad practices, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are all drawn forth from one's own mind; never has a single dharma or a single practice been obtained outside of the mind.

This is practice. Regarding the realization of the awakening mind (*bodhicitta*): from the first stage (*bhūmi*) through the tenth stage, one realizes it precisely because one has set out toward the Buddha-way from the very first moment of generating that mind.
Question: Since faith reveals that the mind itself is [Buddha], what further need is there for cultivation?

Answer: It is precisely because it *is* [Buddha] that one must cultivate further. It is like iron that is not gold; if it were already gold, one could not smelt it to form a wondrous vessel. Question:
Regarding the practice herein, is it sudden or gradual? Answer: If one considers the practice itself, it is sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation.
If one considers the severing of hindrances, it is like the sun rising suddenly while the frost and dew gradually dissipate. If one considers the perfection of virtues, it is like a child just born.

Thus, the limbs and body are fully formed, nurtured until one becomes an adult, and one’s will and spirit gradually take shape. Therefore, a sutra says: "At the very moment of first generating the resolve for enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening.
Yet, the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood are cultivated and realized in succession; this is truly because such practices do not flow directly from the ultimate reality.

Without this, one cannot accord with the Truth. If one has not heard this Dharma and has not entered this gate, then even if one passes through many kalpas practicing the six perfections and the myriad deeds, one will ultimately not realize the Truth.
Furthermore, a person of sudden enlightenment is like a lion cub; at the moment of birth, it is already a lion.
One who has not first attained sudden enlightenment is like a jackal that follows a lion for a hundred [kalpas].
For a thousand kalpas, one will ultimately fail to become a lion; thus we know that if one does not first realize one's own mind, how can one achieve the Perfect and Sudden?
To follow others' deluded studies is to fail to enter the True Vehicle. Furthermore, if one practices based on awakening, this constitutes awakening through understanding.

Awakening through cultivation is precisely what constitutes realization; thus, one should know that directly comprehending the True Suchness of the One Mind is itself called Buddhahood—this is the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuanton zong*).
If one relies on this mind to resolve upon the path and practice, this is the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*) of the Mahāyāna.

For those who accord with the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuan-dun jiao*) and realize that the mind is inherently complete, all their meritorious practices increase day by day by a factor of ten million. Therefore it is said:

"Those who realize the mind are swift; those who resolve to practice are slow. Question: Since the essential purport of this treatise has already been entered through faith, [what further remains to be done?]
Regarding the arousal of the mind for cultivation and realization, under which teaching is this subsumed? Answer: This is to clarify the Perfect Teaching by borrowing from the Distinct Teaching.

As for those who have achieved faith and aroused the mind (the ten levels of faith), upon what kind of person do they rely, and what practices do they cultivate, so as to achieve the fulfillment of faith and become capable of arousing the mind?

It is said that they rely on sentient beings of the indeterminate group (ordinary people at the ten levels of faith). Because they possess the power of the roots of goodness from past熏習 (*vāsanā*)—both internal causes and external conditions—they believe in the retribution of karma.

Recompense (the non-deviation of cause and effect). One is able to give rise to the ten wholesome deeds (ceasing evil and practicing good). One grows weary of the suffering of birth and death (contemplating the three realms as a prison).

Desiring to seek unsurpassed bodhi, one encounters various Buddhas, personally receiving their teachings and making offerings. One practices with faith; because this faith is perfected after ten thousand kalpas (due to diligence, though for those of dull faculties, there are four types who all require ten thousand kalpas to achieve the dharma-characteristics), the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas (as external conditions) instruct them to resolve upon the mind.

Or, out of great compassion (because they view all sentient beings as of one body, it is called great compassion), they are able to resolve upon the mind themselves. Or, because the True Dharma is about to perish, by...

Due to the causes and conditions for protecting the Dharma—seeing that the True Dharma is about to perish, the Bodhisattva acts as if their own practice were perishing and thus protects the Buddha-Dharma—they are able to generate the mind [of enlightenment] themselves.

One who achieves such faith and generates this mind enters the stage of right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*) and never regresses; they are said to dwell within the lineage of the Tathāgata and be in accord with the true cause.

There are three groups [of beings]. The first consists of those from the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) upward who possess irreversible faith; these are called the group of right certainty (*samyaktvaniyatarāśi*).

Those who have not yet entered the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and do not believe in True Suchness (*tathatā*), the Three Jewels (*triratna*), or cause and effect are called the group of wrong certainty (*mithyātvaniyatarāśi*).

Between these two [categories], those who seek the Mahāyāna but whose minds are not yet resolved—wavering between advancing and retreating like a hair in the sky—are called the "indeterminate group" (*aniyata-rāśi*).
Now, based on such persons, the practice is elucidated. The passage beginning with "There is permeation" (*asti vāsanā*) below distinguishes the causal practice.

It refers to having previously heard the power of the ten wholesome dharmas from a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), as well as the internal permeation of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-pratibhāsa*).
Because of this power, one is able to believe in the retribution of karmic actions and cultivate the ten wholesome deeds; one grows weary of birth and death and seeks bodhi.
Having this internal cause, one invokes the Buddhas as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

By serving the Buddhas and practicing with faith for ten thousand kalpas, one finally achieves success. There are ten stages within the position of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*): namely, faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, giving, [precept, patience, vigor, and meditation].

Precepts, protection, relinquishment, and vows. Regarding the ten thousand kalpas, there are four distinctions based on the sharpness or dullness of one's faculties: first, those with sharp faculties who are diligent;
second, those with sharp faculties who are not diligent; for both of these, the number of kalpas cannot be fixed. Third, those with dull faculties who are diligent.
The longest duration is ten thousand kalpas. For those of dull faculties who lack diligence, the number of kalpas cannot be fixed;

here, we take only the third case, hence it says "ten thousand kalpas. Regarding those who achieve faith through the Buddha’s teachings and are inspired to resolve their minds [for enlightenment], this refers to entering the stage of "Abiding in the Resolve" (cittotpāda-vihāra) by means of awaiting the Buddha’s grace and being encouraged and exhorted. Alternatively, there are those who do so through great compassion.
It is for the sake of sentient beings. Or, "due to the True Dharma" means for the sake of the Buddha-dharma.
One who is able to spontaneously resolve their mind (bodhicitta) is said to have it flow from within their own breast, without waiting for the exhortation of the Buddhas;

such a person is able to shoulder both sentient beings and the Buddha-dharma upon one shoulder and directly enter the stage of the Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*). The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that by means of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), one perfects...

One achieves a single mind; this is called the Stage of Resolving the Mind (*cittotpāda-vihāra*). Having entered and abided in faith, one never regresses and attains communion with the portion of the Tathāgata’s essence.
Thus, one dwells within the lineage of the Tathāgata. Therefore, while in the stage of abiding, one receives the names of entering the womb, emerging from the womb, and the youthful Prince of Dharma.
As for what is called the "Tathāgata lineage," it refers to compassion as the Buddha-eye.
Right mindfulness is the Buddha’s head; wondrous sound is the Buddha’s ear; the fragrant forest is the Buddha’s nose; ambrosia is the Buddha’s mouth;
the four analytical knowledges are the Buddha’s fragrance; the six perfections are the Buddha’s body; the four means of integration are the Buddha’s hands; equanimity is the Buddha’s fingers;
precepts and meditative concentration are the Buddha’s feet; and the knowledge of all modes is the Buddha’s mind. Such is the case.

If there are sentient beings whose roots of goodness are meager and whose afflictions have been deep-seated for a long time, even though they encounter a Buddha and are able to make offerings, they will only plant the seeds of humans and devas or the seeds of the two vehicles.

Even if some among them seek the Mahāyāna, their faculties are unstable, fluctuating between progress and regression; or there may be those who make offerings to various Buddhas for less than ten thousand [eons].

Throughout kalpas, there are occasions when one encounters conditions and gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*). That is to say, one may give rise to this mind upon seeing the physical marks of a Buddha;
or one may give rise to it because of making offerings to the Sangha; or one may give rise to it because of being taught by those of the Two Vehicles;
or one may give rise to it by emulating others. Such instances of giving rise to the mind are entirely uncertain; if one encounters adverse conditions, one may even regress.
One falls away from and enters the stages of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).

This section serves as the foundation for the subsequent "Section on the Practice of Faith" (*śraddhā-pratipatti-bhāga*). The preceding passage spoke of entering the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) from the stage of indeterminate beings (*aniyata-rāśi*);
this section specifically addresses those in the stage of indeterminate beings. This occurs because their roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*) are weak and their afflictions (*kleśa*) are powerful.

Because their roots are shallow, even if they encounter a Buddha, they are unable to give rise to the bodhicitta; instead, they may plant the seeds of the human or celestial realms, or of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).
Even if some should seek the Mahāyāna, they lack a resolute will and thus vacillate between advancing and retreating.

Or, there may be those who encounter conditions and give rise to the mind, yet this does not proceed from themselves but from others. This is what is called the "inferior" [type], which is the giving rise to the mind through the perception of signs.

Furthermore, "following the instruction of others" means complying with another's verbal lead. "Learning from others" means imitating them. These all involve being led by others and lacking self-mastery;

because the foundation of one's practice has not yet been hidden, one advances when encountering favorable conditions and retreats when encountering adverse ones—all such states are termed "indefinite.
As the ancient masters said: "Unless you understand it yourself, you will fall back."

Riding the ox, one’s entire life is never spent following after others; this is to know that the wondrous gate of the single mind cannot be contemplated by those without great wisdom, nor can it be believed in by those without great roots.
To contemplate it is to equal the Buddha-wisdom; to believe in it is to enter perfect penetration (*samyag-vyavacāra*).
How easy is it to speak of the single word "belief"? Question: The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Upon hearing the two characters for 'eternal abiding'..."

One may still attain the merit of not falling into hell for seven lifetimes. Why, then, does the Sūtra state that those in the sixth stage of mind and those at the level of ordinary faith (śraddhā-bhūmi) are still subject to regression?
Answer: Within the ten stages of faith (daśa-śraddhā), resolute conviction (adhimukti) has not yet been perfected; they have not attained what they claim to have attained.
They will then give rise to arrogance; they will not seek virtuous friends and will not respect the worthy and good.

Because of such indolence, even though they dwell for a long time among humans and devas, they are able to accomplish the karma of the great hells. If one possesses even a single moment of faith and is not arrogant, constantly seeking superior friends, then these faults will not occur.
Therefore, a sutra says: "If, upon hearing the name of the Tathāgata and the Dharma he preaches, one does not believe... [it continues: "just as..."
They are able to reach the stage of adamantine wisdom in the ultimate sense; how much more so for those who practice with faith!
Furthermore, regarding those who have accomplished faith and give rise to the mind [of awakening], what kind of mind do they generate? Briefly stated, there are three types. What are these three?

First is the straightforward mind, because it maintains right mindfulness of the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness). Second is the profound mind, because it delights in accumulating all kinds of wholesome practices (*kuśala-karman*).
Third is the mind of great compassion, because it desires to uproot the suffering of all sentient beings.
This statement means that once the mind of faith is accomplished, one further gives rise to three minds. Regarding "directness":

not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, having no desires and no reliance—therefore it is called the direct mind. To maintain right mindfulness of True Suchness (Tathatā) means not giving rise to a single thought;
to give rise to even a momentary thought is to understand erroneously, to understand crookedly, and to fall off the path and into the weeds.
This upright mind (*ṛju-citta*) is the foundation of these two practices. Regarding the "profound mind" (*gambhīra-citta*), it refers to the cultivation of every wholesome quality.

The Great Master Zhiyi’s commentary on the *Sūtra of Contemplation* states: "Profound" means that the fruit of Buddhahood is deep and sublime; because one seeks it with the mind, it is called the profound mind.
It arises from the profound principle and also arises from the thick roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*). Thus, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* says: [text follows]
Entering the profound and vast mind. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "When roots are deep, they are difficult to uproot"; hence it is called the "profound mind" (*gambhīra-citta*).
Regarding the three minds beginning with the "direct mind" (*ṛju-citta*), these correspond in meaning to the three minds described in the *Sixteen Contemplations Sūtra*.
That text says: first, the mind of utmost sincerity; second, the profound mind; third, the mind of dedication and aspiration. Here, the first is termed the "direct mind."

That is precisely the mind of utmost sincerity. As for the "mind of utmost sincerity," it refers to sentient beings who practice according to reality. "Utmost" (*zhi*) means single-mindedness; "sincerity" (*cheng*) means reality.
It is not merely a straightforward mind or right mindfulness of *tathatā* (suchness). How could this be called a single-minded and realistic understanding of the profound mind?

Although that commentary [the *Bhāṣya*] presents three meanings, they do not exclude one another. To seek the lofty and profound fruit, one must accord with the profound principle. Desiring to accord with the profound...
In principle, one must deeply cultivate the roots of goodness; this constitutes establishing practice based on principle to seek the fruit.
That sutra establishes three profound meanings, none of which exceed this joy of accumulating all virtuous deeds.

The mind of dedication and aspiration in that sutra is precisely the meaning of great compassion uprooting suffering; for it is through true suchness and right mindfulness that one proceeds toward the fruit.

The virtuous mind. Skillfully dedicating the merit of these two minds, one makes the vow to be born in the Pure Land, swiftly realize the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), and extensively uproot the suffering and affliction of all sentient beings. Furthermore, these three minds accord with three dharmas. Which are they?

The first thought accords with the single nature of the equality of *tathatā* (suchness). The latter two are precisely the two types of cultivation: self-practice and the practice of transforming others. Since—
This cultivation of the two natures as one is the arousal of the mind based upon the perfect fusion of the three dharmas. Now, these three minds are cultivated within a single thought-moment;

the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and the *rajas* of the sands of Ganges (*pāṃsu-gaṅgā-rajas*) are spontaneously eliminated first. Upon entering the tenth stage of faith, this is "Great Compassion."
There is nothing that is not delivered through non-arising. Thus we know that the source from which the myriad practices arise is True Suchness (tathatā).

That into which they enter through the convergence of conditions is True Suchness. When a Bodhisattva resolves their mind, they first contemplate True Suchness; when a Bodhisattva gives rise to faith, they first believe in True Suchness;
when a Bodhisattva attains realization, they first accord with True Suchness. Question: What are the characteristics of True Suchness? Answer:

To have no faith in any phenomena is to have faith in *tathatā* (suchness). Since, within the principle of *tathatā*, all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, if one perceives phenomena as being existent, one has faith in phenomena and lacks faith in *tathatā*.
Therefore, if one has not previously planted the vast seeds of bodhi, it is difficult to gain such faith suddenly. Thus, the Patriarch said: "The great condition unites with faith."
Therefore, know that one who is able to believe in this Dharma does so for no small reason. Yet the principle of True Suchness (Tathatā) has neither self nor other;
it is neither one nor different. It encompasses the single vital breath and pervades all phenomena.

Furthermore, if there is a person whose self-nature is pure, who is born containing this [principle], and who is devoid of deluded thoughts within, such a one is called a sage. Now, within True Suchness...
Furthermore, there is not even so much as a speck of difference in the dharmas of the noble ones, not even the size of a mote of dust.

If, moreover, there is a person whose self-nature is pure, born containing [this purity] from the beginning, yet who possesses delusive thoughts that naturally become turbid and chaotic, they are called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Nevertheless, within true thusness (*tathatā*), there is not even so much as a speck of difference in the dharmas of an ordinary person, not even the size of a mote of dust. Therefore, a sutra says:

The Buddha-nature is vast and immeasurable; it is non-dual between the holy and the ordinary. It is perfectly complete in all things, pervading even grasses and trees, extending throughout ants and insects, and reaching down to the finest motes of dust and the pores of the skin—there is nothing that does not arise as a manifestation of this One. Therefore, it is said:
"When one is penetrated, all matters are completed. Thus, right mindfulness of True Suchness (Tathatā) is the source of all practices.

Question: Since it was taught above that the Dharma-realm has a single characteristic and the essence of the Buddha is non-dual, why does one not simply contemplate True Suchness alone, but must further seek and practice various wholesome deeds? Answer:

It is like a great maṇi jewel whose essential nature is luminous and pure, yet which possesses the impurities of ore and filth (though its essential nature is fundamentally pure, this does not preclude the presence of defilements). Even if a person contemplates the nature of the jewel, if they do not employ skillful means to grind and polish it in various ways, it will ultimately [not shine].

There is no attainment of purity. Thus, the *tathatā*-dharma of sentient beings (all equally possessing the essence of *tathatā*) is empty and pure in its essential nature (*svabhāva*), yet it is defiled by immeasurable afflictions (*kleśa*).

Even if a person contemplates *tathatā*, if they do not employ various skillful means (*upāya*) to cultivate and perfume themselves through the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*), there will likewise be no attainment of purity.
This is because the defilements are immeasurable and pervade all phenomena (*dharma*). Therefore, one must cultivate all wholesome practices as an antidote (*pratipakṣa*). If...
When a person practices all wholesome dharmas, they naturally accord with the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness).

The nature of a jewel is used as a metaphor for *tathatā*, while mineral impurities are used as a metaphor for ignorance (*avidyā*). If one merely recollects the nature of the jewel without polishing it, it will never become pure;

likewise, if one possesses innate truth but does not cultivate it, it will never manifest its function. Therefore, one should maintain right mindfulness of *tathatā* and further cultivate wholesome practices.
Practice means acting and performing deeds that naturally accord with True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Briefly stated, there are four kinds of skillful means (*upāya*). What are these four? First is the fundamental skillful means of practice (benefiting oneself and others), which refers to contemplating that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena within the ten dharma-realms is non-arising (originally and inherently non-arising).
Thus, one is free from false views and does not abide in birth-and-death (unlike ordinary beings, one attains the principle of true emptiness). One contemplates the causes of all phenomena...

Through the harmony of conditions, the fruits of karma are never lost. Giving rise to great compassion, one cultivates all manner of merit and virtue to gather and transform sentient beings, yet does not abide in nirvana, because one accords with the non-abiding nature of reality.
This takes non-abiding as the fundamental expedient for practice. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established.
Therefore, the former masters said: "Birth is non-birth; the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is profound stillness.
Thus, one does not grasp at any dharma and commits no evil, thereby perfecting great wisdom. One does not abide in birth-and-death, yet through non-arising, there is arising.
The fruits of karma remain steadfast; therefore, I do not abandon a single dharma, but extensively practice all manner of goodness to perfect great compassion.
I do not dwell in nirvana, for the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is fundamentally non-abiding; thus, I also follow this nature of phenomena and am without abiding.
Second is the skillful means of cessation, namely: shame (*hrī*), remorse (*apatrāpya*), and repentance (*deśanā*).
These can arrest all unwholesome dharmas so that they do not increase, because by conforming to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one becomes free from all faults.

Shame (*hrī*) has as its nature the honoring and revering of the noble and good by relying on the power of oneself and the Dharma; its function is to counteract lack of shame and to bring unwholesome conduct to rest.
Embarrassment (*apatrāpya*) has as its nature the disparaging and rejecting of violence and evil by relying on the power of the world; it counteracts lack of embarrassment.
The function of *śīla* (restraint) is the cessation of unwholesome conduct; it is the second of the eleven wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*).
Regarding *kaukṛtya* (remorse), it is one of the four indeterminate factors (*aniyata-dharma*). As the *Yi Jing* says: "That there is no blame in *zhèn* (the hexagram Zhen) depends upon remorse.
When these three [factors] are present, unarisen evil is not allowed to arise, and arisen evil is not allowed to increase. This is what is meant by "all evils..."
It is so because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally free from faults and evils; therefore, by conforming to that nature, one likewise remains free from faults and evils.

Third is the skillful means for initiating and increasing roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), which refers to diligently making offerings to and prostrating before the Triple Gem, praising and rejoicing in their merits, and entreating all Buddhas.
Because of a heart of profound love and reverence for the Triple Gem, one’s faith increases, and thus...

They are able to aspire to the unsurpassed path. Furthermore, because they are protected by the power of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, they are able to eliminate karmic obstructions and their roots of goodness do not regress;
for, by conforming to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they are free from the obstruction of delusion.
To cause unarisen wholesome states to arise and to cause already arisen wholesome states to grow—this is what is meant by "practicing all manner of wholesome deeds.
Diligence refers to *vīrya* (exertion), for there is no wholesome state that does not arise from exertion. This includes making offerings to and prostrating before the Triple Gem.
Physical action (*kāyakarman*). Praising and requesting [the teaching] is verbal action (*vākkarman*). Rejoicing (*anumodana*) is mental action (*manaskarman*).
"Loving respect" means drawing near without indolence and without treating [the teacher] with levity. "Sincerity and thickness" means being dignified and profound, rather than inferior or thin.
"Seeking with resolve" means the mind and speech being in accord, not acting in a casual manner. "Increasing" means there is daily benefit.
One shall not fall back into regression. All that has been mentioned above constitutes virtuous causes. That which is protected by the Triple Gem constitutes virtuous conditions.

When causes and conditions are fully present, karmic obstructions diminish daily, and roots of goodness advance daily. This is because, by the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is fundamentally no obstruction of delusion.
Therefore, by conforming to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is likewise no obstruction of delusion.

Fourth is the skillful means of the equality of great vows, namely, the making of a vow to bring all sentient beings to transformation and deliverance until the end of the future, leaving none remaining, and causing them all to reach ultimate *nirvāṇa* without remainder at unsurpassed *bodhi*. This is because it conforms to the nature of phenomena.

Because it is severed [of all defilements], the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is vast and expansive, pervading all sentient beings, equal and non-dual, without thoughts of self or other, and ultimately quiescent.
Because the Bodhisattva gives rise to this mind, they obtain a partial vision of the *dharmakāya*.
By virtue of seeing the *dharmakāya*, according to their power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), they are able to manifest eight ways of benefiting sentient beings, namely: from Tuṣita...

Following the heavens, he entered the womb; while dwelling in the womb, he was born through the transformation of the Dharma. Emerging from the womb, he left the city; at the appearance of the morning star, he attained the Way; he preached the Dharma, turning the wheel of the Law; and finally, he entered Nirvana beneath the twin śāla trees.

However, this bodhisattva is not yet called the Dharmakāya because, due to the out-flowing karma (*sāsrava-karma*) accumulated over immeasurable past eons, they have not yet been able to definitively sever it;

thus, wherever they are born, they do so through the power of their vows rather than being dragged by karma, and while they experience slight suffering, they are not bound by karma, owing to the sovereign power of their great vows.
As stated in the Sūtras, there are those who speak of falling back into the evil destinies, but this does not apply to them.

This is a provisional teaching given from the perspective of [the ultimate] reality for the sake of those beginner bodhisattvas who have not yet entered the stage of certainty and are prone to indolence; it is intended to inspire them toward valor by instilling a sense of awe.
Furthermore, once a bodhisattva has resolved their mind [on enlightenment], they remain forever free from cowardice and never fear falling into the stages of the two vehicles.
This is because they have heard that even after practicing difficult austerities for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one finally attains *nirvāṇa*.
Nor is he timid; for through faith he knows that all dharmas have been in nirvāṇa from the very beginning (if they are originally in nirvāṇa, how could there be any falling back?).
To make the vow to deliver sentient beings until the end of the future is because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is uninterrupted.

To accord with the nature of phenomena means that one must transmit the Dharma and deliver sentient beings, thereby continuing the Buddha’s life of wisdom. Below the section on the nature of phenomena, the reason for delivering sentient beings is set forth:
because the nature of phenomena is all-pervasive, entirely equal, devoid of self and other, and ultimately quiescent. Bodhi...
While the Bodhisattva is in the stage of the ten abodes, he makes this great vow; by the power of that vow, he then partially perceives the Dharmakāya and dwells within the lineage of the Tathāgatas.
Relying on the power of this vow, he manifests among humanity, attains enlightenment, turns the wheel of Dharma, and delivers all sentient beings.
Nevertheless, this Bodhisattva is merely called a "vow-body" (praṇidhānakāya) and not a "Dharmakāya," because he has not yet exhausted the afflictions.
Because they have not yet definitively severed their afflicted, outflow-tainted karma (*sāsrava-karma*), they experience a degree of subtle suffering in the place where they take birth.
However, because they are sustained by the power of great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna-bala*) and act with mastery according to their will, they are not dragged along by karma. This is as explained below.
This is the exercise of skillful means (*upāya*). "Those who have not yet entered the state of correctness" refers to those who have not yet entered the stage of the *dharmakāya*.

To cause them to be courageous by instilling fear means: if even Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), who have already seen the *dharmakāya*, can still fall back, how much more so for those like us who have not yet seen the *dharmakāya*—how could we dare to be indolent? Furthermore, from "Moreover, this" below, the reality is revealed. It says: "This is the Bodhi..."

When a Bodhisattva makes the Great Vow, they shoulder all sentient beings upon their own shoulders and immediately cause them to enter into masses of fire and mountains of blades without giving rise to fear or timidity; how much less would they fear falling into the stages of the Two Vehicles?

Even when hearing that one must undergo countless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of difficult practices and ascetic austerities before attaining Buddhahood, they do not feel fear or timidity, because they have self-confidence that they are fundamentally Buddhas from the beginning.
Because it does not depend on further cessation, one should know that the mind generated by those practicing through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) is even more superior.

This is because these bodhisattvas, from the time of their initial right faith until the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa is about to be completed, have attained a profound realization that manifests within the dharma of *tathatā*. Regarding this...

One cultivates the characteristic of detachment. Because one knows that the essence of the dharma-nature is devoid of stinginess and greed, one practices the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) in accordance with it.
Because one knows that the dharma-nature is unstained and free from the faults of the five desires, one practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) in accordance with it.

Because one knows that the dharma-nature is without suffering and free from anger and affliction, one practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) in accordance with it. Because one knows...
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is devoid of the characteristics of body and mind; because it is free from indolence, one practices the *vīryapāramitā* in accordance with it.
Because the nature of phenomena is eternally settled and free from confusion, one practices the *dhyānapāramitā* in accordance with it.
Because the essence of the nature of phenomena is luminous and free from ignorance, one practices the *prajñāpāramitā* in accordance with it.

"Understanding" refers to the ten abodes (*bhūmi*). "That which is" refers to the ten practices (*caryā*). These two constitute the capacity for arousal, while the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) constitute that which is aroused.

Because one arouses the mind of dedication, the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) practiced therein become increasingly superior to what preceded them. This is the stage when one is about to complete the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.

This refers to the period from the initial stage of right faith until the dedication of merit and practice is nearly complete—spanning one *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa—at which point one is about to enter the first stage (*bhūmi*).

"The profound understanding manifests as the cultivation of signlessness" means that one is on the verge of awakening to and entering *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), yet has not yet actually entered it because there is still something apprehended (*upalabdhi*). Therefore, within the four stages of application (*prayoga*), one simultaneously seals both [aspects].

Only through emptiness can one attain the state of cultivation that is free from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). From the words "Because he knows" (*yī zhī*) onwards, the text correctly explains this freedom from characteristics.

Because Bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings have not yet seen the *dharmatā*, they perceive the existence of greed, hatred, and delusion, and therefore deliver beings by means of the *dānapāramitā* and the other perfections.
These Bodhisattvas, however, have already seen the *dharmatā*; they know that within that *dharmatā*, greed, hatred, and delusion are fundamentally non-existent.
Nevertheless, this does not hinder one from practicing the six perfections in accordance with the nature of awakening.
Although one practices the six perfections, one does not perceive the marks of giving and so forth; therefore, it is said that "the cultivation is free from marks.

Every single perfection and every single practice cultivated by this Bodhisattva accords with the principle of True Suchness and the Dharma-nature of the One Mind; it is not something that exists separately outside of self-nature.
Because that which is cultivated accords with the nature of the mind, all meritorious qualities arise from that very nature;
they are inexhaustible and unconditioned, neither grasped nor abandoned. Thus, through the mind’s relinquishing, the cause of *dāna* (generosity) perfects the gate of pure giving;

through the mind’s upholding, the cause of *śīla* (precepts) accomplishes the pure discipline of self-nature; through the mind’s enduring of insults, one possesses the great patience of non-arising; [and through the mind’s exertion,] *vīrya* (diligence)...

It is produced by the mind. To be fully prepared with firm and strong resolve as one enters the gate, and to be able to contemplate the nature of the mind, is called "supreme concentration" (*adhyāna*).
Thus, dhyāna arises from the mind. When *prajñā*—the spiritual mirror—reaches the profound and penetrates through to the ultimate, wisdom arises from the mind. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
With a single mind, unmoving, one is fully endowed with the six *pāramitās*. Why is this? A sutra states: "That for which there is nothing to give is called generosity (*dāna*).

How could there be any phenomenon outside the mind upon which one might dwell as a sign? Furthermore, it says: "The nature of precepts is like empty space; those who uphold them may fall into delusion.
