How could one cling to phenomenal dharmas by distinguishing between partial observance and violation? It further says: "As for patience (*kṣānti*)," regarding...
In a single kṣaṇa, all marks (*nimitta*) and all objects of perception (*ālambana*) are exhausted.
How could this be a matter of applying an antidote to external objects and subduing one’s own mind through patience? Furthermore, it says: "If the mind does not arise, diligence will be boundless.

How could one then cling to conditioned phenomena and give rise to vain, exhausting deliberations? It also says: "Not seeing the characteristics of the mind is called right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*). How could this be...?

Is this avoiding clamor and confusion to maintain stillness amidst the dust? Furthermore, it is said that not seeking the intrinsic nature, characteristics, causes, or conditions of all phenomena is called right wisdom (*samyag-prajñā*).
How could one externally pursue names and words to forcibly produce intellectual understanding? To perceive phenomena as existing outside the mind is what is called being an outsider (*tīrthika*).
If one directly realizes one's own mind and is not moved by various views, this is called "conformity" (*anuloma*).
Suchness. Furthermore, at the moment one abandons [all things] in accord with a single thought-moment, one is immediately endowed with the ten perfections (*pāramitā*).

Abandoning without grasping is called generosity (*dāna*); being unsullied by various marks is called morality (*śīla*); accepting what is non-dharmic is called patience (*kṣānti*); being free from the marks of body and mind is called vigor (*vīrya*);

being tranquil and unmoving is called meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); definitively realizing non-arising is called wisdom (*prajñā*); and although empty, not obstructing any phenomena is called skillful means (*upāya*).

Skillful means (*upāya*) is their mutual manifestation; the aspiration to attain equality with the fruit of Buddhahood is their vow (*praṇidhāna*); unwavering discernment is their power (*bala*); and decisive clarity is their wisdom (*jñāna*).

Therefore, when a single thought-moment is in accord [with the mind], the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*) are fully realized. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "In every moment of thought, the ten pāramitās are complete.
Thus, if the ten perfections are perfected, the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates are simultaneously and equally fulfilled.

It should be so. All that constitutes the holy teaching must be integrated within the mind; in principle, there is nothing that does not correspond to it. If one acts according to phenomena outside the mind, one will merely grasp at saṃsāra;
even if one passes through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, it will ultimately result in nothing but deluded thought. Therefore, the Confucian classic states:
"In the past, throughout countless kalpas, I gave away my kingdoms, wealth, and life to others innumerable times; yet because I gave with a deluded mind, it was not [true giving]."
It is for the sake of giving. Only when one gives the five flowers to the Buddha today with a mind of non-arising can it truly be called "giving.

Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Even if one were to give wealth and treasures to the Buddha throughout countless kalpas, if one does not know the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the Buddha, this is still not called giving.
An ancient master said: "All things must return to the fundamental essence to find equilibrium; right and wrong naturally merge within the mind."

Regarding the realization of the awakening mind (*bodhicitta*): from the Stage of Pure Mind (*śuddhacittabhūmi*) up to the Ultimate Stage of the Bodhisattva (*bodhisattvanisthābhūmi*), what kind of sphere (*viṣaya*) is realized?
It is called the sphere of *tathatā* (suchness) based upon the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*). Yet, for this realization, there is no sphere;

it is solely the wisdom of *tathatā* (the fundamental wisdom) that is termed the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). It is through this that a bodhisattva, in a single moment of thought, is able to reach all ten directions without exception.
Throughout the worlds, he makes offerings to all Buddhas and entreats them to turn the wheel of Dharma, solely for the purpose of guiding and benefiting sentient beings without relying on mere words.
To those whose faculties are weak, he may manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment by transcending the stages;
to those who are indolent and lax, he may say, "I shall attain the Buddha-way only after practicing for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. Thus, he is able to manifest [these various teachings].
Thus, although there are countless inconceivable skillful means, in reality, the bodhisattvas’ (Mahāyāna) spiritual lineage (*gotra*), faculties (*indriya*), and so forth are equal;
their resolve (*cittotpāda*) is equal, and what they realize is also equal. There is no dharma by which one may surpass another, for all bodhisattvas pass through three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
It is only according to the differences among sentient beings and worlds—their perceptions, hearings, faculties, desires, and natures—that [distinctions appear].
Because they differ, the practices demonstrated also have distinctions.
"Realization" refers to entering the gate of *tathatā* (suchness). What is called *tathatā* here refers to the ten kinds of *tathatā*:
first, universal; second, supreme; third, superior flow; fourth, non-appropriation; fifth, non-differentiation of categories; sixth, non-defilement.
Purity. Seventh, the non-distinction of dharmas. Eighth, neither increasing nor decreasing. Ninth, mastery over the eight knowledges. Tenth, the suchness that is the basis for mastery over karma.
From the first stage through the tenth stage, because karmic consciousness has not yet been exhausted, the obstacles severed at each stage are distinct.
That which is realized is also distinct; thus, ten kinds of objective appearances manifest. This does not mean that there are ten kinds of *tathatā* (suchness).

When the *karmic consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*) is exhausted, only the principle of suchness (*tathatā-nyaya*) and the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*) remain alone; this is called the *dharmakāya*.
Because there is no distinction. Question: Regarding the principle of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), is it established by means of existence, or is it established by means of non-existence?
Is it established by means of arising phenomena, or by means of ceasing phenomena? Is it established by means of a single phenomenon, or by means of diverse phenomena? Answer:

The True Doctrine of Original Enlightenment, the ground-nature of the Dharma-body, is such that words fail when one attempts to speak of it, and thought ceases when the mind attempts to engage with it. Why is this so? Because it is taught that...
If one speaks of existence, the wondrous essence is void and profound; if one speaks of non-existence, the Way is omnipresent. If one speaks of birth, the three realms are devoid of substance;
if one speaks of extinction, the single nature is eternally numinous. If one speaks of unity, each assumes its own form;

if one speaks of difference, all return to the same true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, it cannot be measured and cannot be hoped for; to be able to transcend the four propositions is precisely this.

Regarding the *dharmakāya*, the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* states: Mañjuśrī said, “World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata sat beneath the Bodhi tree and attained bodhi, there were two characteristics of the Tathāgata: first, the Tathāgata; second, bodhi.
How is it that the Tathāgata has already abandoned these two characteristics? The Buddha said, “Good son, bodhi is the one [nature] of all sentient beings.”
All dharmas are equal and without distinction; they are of one flavor and one nature.
When the Tathāgata sat beneath the Bodhi tree, he perceived these dharmas in this way; therefore, it is called "attaining bodhi.
I do not see any other dharma apart from bodhi, because all dharmas are entirely equal. This equality does not enter into numerical reckoning; therefore—

"Equanimity is called the Dharma-body. From "This is Bodhi" onwards, its great function is revealed. "Not relying on words and letters" means clearly understanding that what is pointed out is ultimately not the moon;
therefore, it directly points to the human mind so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha.
This is precisely the school of Bodhidharma which does not establish written words. "Or he shows" reveals his provisional teachings. As for "but in reality," it reveals... [the ultimate truth].

"True words. *Asaṃkhyeya*—here translated as "innumerable"—is also an indeterminate designation. For example, if one does not see someone for the entirety of a day, one says, "it has been an innumerable amount of time";
if one does not meet them again after a year, one likewise says, "it has been an innumerable amount of time. Therefore, the *Zongjing* asks:

regarding the teaching of attaining Buddhahood, some say it occurs in a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), while others speak of three *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas; I do not yet know which is definitively taken as the standard.

Question: How does one use these texts to instruct later students? Answer: The essential principle of attaining Buddhahood does not depend on the duration of kalpas or the number of years required for its attainment;

rather, this belongs to the realm of expedient means (*upāya*). Therefore, for those who are courageous and vigorous, it is taught that attaining Buddhahood occurs in a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*);

whereas for those who are indolent and lax, it is taught that realizing the fruit requires the completion of three *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas. However, as these are merely the traces of formal teachings, they all belong to the category of expedient means. Thus, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*...
The Commentary states: "Kalpa" means time. Within it there are the periods of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness; all of these are induced by the deluded perceptions of sentient beings.
Furthermore, when deluded perception first moves, it externally induces the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*). Because of the arousal of craving, it externally induces the water-circle (*jala-maṇḍala*).

Because of firm attachment, it externally induces the earth-circle (*pṛthivī-maṇḍala*). Because of investigative seeking, it externally induces the fire-circle (*tejo-maṇḍala*). This is because of the existence of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
There are the six sense faculties. Because there are the six sense faculties, one perceives the six sense objects. Because there are the six sense objects, there is the dimension of time.
If one thoroughly understands the root of ignorance—the single moment of deluded mind—then one will know that [time] arises from the mind.

The three realms are ultimately non-existent. Furthermore, time arises dependent upon objects; since objects are fundamentally empty, time likewise has no substance. Why then need one further discuss kalpas?
Regarding the number [of kalpas]: if one can forever sever ignorance in a single thought-moment, why rely on further passing through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*?

Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Without passing through the *kalpas*, one attains the Dharma-body. It also says: "A snap of the fingers transcends the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). And it says: "Resting is itself Bodhi.
Therefore, we know that the length of the *kalpas* arises from a single thought-moment. The progression toward the fruits within the triple world is likewise [dependent upon this].
This is spoken from within a dream upon waking; yet when one has truly awakened, there are in fact no many kalpas.
Therefore, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, half a day is manifested as fifty minor kalpas, and in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, seven days are manifested as one kalpa.
Thus it is said: "The ten periods of past and present, beginning and end, do not depart from the present thought-moment. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states regarding Pūrṇamukha:

There was a butcher who slaughtered a thousand sheep every day. Later, he developed the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). The Buddha said to him, "In this Bhadrakalpa, you shall attain Buddhahood.
All the great Bodhisattvas and Arhats were filled with doubt, saying, "When we attain Buddhahood, it will be after many kalpas have passed;
why is it that this Broad-Forehead shall attain Buddhahood so soon? The Buddha said, "To those who wish to achieve swift accomplishment, I grant [this]."
If one desires to achieve the distant goal, it is granted immediately. If one perceives True Suchness (Tathatā) all at once, one attains Buddhahood in a single thought-moment.
Thus, we know that sharpness or dullness depends on the person; slowness or speed is determined by oneself and has nothing to do with the number of kalpas.
This is explained according to those of the highest capacity who attain sudden enlightenment and engage in sudden cultivation.
Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of the Bodhisattva’s arousal of the mind, there are three kinds of mind with subtle marks. What are these three?

First is the true mind (*tathatā-citta*), because it is free from discrimination. Second is the mind of skillful means (*upāya-citta*), because it spontaneously and universally acts for the benefit of sentient beings.
Third is the mind of karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna-citta*), because its arising and ceasing are subtle.

These are the three kinds of minds generated by a Bodhisattva who has ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*). Compared to those prior to the stages, these three kinds of mind are increasingly continuous and dense;
therefore, they are called "subtle. Regarding the phrase "because the true mind is without discrimination": this refers to the time of entering the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*).

Because the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) has been severed through discernment, one attains non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). Because one realizes the universally pervasive suchness (*sarvatraga-tathatā*), one attains the true mind (*bhūtacitta*).
As for the expedient mind (*upāya-citta*), it universally practices the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) to extensively benefit sentient beings;

yet all these arise from the True [Mind] as practice, without any artificiality or forced effort, and are thus called "spontaneous" (*svabhāva*). As for the karma-consciousness mind (*karma-vijñāna-citta*), because ignorance (*avidyā*) is not yet exhausted, it flows...
The commentary states that it is not yet empty, because there still exists subtle arising and ceasing. Question: Why is this karmic consciousness also called "arousing the mind" (*cittotpāda*)?
Answer: Because as long as discrimination has not been severed and ignorance has not yet been fully exposed, once discrimination is severed, ignorance momentarily manifests;
therefore, it is also called "arousing the mind."
Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva’s merits have reached full completion, he manifests a body of supreme height and magnitude throughout all worlds in the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
This means that through wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, ignorance is suddenly exhausted; this is called the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Spontaneously, there arise inconceivable activities capable of manifesting throughout the ten directions to benefit sentient beings.

This statement indicates that the Bodhisattva, having reached the end of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, manifests the attainment of Buddhahood. The "Abode of Ultimate Form" (*Akaniṣṭha*) is the summit of the Realm of Form (*Rūpadhātu*).
Regarding the "body of supreme magnitude," in the Heaven of Ultimate Form, the body’s measurement is sixteen thousand *yojanas*.
The body of the Śakra-devānām-indra King measures thirty-two thousand yojanas.
When a Bodhisattva of the Tenth Ground manifests as the Śakra-devānām-indra King, his body is twice that size; therefore, it is called the "supremely tall and large body.
Because no physical form is greater than this deity, the Bodhisattva in his final birth manifests the appearance of attaining Buddhahood within that heaven. That is to say:
It is the transformation of the body of a Bodhisattva of the ten stages into the body of a Buddha.

"Wisdom corresponding in a single thought-moment" refers to the very first moment of initial accord between the beginning and the fundamental; this is called a "single thought-moment. By means of this single thought-moment, one illuminates and shatters ignorance.
To realize the nature of the mind is called attaining the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Spontaneously, there arise inconceivable karmic functions:

manifesting infinite bodies, responding in infinite lands, and delivering infinite sentient beings. This is what is meant by the great, perfect, and stainless [wisdom] arising simultaneously, universally illuminating the dust-motes and lands throughout the ten directions.
Question: Because space is limitless, worlds are limitless; because worlds are limitless, sentient beings are limitless;
and because sentient beings are limitless, the distinctions in their mental activities are likewise limitless.

Such a realm cannot be divided or exhausted; it is difficult to know and difficult to understand. If ignorance is severed and no mental conceptions remain, how can one comprehend it? This is called "all."

[Question]: What is the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*)? [Answer]: All objective spheres are fundamentally the one mind, free from conceptualization (the mind is inherently free from thought).

Because sentient beings falsely perceive objective spheres, the mind has limitations. Because they falsely give rise to conceptualizations that do not accord with the *dharmatā*, they are unable to comprehend it.
The Buddhas and Tathāgatas are free from perceived objects and characteristics; because their minds are true, they are omnipresent. This is precisely the [knowledge of all modes].
The nature of the Dharma inherently illuminates all deluded phenomena; it possesses the function of great wisdom and immeasurable skillful means.
According to what each sentient being should understand, it is able to reveal various meanings of the Dharma. For this reason, it is named "All-Knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*).
This doubt holds that if there were no mind, one could not be called "Omniscient" (sarvajñā). The intention [of the objection] is this:
the realms and distinctions of sentient beings are immeasurable, difficult to fathom, and difficult to know.

If ignorance has been exhausted and mental conceptions have also become empty such that there is no mind, by what means would one discern the various realms to clarify omniscience? Answer: All... [text continues]
The objective realm is free from conceptualization; fundamentally, it has no various distinctions, nor does it have boundaries.

It is because sentient beings falsely perceive the objective realm that there appear the characteristics of distinctions and boundaries—such as large and small, high and low, defiled and pure—which cannot shine universally.
Because they give rise to false conceptualizations, they obstruct the radiance and fail to accord with the *dharmatā*, thereby turning it into nothingness.

Because it is luminous, it cannot be fully comprehended. The Buddhas are not so; because they are free from the marks of seeing, they do not perceive the marks of objective realms, and thus there is nothing they do not pervade.
Because they are free from ignorance (*avidyā*), they attain the vision of the true mind.

This true mind is precisely the self-nature of all phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*). Having seen the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one gives rise to the function of great wisdom from within that dharmatā.
He illuminates all delusive phenomena and, through immeasurable skillful means, teaches various dharmas and reveals various meanings in accordance with the minds of sentient beings,
causing each of them to attain understanding. Therefore, it is only those who accord with the mindless state who can attain the wisdom of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).

He asked again: "If all Buddhas possess spontaneous karma (*anābhoga-karman*) that can manifest in all places to benefit sentient beings, then all sentient beings—whether they see their bodies, witness their miraculous transformations, or hear their teachings—would surely obtain benefit."
Why is it that most in the world are unable to see the Buddha? The answer is: The *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is equal and pervasive in all places;

because it is devoid of volitional effort (*manasikāra*), it is said to be spontaneous (*svayambhū*). It manifests solely in accordance with the minds of sentient beings. As for the minds of sentient beings:
It is just like a mirror: if the mirror is defiled, the reflected image does not appear.
In the same way, if the minds of sentient beings are defiled, the *dharmakāya* does not appear (and thus they do not see the Buddha-body). This concludes the section on the explanation.
This doubt—that sentient beings do not see the Tathāgata—means that they cannot be said to receive inconceivable benefits for sentient beings. [The objection is:

Since the Tathāgata possesses spontaneous karmic activity (*nirmita-karma*), manifesting infinite bodies to universally benefit sentient beings, then all sentient beings ought to be able to see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and be universally moistened by its benefits. Why, then, do they not see him? The answer is: The Tathāgata...

The Dharmakāya is omnipresent, reaching everywhere. Whether it manifests or does not manifest depends entirely upon whether the minds of sentient beings are defiled or pure; it is not that the Tathāgata himself has manifestation or non-manifestation. Thus, the *Zongjing* asks: "The Dharmakāya is universally present within the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings. Since all beings share this same mind, why is there manifestation and non-manifestation? The answer is as follows: ...like [the reflection of the moon in water]. When the water is turbid, the moon is not seen; when the water is clear, the moon appears. It is not that the moon itself has appearance or non-appearance; it is simply due to the clarity or turbidity of the water. The Dharmakāya is likewise like this. It is not that the Tathāgata has appearance or non-appearance; it is solely because the minds of sentient beings are either defiled or pure. If one’s own mind is pure, the Buddha immediately appears before one. If one’s own mind is defiled, the Buddha does not appear. It is not that the Buddha is far away; it is only because one’s own mind is obstructed by afflictions (*kleśa*). If one’s mind is pure, the Buddha is near at hand. If one’s mind is defiled, the Buddha is distant. Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "If one wishes to see the Buddhas of the ten directions, one should purify one’s own mind. This is what is meant. If one’s mind is pure, one sees the Buddha; if one’s mind is defiled, one does not see the Buddha. It is not that the Buddha has appearance or non-appearance; it is only because the mind is either pure or defiled. Thus, the *Mahāyāna-samparigraha-śāstra* states: "The Dharmakāya is omnipresent, yet it appears or does not appear according to the purity or impurity of the minds of sentient beings. This is the meaning. It is not that the Tathāgata has appearance or non-appearance; it is only because the minds of sentient beings are either pure or defiled. If one’s own mind is pure, the Buddha immediately appears before one. If one’s own mind is defiled, the Buddha does not appear. It is not that the Buddha is far away; it is only because one’s own mind is obstructed by afflictions. If one’s mind is pure, the Buddha is near at hand. This is the meaning. It is not that the Tathāgata has appearance or non-appearance; it is only because the minds of sentient beings are either pure or defiled. If one’s own mind is pure, the Buddha immediately appears before one. If one’s own mind is defiled, the Buddha does not appear. It is not that the Buddha is far away; it is only because one’s own mind is obstructed by afflictions. If one’s mind is pure, the Buddha is near at hand. If one’s mind is defiled, the Buddha is distant. Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "If one wishes to see the Buddhas of the ten directions, one should purify one’s own mind. This is what is meant. If one’s mind is pure, one sees the Buddha; if one’s mind is defiled, one does not see the Buddha. It is not that the Buddha has appearance or non-appearance; it is only because the mind is either pure or defiled. Thus, the *Mahāyāna-samparigraha-śāstra* states: "The Dharmakāya is omnipresent, yet it appears or does not appear according to the purity or impurity of the minds of sentient beings. This is the meaning. It is not that the Tathāgata has appearance or non-appearance; it is only because the minds of sentient beings are either pure or defiled. If one’s own mind is pure, the Buddha immediately appears before one. If one’s own mind is defiled, the Buddha does not appear. It is not that the Buddha is far away; it is only because one’s own mind is obstructed by afflictions. If one’s mind is pure, the Buddha is near at hand. If one’s mind is defiled, the Buddha is distant. Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "If one wishes to see the Buddhas of the ten directions, one should purify one’s own mind. This is what is meant. If one’s mind is pure, one sees the Buddha; if one’s mind is defiled, one does not see the Buddha. It is not that the Buddha has appearance or non-appearance; it is only because the mind is either pure or defiled. Thus, the *Mahāyāna-s
The Dharmakāya constantly manifests; there is no time when it does not manifest. It may manifest instantaneously within a single atom, or it may manifest universally across all atoms.

Regarding its instantaneous manifestation within a single atom: this is like the eyelashes of the Tathāgata, the jewel crown of Mañjuśrī, the pavilion of Maitreya, the pores of Samantabhadra, the chamber of Vimalakīrti, the womb of Māyā, and even down to a mustard seed or the point of a needle.

Near dust and distant dust each manifest instantaneously. That all dusts manifest universally means they encompass all places, penetrate all times, interpenetrate in layers of depth, and are universally fused without obstruction. An ancient master said:
"That all inconceivable phenomena can be universally manifested within a single phenomenon—can this be anything other than the functional application of the pure *dharmakāya*? Regarding this:
It is said: "If one can contemplate the non-duality of the mind with true discernment, only then will one see the pure body of Vairocana.

If a single thought of evil arises, the Dharmakāya immediately manifests according to that evil; if a single thought of goodness arises, the Dharmakāya immediately manifests according to that goodness.
Even down to seeing form, it manifests in the locus of form; seeing emptiness, it manifests in the locus of emptiness. This is called 'manifesting everywhere. Be most careful not to [miss this]."
To seek the Dharma-body of all Buddhas afar is to realize that it is precisely this single thought-moment of emptiness.

If it does not manifest, it is because it is obscured by adventitious defilements and separated by the net of one's own views; it is not the fault of the Dharma-body. It is like the sun and moon adorning the sky, yet the blind do not see them;
or like thunder and lightning shaking the earth, yet the deaf do not hear them. Thus, for those with merit, as soon as they are born, the precious jewels appear before them.
When those of meager merit emerge, thorns and brambles grow; all this arises because their own minds are either pure or defiled, such that things appear or do not appear accordingly.
If one realizes that within one's own mind they manifest simultaneously and with equal nature, [all obstacles vanish].

Next, the Section on Cultivating Faith is explained (this explains that sentient beings of dull faculties and meager merit who have entered the stage of right determination must apply diligent effort).

This is for the cultivation of faith by those sentient beings whose roots of goodness are slight; for those who, before ten thousand kalpas have elapsed, enter the assembly of right determination, the four unbreakable faiths are taught to bring them to the fulfillment of faith.
In this context, because it concerns sentient beings who have not yet entered the stage of the correct determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), the cultivation of faith is taught.
What is faith? How is it cultivated? Briefly stated, there are four kinds of faith. What are the four? First is faith in the root, which is True Suchness (*tathatā*).

The first is to joyfully recollect the Dharma of True Suchness (the Teacher of all Buddhas), which brings delight to body and mind as one practices in accordance with it. Second is faith in the Buddha:

because he possesses immeasurable merit (as previously described through the three wheels), one constantly recollects him, draws near to him, makes offerings, and shows respect, thereby generating roots of goodness and aspiring for omniscience. Third is faith in the Dharma:

because it provides great benefit, one constantly recollects and practices the various *pāramitās*. Fourth is faith in the Saṃgha (referring to Bodhisattvas of the ten stages): they are able to practice correctly.
Benefiting oneself and others, one should always delight in drawing near to the assembly of Bodhisattvas, for the purpose of seeking and studying the practice of true cultivation.
One’s habitual nature is easily influenced, just as plain silk may be dyed blue or green; it is like turbulent water that may flow east or west;
and it is like a measuring inchworm that may appear dark green or yellow. This is because the eight consciousnesses contain the seeds of the ten dharma realms.

O son, those who, upon hearing the Dharma as it is taught, immediately give rise to its actualization, are called sentient beings who have not yet entered the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Now, for the sake of such sentient beings, these four indestructible faiths (*avetyaprasāda*) are taught;
because by hearing these four indestructible faiths, they do not fall back or decline. "Faith in the root" refers precisely to faith in the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma. "Delight" means...

Joyful aspiration and mindfulness—mindfulness here refers to clear recollection. If one has joy but lacks mindfulness, that joy will not endure. If one has mindfulness but lacks joy, that mindfulness will not be authentic.
One must be like a bee mindful of fine honey or one parched with thirst longing for nectar; even in moments of haste or distress, one must keep this in mind and hold it fast without interruption.
This is called true joyful mindfulness. If there were anyone who could fall away while possessing such [mindfulness], it would be impossible.
For this reason, it is said that for those who have accomplished faith, it is called "right mindfulness" (*samyak-smṛti*);

for those who have not yet accomplished faith, it is called "delightful mindfulness. Both of these refer to faith in the Three Jewels. If one has not yet believed in True Suchness (*tathatā*), the Three Jewels one believes in remain outside the mind;
thus, they do not accord with reality. Should one encounter external conditions, there may arise a falling away or loss [of that faith].
If one first has faith in True Suchness (tathatā), then the Three Jewels in which one places faith are entirely True Suchness. Through this, one progresses until faith is fully accomplished.
There are five gates of practice that can assist and perfect this faith. What are these five? First is the gate of giving (dāna-pāramitā). Second is the gate of precepts (śīla)...

1. The gate of ethical discipline (*śīla*); 2. The gate of generosity (*dāna*); 3. The gate of patience (*kṣānti*); 4. The gate of diligence (*vīrya*); 5. The gate of tranquility (*samatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) (the union of meditative concentration and wisdom).
To believe without practicing is mere belief; how can belief alone be fulfilled? Only when one is able to practice these five things is belief truly perfected.
This is precisely what was previously described as the joyful accumulation of wholesome conduct—the method for removing impurities from ore.
How does one practice the gateway of giving? If one sees anyone who comes seeking anything, one should give away all one's wealth and possessions according to one's ability;

by this self-benefit of abandoning stinginess and greed, one causes others to rejoice. If one sees those beset by calamity, fear, or peril, one should, to the best of one's capacity, grant them fearlessness (this giving is superior to the former).
If there are sentient beings who come seeking the Dharma, one should [teach] according to what one can understand.
He then spoke for him: "One should not greedily seek fame, profit, or honor; rather, one should contemplate only benefiting oneself and others, dedicating such merit toward Bodhi.

There are three kinds of giving: namely, the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*), the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*), and the gift of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*). 'If one sees all those who are lowly' refers to the gift of material wealth."

Furthermore, "if one sees those in distress" refers to the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*). "If there is [a recipient]" refers to the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*). Master Fu’s Verse on Giving states:

"The gate of giving encompasses the six practices (the six practices being the six perfections). The six practices are subsumed within the three types of *dāna* (the three *dānas* being: the *dāna* of material goods, the *dāna* of fearlessness, and the *dāna* of Dharma).

Giving constitutes the *dāna* of material goods, for it provides sustenance for the growth of all wholesome dharmas; thus it is called the *dāna* of material goods. Observing the precepts and practicing patience constitute the *dāna* of fearlessness, because through the purity of the precepts, one remains unmoved by insults and humiliation."

The mind is free from fear; therefore, it is called the *dāna* of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*). As for the *dāna* of the Dharma (*dharma-dāna*), it consists of diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). Because compassion arises from concentration and various dharmas arise from wisdom, it is called the *dāna* of the Dharma. These six practices are grouped into three types of *dāna*: the *dāna* of material goods, the *dāna* of fearlessness, and the *dāna* of the Dharma.

Let sound and form not interfere with one another. Do not establish the two extremes; there is no need to settle upon the Middle Way. (To "settle" on the extremes refers to the two extremes of existence and non-existence.

If these are not established, both existence and non-existence are discarded. What "Middle Way" could then be settled upon? Zhao says: ordinary people cling to existence and do not see the emptiness within existence; those of the Two Vehicles cling to emptiness and do not see [the reality] within emptiness.)

Therein lies the subtle existence; do not cling to views regarding the two extremes, nor grasp at characteristics within the Middle Way (for this is known only by the Buddha’s knowledge and vision). If you wish to recognize the place of non-arising, turn away from objects and observe the mind.

How does one practice the gate of precepts? It is said: not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not using double-tongued speech, not speaking harshly, not lying, and not engaging in frivolous chatter (exaggerating faults or glossing over errors).

One should distance oneself from greed and envy (greed, anger, and delusion), deceit and fraud (the ten non-virtues), flattery and crookedness, malice and resentment, and false views (delusion; guarding against wrongdoing and ceasing evil).

If one is a renunciant, for the sake of subduing the afflictions (it is necessary to subdue the afflictions), one should likewise distance oneself from bustle and clamor, always dwelling in tranquility, and cultivate [these practices].

Having few desires (not seeking much), being content (giving rise to shame and remorse), and practicing the dhūta austerities (these twelve practices which shake off defilements); furthermore, feeling fear toward even minor transgressions, one feels shame and remorse, and reforms.

One must not treat lightly the prohibitions and precepts established by the Tathāgata; one should guard against reproach so as not to cause sentient beings to give rise to false transgressions and faults.

There are three types of precepts: namely, the precept of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*). These are referred to as the "lower" [precepts].

"This is the restraint of the code of discipline (*saṃvara-śīla*). 'To distance oneself from the lower' refers to the gathering of wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*). 'One should protect the lower' refers to benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*).
As for the statement 'not killing,' it universally encompasses all beings and does not refer to humans alone. As for 'not stealing,' it includes even a single needle or a single blade of grass."
Not only regarding the five coins; as for non-celibacy, one commits the offense by merely giving rise to the thought, not only through physical contact.
As for double-tongued speech, it means instigating discord between two parties. As for harsh speech, it means acting willfully with biting and stinging words.

As for false speech, it refers to groundless talk. As for frivolous speech, it refers to flowery and embellished rhetoric. Greed means seeking much. Envy means jealousy and resentment. One should consider that these arise from ignorance and lack of vision.
To deceive another is called "fraud" (*ch'i*). To probe into others while knowing and seeing their true nature is called "guile" (*cha*).
The sycophant uses excessive courtesy and a pleasing countenance to flatter others. The one full of anger rages and acts ferociously to vex others.
The one with false views does not contemplate *tathatā* (Suchness) but seeks externally. The one with few desires does not indulge in the world.
This is the flavor [of the Dharma]. "Contentment" means being satisfied with what one has received in small measure. "Dhūta" (ascetic purification) means shaking off the dust of dharmas.

"Fearing even minor transgressions" means preventing small faults from developing into great ones. "Guarding against reproach and suspicion" refers to practicing that which is not in accordance with the Vinaya or possessing things that are not in accordance with the Dharma;
these all invite public censure and slander, thereby giving rise to offenses in others. That such offenses arise in others is truly due to...

Therefore, one must guard it. Question: If worldly defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) are that which is to be remedied and supramundane pure phenomena (*lokottara-śuddha-dharma*) are the remedy, then the ultimate and the conventional are mutually manifest as the object and the subject of counteraction. Why, then, do you speak only of the principle of the "One Mind" as being able to dispel all phenomena?
Answer: The ultimate Way is rooted in the One Mind; the nature of the mind is rooted in non-abiding. This non-abiding mind...
As for the essence: when spiritual awareness is not obscured, the myriad things arise; they all take the non-abiding one mind as their essence.
Apart from the mind, there is no separate dharma. It is like the multitude of waves relying on water—apart from water, there are no waves;
or like myriad forms relying on space—apart from space, there are no forms. Therefore, the Buddha said: "I do not see any dharma other than greed that can emerge [from it]."
The same applies to hatred and delusion. Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature apart from the *dharmadhātu*, the *dharmatā* of desire and so forth receives the names "desire" and so on.
This explains that the *dharmatā* of desire and so forth can bring about the transcendence of desire and so forth. Thus, a verse says:
"By giving rise to right reflection regarding desire, one attains liberation from desire; therefore, it is said that desire transcends desire. The same holds true for hatred and delusion.
The commentary states: Apart from desire, there is no separate phenomenon. This is because the dharma-realm of desire is the very gateway through which all phenomena proceed toward desire.
If one correctly contemplates this gateway of desire and realizes that desire lacks intrinsic nature, one then attains liberation from desire and the like.
If one gives rise to false thoughts regarding desire and, being deluded by desire, develops attachment, then one is bound by that desire.

This bondage and liberation thus constitute the two gates of the ultimate and the conventional. Within these two gates of the ultimate and the conventional, all phenomena—both defiled and pure—are fully encompassed.
Since this is the case for the phenomenon of desire, it is likewise for hatred and ignorance, as each individually pervades the entire dharma-realm. If one is deluded...
Skillful means involve craving for various doctrinal gateways; this is like being swept away by the surging waters of doubt or casting one's feet toward a city of Gandharvas.
Relying on the void leads only to self-destruction. Once the reality is attained, what cause for worry remains? This principle of the single mind is where all myriad virtues converge.
Whether good or evil, it can turn them both around; whether favorable or adverse, it causes them all to be perfected as good. Thus, the ten mysteries...
Within this gate, there is the "Gate of the Perfect Accomplishment through the Revolving of Mind-Only. Therefore, one cannot definitively state whether the nature is pure or impure.
Thus, we know that inversion and conformity arise solely from the revolving of the mind; suffering and pleasure follow their respective conditions.

The true mind, which does not abide for even a single thought-moment, has never changed throughout kalpas as numerous as motes of dust; it is merely what is perceived according to the distinctions made by wisdom.
They are simply different. Master Fu’s Verse on Upholding the Precepts says: "Precepts (śīla) attain purity; they are the cause from immeasurable kalpas past.

Delusive thoughts are like vengeful thieves; craving and attachment are like the stars Shen and Chen (Shen and Chen refer to the two constellations Shen and Shang; one rises while the other sets, always remaining far apart)."

Amidst desire yet free from desire; dwelling in the dust yet unstained by the dust. Temporarily relying on the Ground Free from Defilement (Vimalā-bhūmi), one shall realize the body of the Dharma King (the Buddha, sovereign of all dharmas).

How does one practice the gate of patience? It means that one should endure the afflictions caused by others—just as a pig remains unmoved when trampled upon a mountain of gold—and harbor no intent for retaliation.
Furthermore, one should likewise endure the dharmas of gain and loss, defamation and praise, fame and insignificance, suffering and pleasure.
To endure affliction without retaliating is the patience toward resentment (*āghātamarṣaṇakṣānti*). To endure the eight winds (*aṣṭau lokadharmāḥ*) is the patience of acceptance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).

"Gain" refers to when shoes fill the space outside one's door; "loss" refers to when crows perch in rows before one's gate. "Censure" refers to being treated with malice despite having committed no fault;

"praise" refers to being attributed with goodness despite possessing no virtue. "Fame" refers to the extolling of one who truly possesses virtue; "slander" [refers to the disparagement of one who does not].
To truly lack virtue yet to prick others with it—this is what is meant by the affliction of body and mind; for body and mind to be at ease and relaxed—this is what is meant by joy.
When these winds of the eight kinds of objects arise, one who can settle the mind and remain unmoved is none other than one possessed of great patience (*mahākṣānti*).
Huang Tingjian said: "These eight things are the seeds of ignorance (*avidyā*); human beings arise from ignorance."
Born from seeds, complete with skin and bone—how could there be any place to escape?

Yet, when viewed through the lens of a hundred years, both others and myself, as well as those eight things, all become one emptiness. An ancient said: "The bodies of sentient beings are identical to the great void;
where can afflictions find a foothold? Reflect deeply and contemplate thoroughly: from where do afflictions arise? They have no origin.
Is it beneficial for one’s affairs? Is it beneficial for the person?

The waves of the eight winds are vast and boundless, yet with a life of a hundred years that has its own limit, one calculates in various ways, desiring profit, loathing decline, resenting disparagement, rejoicing in praise, and seeking renown.

To avoid censure, to loathe suffering, and to pursue pleasure—without understanding gain and loss, and moreover possessing one's own karmic causes from past lives—one must simply act without calculation.
Furthermore, to leap like a monkey and gallop like a horse until one is utterly exhausted before resting cannot be called wisdom.
Nor does one know the path that approaches the Way; thus, one is brought to an end here. As Layman Lanan said: "This..."
The eight objects are the seeds of ignorance. If one can attain a point of resolution within the *huatou*, then the seeds of ignorance will be entirely transformed into the true suchness of *prajñā*.
Once they have been entirely transformed into the true suchness of *prajñā*, [the state of liberation is realized].
Thus, even dressing and eating are like this; sitting in stillness and sleeping at ease are also like this.

Even if one were to seek again for the seeds of ignorance, they would be utterly unfindable. This is what the ancient Buddhas meant when they said that the bodies of sentient beings are identical to the great void;
where could afflictions find a foothold? Is this not truly joyful! This is the forbearance of Master Fu.

The verse says: Patience is like an illusion or a dream; the objects of insult are like the hair of a tortoise (the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says that seeing them is like [seeing] the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit).
If one can constantly cultivate this contemplation, one will become even more steadfast when encountering difficulties. There is neither wrong nor right; there is neither low nor high.
To extinguish the thieves of greed and hatred, one must wield the sword of wisdom.
How does one practice the gateway of diligence? It is said: regarding all wholesome deeds, the mind never slackens or retreats, and one’s resolve remains firm and strong.
One should remain far removed from cowardice. One should reflect that since the distant past, one has pointlessly endured all manner of great physical and mental suffering without any benefit.
Therefore, one should diligently cultivate all meritorious virtues to benefit oneself and others, and to distance oneself from all forms of suffering.

Furthermore, even if a person practices with faith, because they have accumulated many grave sins and karmic obstacles from previous lives, they may be harassed and disturbed by malevolent spirits and ghosts; or they may be entangled by various worldly affairs;
or they may be afflicted by the suffering of illness. Since there are many such obstacles, one should therefore be courageous...

With fierce diligence, throughout the six periods of day and night, one should prostrate to all Buddhas, repent with a sincere heart, entreat them to teach, rejoice in merit, and dedicate it toward Bodhi, never ceasing or abandoning this practice.
By doing so, one shall escape all obstacles and cause one's roots of goodness to increase.

"One whose mind does not slacken or retreat" means that one advances further as one practices more. "One whose resolve is firm and strong" means that one does not alter one's commitment because of setbacks or discouragement.
"One who stays far removed from cowardice and weakness" means that one does not cease halfway due to the fear of difficulties.
"Regarding 'should reflect upon the past'" means that by contemplating the past, one exerts oneself in this present life. Furthermore, regarding the subsequent phrase, it serves as an obstacle.
The "heavy" refers to the application of skillful means. Those who wish to eliminate obstacles by prostrating to the Buddha are like a person in debt who seeks the protection of a king;
no one can then harm them. Through repentance, one eliminates the obstacle of evil karma; through exhortation, one eliminates the obstacle of slandering the Dharma.
Rejoicing removes the obstacle of jealousy; dedication removes the obstacle of the three realms of existence. Master Fu’s Verse on Diligence says:

Diligent cultivation is called the Stage of Flames (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi), Precisely because the light of wisdom unfolds. The two types of knowledge are dispelled within the mind, And the three types of emptiness are eliminated from the objective realm.
Ignorance is extinguished moment by moment, And attachment to high and low is removed. If one contemplates the mind without interruption, How could one not reach [the goal]?
Without remainder (the two wisdoms of the ultimate and the conventional).

How does one practice the gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*? That which is called *śamatha* refers to the cessation of all objective appearances that distract the mind, because it accords with the meaning of *śamatha* (which is stillness while constantly illuminating, the pure conduct).
That which is called *vipaśyanā* refers to the discernment of the characteristics of arising and ceasing through causes and conditions, because it accords with [the realization of] *tathatā*.
Because vipaśyanā (i.e., contemplation) contemplates the meaning [of reality], how does one accord with it?

By means of these two meanings, one gradually practices them without separation, so that both are manifested simultaneously (the union of śamatha and vipaśyanā, the simultaneous manifestation of samādhi and prajñā).
"Stopping" (śamatha) refers to forgetting objects and ceasing thoughts; it means not thinking of any phenomena in the world, but thinking solely of mind-only.
"Contemplation" (vipaśyanā) refers to discerning arising and ceasing; it means observing the body, sensations, mind, and dharmas, asking from where arising comes and to where ceasing goes.
Master Ouyi said: "In stopping, one does not follow after deluded thoughts, but remains in a single mark."

"Perpetually pure": through contemplation, one does not stagnate in empty quiescence, yet wondrous function constantly arises. "Not mutually abandoning" means that because one can bring about the cessation of discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), one is able to observe;
because one is able to observe, one can bring about the cessation of discursive thought. This is because both are manifested simultaneously.
Awakening and stillness flow as a dual stream (to illuminate stillness is called contemplation; to contemplate is called stillness).
If one practices stillness, one should dwell in a quiet place, sit upright, and maintain right intention, neither relying on the breath nor relying on forms and colors.
Do not rely on emptiness; do not rely on earth, water, fire, or wind; and so forth, do not rely on seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing.
Eliminate all conceptualizations as they arise through recollection, and even eliminate the thought of elimination itself, for all phenomena are fundamentally without conceptualization.

(All phenomena) do not arise from moment to moment, nor do they cease from moment to moment. Furthermore, one should not follow the mind’s outward wandering toward objects and subsequently use the mind to eliminate the mind.

If the mind wanders and scatters, one should immediately collect it and abide in right mindfulness. This right mindfulness—which takes True Suchness as its object—should be known as being solely mind.
There are no external objects; this mind itself likewise lacks any intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa*). Moment by moment, they do not encounter one another.

Whether rising from one's seat, going or coming, advancing or stopping, or performing any action whatsoever, at all times one should constantly maintain mindfulness of skillful means (*upāya*) and observe accordingly.
Through long-term practice until it becomes pure and mature, the mind attains stability. Because the mind abides, one gradually attains a sharp and intense state of conformity.

They enter the samādhi of true thusness (*tathatā*), deeply subduing their afflictions (*kleśa*). Their faith increases, and they swiftly achieve the stage of non-retrogression (referring here to those previously mentioned who possessed dull faculties).
This excludes only those with the heavy karmic obstructions of doubt, lack of faith, slandering [the Dharma], pride, and indolence; such persons are unable to enter it.
This is the practice for a beginner in the study of Chan. "Sitting upright with a correct intention" means that both body and mind are aligned.
"Not thinking of anything" is called right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "When you sit at the site of enlightenment, dissolve all thoughts.
Regarding "vital breath," this refers to practices such as regulating the breath, counting the breath, or guarding and guiding the vital energy. Regarding "the form,"...

"Contemplating the body" refers to practices such as visualizing the skeletal chain or meditating on the stabilization of the physical form. "Form" refers to the cultivation of the ten universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*), or the visualization of the *padma* (lotus), the sun, the moon, and so forth.
"Space" refers to the cultivation practiced by those of the three vehicles, or that practiced in the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*).

"The four great elements" refers to the analytical investigation of the four elements, or practices such as serving fire or serving wind. "Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing" [refers to the respective sensory cognitions].
"Those who [practice] such things as extinguishing the heart-mind and severing consciousness are all practicing the meditations of the Śrāvakas and non-Buddhists;
therefore, none of these are relied upon. Here, meditation is defined as the unmoving single mind and right mindfulness of *tathatā* (suchness);

this is precisely the Tathāgata-meditation and the Patriarchal Meditation. As for 'all conceptualizations being eliminated in accordance with mindfulness,' it refers to what is called the pure, naked, and bare state."
Sprinkle the wine. To act throughout the twelve periods of the day without relying on a single thing is precisely this. Furthermore, one must eliminate even the notion [of non-reliance];
that is to say, even having a trace of breath is a sickness. Therefore, one must eliminate it again and again.
Since all phenomena are solely suchness (*tathatā*), fundamentally devoid of conceptualization and without arising or ceasing, there is no room for a single deluded thought to arise.
If at times you have not been maintaining constant vigilance, yet a thought arises, you must immediately become aware of it. As the saying goes: "One does not fear the arising of a thought;
one only fears that awakening is late. By all means, do not follow after external thoughts and objects, and then subsequently attempt to use the mind to eliminate the mind.
If you use the mind to eliminate the mind, thoughts will arise in succession, and this is not the method for bringing the mind to rest.
"If the mind wanders and scatters, one must immediately collect it and abide in right mindfulness.
This is what is meant by "once it has wandered off into the grass, pull it back by the nose. Da'an said:
"For thirty years I lived at Mount Gui, eating Mount Gui’s rice and defecating Mount Gui’s excrement, yet I did not study Mount Gui’s Chan; I simply watched a single water buffalo. If..."
Falling into the weeds and falling into the grass, he was immediately seized by the nostrils and dragged back. For having temporarily encroached upon the crops, he was whipped and subdued.
Having been thus for a long time, this pitiable creature has come to accept human commands; now he has transformed into a white ox in the open field.
It is right before you, revealed all day long in its vast openness; even if you try to pursue it, it will not go away. Therefore it is said:
"To place it in one location is itself the site of enlightenment for all Buddhas. This is the most critical point for a beginner to apply effort in their practice.

One who possesses right mindfulness should know that "the mind alone exists and there are no external objects"; only when one does not perceive any phenomena existing outside the mind [is this realized].
This is called right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). If one perceives even a single dharma, it is entirely wrong thinking (*mithyā-manasikāra*);

therefore, it is said that the inner mind does not go out and external objects do not enter, and the mind is like a wall or a barrier—only then can one enter the Way. Formerly, Chan Master Fakong resided on Mount Wutai.
Every night he would suddenly hear a voice called "Empty Chan. Fakong was troubled by this, but after a long time, he attained self-awakening.
He said, "All these are objects of my own mind; how could there be any external sound? Thereafter, the sounds ceased entirely.
Furthermore, when Dharma Master Lingrun was traveling in the mountains, a wild fire rushed toward them from afar. His companions all sought to avoid it, but Lingrun walked on with his usual pace.
He said, "Outside the mind there is no fire; fire is truly of the mind itself. If one says that fire can burn, there is no way to escape the fire."
The fire arrived and was extinguished. Furthermore, when Kumārajīva of the Jin dynasty was a child, he accompanied his mother to Khotan.
He carried the Buddha’s alms bowl upon his head and thought to himself, "This bowl is extremely large; why is it so light? Immediately, it became heavy, and he cried out, setting it down.
His mother asked him the reason, and he replied, "Because my mind harbored a sense of discrimination, the bowl consequently felt light or heavy. From this, one knows that—
All phenomena arrive in accordance with mindfulness. When mindfulness has not yet arisen, their measure is equal to the great void.

Thus, although the various categories of presently active discrimination are now in full confusion, why is it that spiritual efficacy is not uniform? It is said: These are all empty and false, chaotic thoughts. They are like matters within a dream;
because the power of the mind is obscured and its capacity is weak and inferior. Alas! No person [understands this].
It was not that they lacked a heart of loyalty and filial piety; yet, when Wang Xiang lay upon the ice, the fish leaped forth, and when Geng Gong prostrated before the well, the spring gushed out.
Why was this? It was because their cultivation of these virtues was single-minded; thus, the response of spiritual efficacy was as swift as a shadow following a form or an echo following a sound.
All of these are illustrations for realizing that there is only mind and no external objects.

Furthermore, this very mind is without characteristics and cannot be apprehended from moment to moment. It is said that if the mind wanders and scatters, one should immediately abide in right mindfulness.
This mind is simply restored; it is not necessary for the mind to further eliminate the mind.
You should know that once this mind is restored, one no longer perceives any self-characteristic of the mind to be grasped, and it naturally becomes settled and at ease.
The above clarifies the practice performed during stillness. From here on, it again speaks of the practice performed during movement, which refers to daily life.
In all places and at all times during the four modes of conduct, one should observe in accordance [with the practice], never forgetting the correct mindfulness of the "mind-only" *huatou*.
This is because it is the great expedient means for entering the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*). As for the term "in accordance":
It is like rowing a boat against swift currents: do not let the *huatou* (the critical phrase) drift away. As for observation, it is like a cat catching a mouse: do not let go of the *huatou*.
In the midst of daily life and ordinary activities, apply yourself with effort in this manner. After a long time, you will naturally become mature;
the mind will no longer wander, and you will abide constantly in right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). Once you abide in right mindfulness, your resolve will naturally and gradually [become firm].
As it gradually becomes more intense and sharp, one is able to accord with and enter the Samādhi of True Suchness (*tathatā*). "Samādhi" refers here to right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
Once one has entered this concentration, discriminative thought does not arise; afflictions are naturally subdued, and faith naturally grows.

Without waiting for ten thousand kalpas, one will swiftly achieve the stage of non-retrogression. This excludes those of inferior capacity and those who lack faith, as indicated by the fivefold discernment.
Those who are icchantikas are those who slander [the Dharma]. Those who destroy the teaching are those who commit the five heinous crimes (ānantarya-karma) and are inhabitants of the Avīci Hell.
Those who possess pride are those who are arrogant and haughty, lacking a sincere heart. Those who are indolent...
Vagrant and heedless—those who do not exert effort. These five types of people all fail to accord with [the teaching], and therefore cannot enter.
Thus, the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "Except for those of sudden enlightenment, even the Dharma does not accord with them."

Furthermore, by relying on this samādhi, one realizes that the dharma-realm has a single characteristic: namely, that the dharma-body of all Buddhas and the bodies of sentient beings are equal and non-dual.
This is called the *ekavyūha-samādhi* (samādhi of the single practice). One should know that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the root of this samādhi;
if a person practices it, they will gradually be able to give rise to immeasurable samādhis.
The Śūraṅgama King Samādhi is the perfection of the ten thousand practices. Here it is called "the one practice. Because of this one practice there are the ten thousand practices;
because of the ten thousand practices there is this one practice. The Mañjuśrī-prajñā Sūtra asks: "What is named the One Practice Samādhi? The Buddha said:
"The Dharma-realm has a single characteristic. To have one's conditions and attachments bound to the Dharma-realm is named the One Practice Samādhi. Those who enter this samādhi..."
One fully knows that the dharma-realm of all Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, is characterized by non-differentiation.
Because this *tathatā-samādhi* (samādhi of suchness) can give rise to immeasurable samādhis, it is called the "root of samādhi. As the *Ghanavyūha-gāthā* says:
"Just as when one grain of rice is known, all the others can be known; so it is with all dharmas—by knowing one, one knows them all. Therefore, it is known.
The myriad dharmas all converge within this school, just as a hundred flowers together form a single honey. If one understands this clearly, then all things are oneself.

Whether ascending or sinking, departing or abiding, let it be as you wish according to conditions; whether speaking or remaining silent, expanding or contracting, always remain in accord with the Way of the Single Truth.
Even in managing one’s livelihood and engaging in worldly production, do not deviate from the gate of the true mark (*dharmatā*). In every movement and application, in every thought-moment...
Apart from the Dharma-realm, whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, one is constantly within it at every step.

Just as a person of clear insight, upon opening their eyes and relaxing their mind, can perceive everything beforehand, so too for those who have not yet met [this realization], their every movement and action is never interrupted;
it is exactly like Sudhana ascending the pavilion or the Dragon Girl offering her pearl—at that moment, one naturally beholds it with one's own eyes.
One must discipline oneself to accomplish the task, forgetting fatigue day and night. If one asks about the journey but does not travel, one’s hometown will only grow further away;
it is like seeing a treasure but failing to take it, resulting once again in poverty.
Therefore, know that within a single thought-moment of birth and death, those who can believe in the inconceivable deeds of the Buddhas are exceedingly rare. (From a verse by Master Fu Dashi)
It is said: "One who is able to resolve their mind in this way should understand the two extremes. Nirvāṇa is without marks; Bodhi is free from objects of perception (Zi Rong says:

As in practice one must resolve to cultivate the bodhisattva path and seek those with the correct knowledge and vision of the Mahāyāna to awaken to the Supreme Vehicle, one must first understand the attachments to the two extremes of existence and non-existence.

Only then can one realize the principle of the markless nature of nirvāṇa; thus, one is free from the mind and its objects of perception). There is neither vehicle nor rider; both person and phenomena are abandoned. One who wishes to reach [this state]..."
Regarding the principle of True Suchness (tathatā), one should recognize its original source.
There may be sentient beings who, lacking the power of roots of goodness, are then deluded and disturbed by various māras, non-Buddhists, and malevolent spirits.
If, while sitting in meditation, one manifests terrifying forms, or manifests the appearances of handsome men, women, and so forth, one should contemplate that these are but the mind;
then the objective realm will cease and will ultimately not cause affliction. Or they may manifest the image of a deva, the image of a bodhisattva, or likewise the image of a Tathāgata.
Endowed with the primary and secondary marks of excellence, he may preach dhāraṇīs; or he may preach generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
or he may speak of equanimity, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the absence of enmity and the absence of kinship, and the absence of cause and effect.
Ultimate emptiness and stillness is true *nirvāṇa*. [The demon] may cause people to know past events from their former lives and also know future events;

he attains the knowledge of others' minds and possesses unimpeded eloquence. He can cause sentient beings to become greedily attached to worldly fame and profit, and can also cause people to frequently become angry or frequently joyful, such that their nature lacks constancy, or else they become excessively compassionate and loving.
They sleep much and fall frequently ill; their minds are indolent. Sometimes they suddenly exert themselves with diligence, only to lapse back into negligence again.

They give rise to a lack of faith, becoming full of doubt and excessive deliberation. Or they abandon their original superior practices to cultivate miscellaneous activities. If they become attached to worldly affairs, they will be entangled by various distractions.
These states can also cause people to attain a semblance of various samādhis, yet all such attainments belong to non-Buddhists.

This is not true samādhi. Or again, it may cause a person to remain in a state of meditative concentration for one day, two days, three days, or even up to seven days, obtaining naturally fragrant and delicious food and drink, with body and mind feeling at ease, neither hungry nor thirsty.
This causes people to become attached; or it may cause a person to eat without moderation, sometimes too much and sometimes too little, resulting in a change in their physical complexion.
For this reason, a practitioner should constantly observe with wisdom so as not to allow this mind to fall into the net of error.

One should diligently maintain right mindfulness, neither grasping nor becoming attached, thereby being able to distance oneself from these various karmic obstructions. One should know that [this applies to] what is taught by the non-Buddhists.
There are samādhis that do not depart from the mind of attachment, craving, and egoism, because of greed for worldly fame, profit, and honor.

The preceding section clarified the realm of the Buddha; this section clarifies the realm of Māra. One must understand that both the Buddha and Māra are merely manifestations of one's own mind. Do not...
Those who come from without and manifest terrifying forms possess the aspect of fearfulness; those who appear as handsome men and women possess the aspect of loveliness.
To maintain the mindfulness that these are merely the objective realms of one's own mind, and thus cause them to vanish, is the method for repelling demons.
As the ancient masters said: "The wiles of mountain ghosts have an end, but the old monk does not heed them, for they are inexhaustible. If, with even a single thought-moment...

If you move, you will be manipulated by them. Long ago, there was a Chan master sitting in the mountains who saw a filial son carrying a corpse and placing it before him, then weeping and saying, "Why did you kill my mother?
The Chan master knew this was a demon and thought to himself, "This is a demonic realm; if I were to strike it away with an axe, I might attain liberation."
He then took an axe and struck the filial son. The filial son fled. Later, he noticed his thigh was wet;
upon looking, it was blood. He had not expected to strike himself. Furthermore, there was a Zen master who, while sitting, saw a pig come before him.
Knowing it was a māra, the master seized the pig by its nostrils and shouted, "Bring fire! When the fire arrived, he then saw—
The Chan master himself cried out, seizing his nose. This occurred precisely while he was sitting in meditation; a view arose within his mind, which then caused an external demon to enter his heart.
Thus one knows that if one realizes "mind-only," all objective realms naturally cease. Where else could there be a realm of demons apart from the mind? Regarding the phrase "or manifests below":
it means manifesting a body according to what [the practitioner] prefers. Regarding the phrase "if he speaks below": it means according to what...

If they delight in preaching the Dharma, he preaches the Dharma. If they delight in *dhāraṇīs*, he preaches *dhāraṇīs*. If they delight in the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), he preaches the six perfections.

If they delight in equanimity, he preaches equanimity. If they delight in liberation, he preaches the three liberations (*trivimokṣa*). If they delight in recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), he manifests the recollection of past lives.

If they delight in the supernormal power of the mind (*cetaḥparyāya-abhijñā*), he manifests the supernormal power of the mind. If they delight in fame and profit, he speaks of fame and profit. Once he has entered...
The human mind is like oil mixed into flour; it can cause the practitioner to alternate between anger and joy, altering their habitual patterns and changing their temperament.
For instance, one who possesses much compassion will feel love upon seeing others, while one afflicted by sleepiness, illness, or indolence will find it difficult to endure spiritual practice.
To arise suddenly and perish suddenly means to be sharp at the beginning but lax at the end. To be born from a lack of faith means to begin with faith but conclude with doubt and hesitation.
To abandon superior practices and cultivate miscellaneous deeds is like leaving the high trees to enter a deep valley.
Such is the nature of having no constant standard; that which is only partially similar is but a mere semblance.
"True. This is the samādhi of reflected images. That which causes people to attain meditative concentration is sustained by the power of Māra.

That the colors change and differ is to dazzle the eyes of men. Although such demonic activities are many, if one observes them with superior wisdom and maintains the mindfulness that they are 'mind-only,' no grasping or attachment will arise, and they will naturally vanish.
If one gives rise to a mind of attachment, one falls under the deceptive designs of others. Therefore..."

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "If one does not give rise to the thought of being a sage, it is called a wholesome state; if one interprets it as being a sage, one will immediately be possessed by various demons.

The passage beginning with "One should know" concludes that the samādhis of Māras and externalists are not genuine, because the samādhis of external paths do not flow forth from True Suchness (*tathatā*);
rather, they all arise from the two delusions of views and thoughts, and from the two attachments to self and phenomena. They are [empty].
This is not because of a craving for fame, profit, or honor. One should know that to falsely claim to practice for the sake of fame and profit is a delusion.
To feign a solemn appearance out of a desire for respect, speaking of emptiness with every word while dwelling on existence with every thought—all such things are the works of Māra.
How can one not be cautious? Master Fu’s verse says: "The dependent nature arises from a single thought; both are products of delusion."

[The views] proceed and thus divide into sixty-three. Nine hundred [errors] run wild both lengthwise and crosswise. (The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Those of meager virtue and little merit, oppressed by manifold sufferings, enter the dense forest of false views—such as 'it exists' or 'it does not exist.

Relying upon these various views, they possess all sixty-two. The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* says: Regarding the sixty-two views, if one gives rise to them within each of the five aggregates, there are twenty for the four [aggregates] and one [for form], totaling twenty.

With twenty for each of the three time periods, they total sixty. Adding the two views that the body is the self and that the body and the self are distinct, they total sixty-two views. [Regarding the first], it is said: within the aggregate of form, form itself is the self; apart from form, there is no self; within the self..."

Form; within form there is a self (these four being present throughout the five aggregates). If one can constantly perform this contemplation—that what has passed away is extinguished yet not extinguished, and that what is yet to come arises yet does not arise—then truth and falsehood will be seen as level and even.

As for the samādhi of *tathatā* (suchness): one does not dwell upon the mark of seeing, nor does one dwell upon the mark of attainment; even upon emerging from meditative concentration, there is no indolence or arrogance.
All afflictions gradually become thin and subtle. If ordinary persons do not practice this method of samādhi, it is impossible for them to enter the lineage of the Tathāgata.
This is because those who cultivate worldly dhyānas and samādhis frequently give rise to attachment to their flavors.
It is an attachment based on the view of self, bound to the three realms, and shared with non-Buddhists; for if one is not protected by a virtuous friend, the views of non-Buddhists will arise.

The former statement refers to what resembles samādhi; this statement refers to true samādhi. Although one remains within meditative concentration, one does not perceive the characteristics of concentration because there is no conceptual discrimination.
One does not perceive the characteristics of attainment because there is no craving or attachment.
That all afflictions gradually become subtle and thin is the evidence of attaining concentration. This continues until, even upon emerging from concentration, one does not give rise to indolence.

"Arrogance" refers precisely to not being diligent while in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), yet becoming lax and negligent upon emerging from it; or not maintaining a mind of reverence while in concentration, yet harboring arrogance upon emerging from it.
This serves as a counter-illustration to show that the application of the mind must be single-minded, regardless of whether one is in or out of concentration.
The phrase "If those below... concludes by clarifying that only one who practices true *samādhi* possesses the correct cause.

One enters the lineage of the Tathāgata by practicing the lower [stages]. This concludes the explanation that practicing what resembles samādhi inevitably leads to falling into the realm of Māras and outsiders.
Worldly samādhis include the four dhyānas, the eight concentrations, the attainment of non-conception, and so forth; because these have not yet emptied the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*).

Because one has views and attachments regarding the objects of meditative concentration, a wise person composes this verse: "Without having reached the principle of True Suchness (tathatā), One abandons the self and enters the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Regarding sentient beings and a life-principle (jīva), All such perceptions of seeing are entirely false. If one awakens to the path of Bodhi,"
Seeking further liberation on the other shore, one should understand the characteristics of phenomena and non-characteristics in this manner.
Furthermore, those who diligently and single-mindedly cultivate this samādhi shall obtain ten kinds of benefits in the present life.

What are the ten? First, one will always be protected and remembered by the Buddhas of the ten directions and by Bodhisattvas (to cultivate true suchness is to cultivate the mind of the Buddhas of the ten directions).
Second, one cannot be terrified by any demons or malevolent spirits. Third, one will not be deluded or disturbed by the ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist paths or by ghosts and spirits.
Fourth, one will remain far removed from slandering the profound Dharma and from the karmic obstructions of grave offenses.
Gradually they become thin and faint. Fifth, one extinguishes all doubts and all evil discursive thoughts (*vitarka-vicāra*). Sixth, one’s faith in the realm of all Tathāgatas increases.
Seventh, one remains free from sorrow and regret, being courageous and undaunted within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Eighth, their resolve is gentle and flexible; they abandon arrogance and are not troubled by others.
