Ninth, although they have not yet attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*), at all times and in all objective spheres, they are able to diminish afflictions and take no pleasure in the world.
Tenth, if they do attain *samādhi*, they are not startled or disturbed by external conditions or any sounds.

This reveals that those who cultivate the true samādhi obtain benefits in the present life. Those who are protected and remembered by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do so because this is the treasury of the eye of the True Dharma (*saddharmacakṣur-garbha*).
That demons and ghosts cannot terrify them is because the seed within the central tree remains unmoved.
They cannot be deluded by non-Buddhists because they possess the "fixed compass" that distinguishes between consciousness and wisdom.
They remain far removed from slander because they have deep faith in *tathatā* (suchness) and thus incur no fault of slandering the Dharma.

They extinguish all doubt because, having already attained right faith, there is nothing left for doubt to arise. Their faith increases and flourishes, beginning with faith, followed by understanding and practice, and culminating in realization.
Because they have realized and entered [the truth], they are not cowed by birth and death; this is because they have already perfected the adamantine jewel-like awakening (*vajra-bodhi*).

They abandon arrogance because they know that all phenomena are equal and non-dual. They diminish afflictions and take no pleasure in the world because worldly flavors are thin and insipid, while their aspiration for the Path is profound and intense.
Their voices are not startled or moved because their inner mind does not issue forth, nor is it affected by external [objects].
Because the objective realm does not enter [the mind]. Master Fu’s verse says: “The faculty of faith gives rise to a single thought, Which all Buddhas are able to know.
The cause for birth arises on this very day; The realization of the fruit occurs at a future time. Throughout three great eons and many kalpas, The six perfections are long practiced and bestowed.
When these have perfumed the seeds of the outflow-free, Only then is one called ‘inconceivable.’”
Furthermore, if a person practices only *śamatha* (calm abiding), the mind will become sunken or indolent; they will take no delight in various virtues and remain distant from great compassion.

Therefore, one should practice *vipaśyanā* (insight). One who cultivates insight should contemplate that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) in the world cannot endure for long and are subject to momentary change and decay. All mental activities arise and perish in every thought-moment. By means of this—
Therefore, it is suffering. One should contemplate all dharmas remembered in the past as being as fleeting as a dream.
One should contemplate all dharmas remembered in the present as being like a flash of lightning. One should contemplate all dharmas remembered in the future as being like clouds that suddenly arise.
One should contemplate all embodied beings in the world as entirely impure, defiled in various ways, and not a single one [is pure].
There is that which is delightful. One should thus reflect upon all sentient beings:
from time beginningless, because they have all been perfumed by ignorance, their minds undergo arising and ceasing, whereby they have already undergone all manner of great suffering of body and mind.

Even now, they are subject to immeasurable oppression; the suffering they will face in the future is likewise without limit. Yet, this suffering is difficult to relinquish and difficult to escape, and they remain unaware of it.
Sentient beings are thus; they are truly to be pitied. Having reflected in this way, one should immediately and courageously establish a great vow:
"May my mind be free from conceptual discrimination, and may I cultivate all virtuous merits throughout the ten directions."
Until the end of the future, by means of immeasurable skillful means, they shall rescue and deliver all sentient beings suffering from affliction,
causing them to attain the ultimate bliss of *nirvāṇa*. Because they have given rise to such vows, at all times and in all places,

they shall practice and study all manner of wholesome deeds according to their capacity, never abandoning them, with minds free from indolence— except when sitting in meditation, during which time they shall maintain single-minded mindfulness.
Regarding cessation (*śamatha*), if there is anything else whatsoever, one should examine in every respect what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
Whether walking, standing, lying down, or rising, one should always practice both cessation and insight (*vipaśyanā*) together. That is to say:

although one contemplates that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is unarisen, one simultaneously contemplates that through the conjunction of causes and conditions, the karma of good and evil and its retributions of suffering and pleasure are neither lost nor destroyed. Although...
One contemplates the causal conditions of the retribution of good and evil karma, yet simultaneously realizes that the nature [of these phenomena] is ungraspable;

this refers to the cultivation of *vipaśyanā* (insight). If one cultivates *śamatha* (calm abiding), and the mind becomes sunken, it is because one is attached to the state of stillness and refuses to let go—this is what the ancients likened to a withered stump or stagnant water. Alternatively, if laziness arises, it is simply...
One contemplates emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). "Not delighting in various virtues" means not seeking the Buddha-way.
"Being far removed from great compassion" means not delighting in the salvation of sentient beings. As it is said, "At night, it is difficult to turn one's body outside the curtain";

therefore, one should cultivate contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) to remedy this. Regarding the section on "cultivation": this causes the practitioner to contemplate in general that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) in the world...
For a long time, the activities of the mind have not been constant. Sentient beings are greedily attached; they do not perceive and do not know, and for this reason they undergo suffering.
One should contemplate the past and so forth, contemplating that all phenomena are without self. One should contemplate the world and so forth, contemplating that the body is impure.
"Thus, below" refers to contemplating that the mind is impermanent. "Having already received, below" refers to contemplating that sensation is suffering.

"The multitude of beings, below" refers to recollecting the suffering of sentient beings and giving rise to the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). "Performing this, below" refers to giving rise to the two kinds of great vows for self-benefit and benefiting others.
"By means of arising, below" refers to cultivating and accumulating all wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma*). "Only excluding, below" refers to the time of tranquility.
One should focus exclusively on *śamatha* (calm abiding) alone. At all other times when there is movement, one should practice both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* (insight) together.
This means that entering the various *dhyānas* with a single, unmoving mind is called *śamatha*, while realizing that objects are unarisen is named *prajñā*.

Just as a chariot requires two wheels and a bird requires two wings, neither can be lacking. This section clarifies the dual practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. [From] the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
It is said: "There is no self, no limit, and no experiencer; yet the karma of good and evil is never lost. Thus, the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) states:

"As a sovereign of the kingdom of Dharma, by means of these two powers, one reaches the bottom of the sea of birth and death. This is entirely dependent upon the dual cultivation [of wisdom and skillful means].
Dispelling delusive confusion is like the wind blowing away clouds; shattering ignorant darkness is like the sun illuminating the world."
It stirs the deep thorns of false views and uproots the thick roots of ignorance. It serves as the yin and yang for the ocean of Great Enlightenment and acts as the parents of the Jewel Flower King.
It prepares the foundation for the One Vehicle and fortifies the walls and fences of the myriad practices.
Through this correspondence, one is able to enter the Mirror of the School (Zongjing). Master Fu’s verse says:

"Like stars, cataracts, lamps, and illusions, All serve as metaphors for impermanence. Wang Rixiu commented: "Regarding 'like stars,' it means they appear when it is dark and vanish when it is light; this metaphorizes how sentient beings exist due to the darkness of ignorance. If they attain clear awakening, these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) cease to exist.

Regarding 'like cataracts,' it means that sentient beings possess inner radiance which is obscured by conditioned phenomena, just as a film obstructs the eyes. Regarding 'like lamps,' it means they are used when it is dark and not used when it is light; this metaphorizes..."

Sentient beings employ conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) because they are mired in ignorance and darkness; once enlightened, they no longer employ them. That which is "like an illusion" refers to conditioned phenomena, for they are not real or substantial. The outflowing consciousness (*āsrava-vijñāna*) cultivates causes and effects; who says these endure for long?
They are as precarious and fragile as bubbles or dew, like the shadow of clouds or a flash of lightning. Even if one were to pass through eighty thousand eons, [they would still perish].
In the end, one falls into emptiness and oblivion. The Great Master Zhiyi’s verse on Perfect Realization (*pariniṣpanna*) says: When characteristics are stilled, names are also dispelled;

when the mind merges, objects likewise vanish. Coming and going can never be seen; speaking and remaining silent are forever without fixed direction. When wisdom enters the principle of perfect realization, [all is complete].

The body is identical to the *dharmatā* and eternal; having realized the truth, one returns to understand the conventional. Without ceasing, one manifests as a bridge for others. Master Fu’s verse on the Gate of *Samādhi* (*Cessation*) says:
"The river of meditation follows the stillness of the waves; the water of concentration pursues the clarity of the ripples. Purifying the spirit gives rise to the nature of awakening."
Calm the mind to extinguish deluded attachments; pervasive conceptualization is empty discrimination. From the beginning, names have been provisionally established.

If one realizes the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), there is no separate *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature). Furthermore, regarding the gate of wisdom-contemplation: the lamp of wisdom is like the bright sun;

the aggregates (*skandhas*) and elements (*dhātus*) are like a city of *gandharvas*. [Zi Rong says: A "city of *gandharvas*" refers to a city of *gandharvas*. It is a manifestation produced by the residual vapors of dragons and mirages upon the sea. People see towers and pavilions, which suddenly vanish. This refutes the delusions of sentient beings.]

Grasping the five aggregates and the physical body as real, when light comes, darkness immediately departs, leaving no leisure for even a moment’s pause. As the deluded mind has not yet been extinguished, one perceives the forms of self and others;
when the perfect illumination of wondrous wisdom shines forth, there remains only the name of "emptiness."

If one cultivates *śamatha*, it serves as an antidote to the ordinary person’s attachment to the mundane world and enables the relinquishing of the timid views of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
If one cultivates *vipaśyanā*, it serves as an antidote to the fault of the two vehicles’ failure to give rise to great compassion and their inferior state of mind;

it also distances one from the ordinary person’s failure to cultivate roots of goodness. For this reason, these gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* mutually assist and perfect one another, never being separated.
If one lacks both *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), one will be unable to enter the path to Bodhi.
This clarifies that the functions of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* each have their respective remedies. Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are attached to the world and cannot relinquish it;
those of the Two Vehicles (*dviyānika*) fail to realize non-arising and thus fear birth and death. Therefore, one is instructed to cultivate *śamatha* to remedy these conditions.
Those of the Two Vehicles do not give rise to great compassion without contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), and ordinary beings do not give rise to roots of goodness without contemplation;
therefore, one is made to cultivate contemplation to remedy this. That is to say: by contemplating emptiness, the myriad practices boil forth;

by engaging with existence, the single path remains pure. From here below, the practitioner is concluded: one must certainly practice cessation (*śamatha*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) together, supporting and perfecting each other. Necessarily...
They are not separate. If these two gates are not both present, one is incapable of entering the Path. The Great Master Zhiyi composed a verse stating:

"Throughout three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the myriad practices were cultivated in their entirety. Having realized the non-existence of self and others, one forever relies upon the flow of the Noble Path."

Only through the two kinds of emptiness does one gradually realize (the contemplation of the emptiness of both person and phenomena); in samādhi (Sanskrit for *samādhi*, here translated as "right concentration" or "cessation"), one wanders at will.
Having newly dwelt on the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), one constantly delights and is thus free from sorrow.
Furthermore, when sentient beings first study this Dharma and seek to attain right faith, their minds may become timid and weak.
Because they dwell in this Sahā world, they fear that they will not always be able to encounter the Buddhas to personally receive them and make offerings;
they dread that the mind of faith will be difficult to accomplish and thus intend to retreat. You should know that the Tathāgata possesses supreme skillful means to gather in and protect such faith.

This means that by means of the causal conditions of single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha, one will, in accordance with one's vows, be born in a buddha-land in another direction and constantly behold the Buddha, forever leaving the evil realms behind.

As it is said in the Sūtra: "If a person single-mindedly mindfully recollects Amitābha Buddha in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss (where ordinary beings and sages dwell together), and dedicates the roots of goodness they have cultivated toward the vow to be born in that world, they shall immediately attain rebirth there. Constantly...

Because they behold the Buddha, they shall never fall back. If they contemplate that Buddha’s *tathatā-dharmakāya* (True Suchness Dharma-body) and constantly and diligently practice it, they will ultimately attain birth [in that realm], for they abide in right concentration and wisdom (*samyak-samādhi-prajñā*). Thus has been explained the section on the cultivation of faith.

The above has opened five gates to cause people to focus their minds and have self-confidence that they are originally Buddhas, thereby directly accepting this truth and further practicing various deeds to refine themselves.

Below this, for those who seek to enter right faith but possess timid hearts, the Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance (Nienfo) is separately opened. The Buddhas are difficult to encounter—this is the first fear. Faith...

It is difficult to give rise to [this mind], for there are two fears. With the mind harboring these two fears, one intends to retreat and fall back into the realms of humans and devas or the Two Vehicles.
Therefore, a distinct skillful means is opened up to lead them to recite the Buddha’s name: first, to protect and sustain their faith so that it may reach fulfillment;

second, to allow them to be reborn according to their vows so that they may behold the Buddha. To speak of "single-mindedness" means that pure mindfulness continues in succession, with the one mind undiverted.
This is confusion. Regarding the causal conditions of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection): the Buddha is the primary cause (*zhengyin*), and recollection is the auxiliary condition (*zuyuan*).

It is only through the harmony of these causes and conditions that one can behold the Buddha. Since the Buddha’s body is omnipresent, it is simply because one’s intention is not single-minded and one’s recollection is not earnest.
Because it is not easily encountered, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are the body of the Dharma-realm;

they enter into the thoughts within the minds of all sentient beings. Therefore, when one contemplates the Buddha with the mind, that very mind is endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. Thus, the Buddhas [are truly...]
The Ocean of Universal Knowledge arises from the mind and thoughts. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"If sentient beings recollect the Buddha and think of the Buddha, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present or in the future. Having seen the Buddha, their faith will certainly never regress. Therefore, [one should practice].
If one contemplates the lower [stages], this is precisely the observation of who it is that practices mindfulness of the Buddha.

This shares the same path as the contemplator of non-thought (*amala-vijñāna*), yet differs in its method, because one ultimately attains birth and abiding in right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"O Mahāmati, you should know that after the Parinirvāṇa of the Sugata, there will be a bhikṣu of great fame and virtue in the land of South India."
His title was Nāgārjuna; he was able to shatter the doctrines of existence and non-existence. In this world, he manifested my Unsurpassed Mahāyāna Dharma.

He attained the first stage, the Stage of Joy, and was reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss. Therefore, know that both Zen meditation and the recitation of the Buddha’s name are swift paths to liberation.
One who can single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name will surely be like one who is resolute in intent to practice Zen. Recite the Buddha’s name!
Yet their minds are not focused; they practice *chan* (meditation) without resolute intent.
For those who wish to be reborn in the Pure Land and see their nature to achieve Buddhahood, this is truly difficult. The *Ten Doubts about the Pure Land* asks:
"The essence of all phenomena is empty, originally unarisen, and equally quiescent. To now abandon this and seek that—does this not contradict reason? The Sūtra says: "The Pure Land..."
First purify the mind; when the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. How is this to be reconciled? Answer: First, there is a general response.

If it is said that seeking rebirth in the Western Land constitutes abandoning this to seek that and is thus contrary to principle, then your own insistence on remaining here without seeking rebirth in the West constitutes abandoning that to cling to this;
this, in turn, becomes a sickness and is likewise contrary to principle. Furthermore, [the argument] turns...
Furthermore, one who does not seek birth in that [other world] nor seek birth in this [world] eliminates the view of annihilationism.

This is the second specific answer. Now, as for "neither arising nor ceasing": within the conditions for arising, the various dharmas come together and do not maintain their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If one seeks the essence of arising, it cannot be found. When this arising occurs, it comes from nowhere; therefore, it is called "non-arising."
When all phenomena disperse, they do not maintain their own nature; thus one says, "I am dispersing and ceasing. At the time of this dispersal and cessation, there is nowhere to which one goes;
therefore, it is said that there is no extinction. This does not mean that apart from what arises through causes and conditions, there exists something else that is neither born nor extinguished.

Nor does it mean that one should not seek birth in a Pure Land and instead call that "non-arising. As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Of those phenomena produced by causes and conditions, I say..."
This is emptiness; it is also called provisional designation, and it is also called the meaning of the Middle Way.

Furthermore, all phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another, nor from both together, nor without cause; therefore, one knows that there is no arising. As the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
Although they know that all Buddha-lands and sentient beings are empty, they constantly cultivate pure lands and transform all classes of living beings.
The wise person zealously seeks birth in a pure land, yet realizes that the essence of birth is unattainable; this is true non-arising.
This is what is meant by "when the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. The deluded person is bound by birth; upon hearing of birth, they immediately [grasp it as real].

They give rise to conceptual interpretations; hearing of non-arising, they immediately form the interpretation of non-arising. They do not know that arising is itself non-arising and non-arising is itself arising.
Failing to penetrate this principle, they arbitrarily engage in disputes over right and wrong, resenting others who seek birth in the Pure Land—how much slander this is!
"This person is a slanderer of the Dharma, a heretic of false views. Thus, it is said in the *Jingtu huiwen* (Questions on the Pure Land):
"Those who practice Chan meditation should most earnestly recite the Buddha's name. Should their faculties be dull, they may fear that they will not attain great awakening in this life;

therefore, they should temporarily rely on the power of Amitābha’s vows to be received and led to rebirth there. It further states: "If you recite the Buddha's name and are not reborn in the Pure Land, I, the old monk..."
"One shall fall into the Hell of the Severed Tongue. Zen Master Zhenxie Liao’s *Discourse on the Pure Land* states:
"The single school of the Dongshan lineage all realize through secret cultivation. What is the reason for this? It is truly because the Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance is a direct path of practice;

it directly accords with the Great Canon to receive those of the highest capacity, while indirectly guiding those of middling and lower capacities. It further says: "This is the way of the Buddhas and the Patriarchs."
Whether in the Exoteric Teachings or in Chan, all cultivate pure karma and return to the same single source.
Once one enters this gate, all immeasurable Dharma-gates are fully realized and entered. This is as true for Tianyi Huai, Yuanzhao Ben, Cishou Shen, and Nanyue Huisi.
Fazhao, Jing’ai, Datong, Huaiyu, Daozhen, Fazhen, Shouna, Beijian Jian, Tianmu Li, and other great elders were all masters of the Chan school.
Their secret cultivation and public teaching in propagating the principles of the Pure Land were identical, though not explicitly agreed upon.
How could it be that only these elders were thus? I have heard an elder say: [The passage continues with the list of names and their shared intent.]
Combining the five schools of the lineage, all Zen monks throughout the world—whether enlightened or unenlightened—there is not one who does not return to the Pure Land.
Master Baizhang Hai was the dharma heir of Mazu; from ancient times to the present, no monastery in the world has dared to contravene even a single matter of his regulations.
Observe how he recited for a sick monk, chanting a verse to extol [the Buddha].
"Amitābha. Again, they recite the Buddha's name together one hundred thousand times. The dedication says: "While remaining causes have not yet been exhausted, may we swiftly attain light ease;

though the great life-span is difficult to escape, may we go directly to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing. Furthermore, when escorting a deceased monk, one says: "The spirit transcends to the pure realm, and karma is shed from worldly toil.
May the lotus flower of the highest grade bloom, and may the Buddha grant the prediction of enlightenment in this very life. [Then follows] the cremation.
At that moment, one should draw out the voice and chant "Amitābha Buddha" loudly; with ten chants and ten responses, one assists others in their rebirth.

Is this not the ultimate destination of the Pure Land teachings? Since the time of Baizhang, all have relied upon this method. Thus, it is surely the case that there are no Chan monks who do not return to the Pure Land.
For this reason, throughout both the Eastern Land and the Western Regions, there are none who do not [rely on this].
This constitutes the ultimate goal and destination. That the Master of the Treatise placed this chapter at the end of the "Section on Cultivating Faith" was also deeply intentional;
it was not a mere forced arrangement. Those who harbor doubts may now place their trust in this principle.
Next, the section on the benefits of exhortation to practice is explained.
This section exhorts people to advance in their cultivation so that they will certainly obtain great benefit.
Such is the Mahāyāna, the secret treasury of all Buddhas, which I have now explained in summary. If there are sentient beings who wish to [attain] the Tathāgata...
Upon entering this profound realm, one attains right faith, remains free from slander, and enters the path of the Mahāyāna;
one should uphold this treatise, contemplate it, and practice it, for through these means one will ultimately reach the unsurpassed way.

If, having heard this Dharma, a person does not give rise to cowardice or weakness, know that this person will certainly succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas (in the causal stage) and will surely receive the prediction of enlightenment from all the Buddhas.
"Thus, below," concludes the preceding text. "If there is, below," encourages the benefit gained from practicing Zen meditation.
"Holding" means not letting go. "Contemplating" means striving with all one's might to reach the ultimate. "Cultivating" means permeating the mind moment by moment.
"Ultimately reaching the Unsurpassed Way" refers to the attainment of benefit. If, upon hearing this, one proceeds with courage...

One may give rise to timidity and weakness. However, if this person’s contemplation of principle is clear and both their practice of the Dharma and observance of the precepts are urgent, then they can accomplish the goal within a single lifetime and will certainly succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas.
Therefore, it is said: "If a single phrase permeates the spirit, one will surely become a Buddha; if a single word passes through the ear, [the result follows]."
For seven generations they shall not sink. In the past, a mud crab was reborn in heaven after listening to the Dharma; a stable elephant ceased its evil ways upon hearing a sutra;
a bhikṣu attained the fruit of the path through laughter; and a woman realized emptiness through reflection.
How much more so for one who hears this Great Liberation Dharma-gate of single-mindedness! The *Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra* states: "First, it reveals the arising of freedom from doubt."

Regarding those who enter the gateway of merit through faith: it refers to sentient beings who, having heard this Mahāyāna Dharma-gate that is profoundly deep, most sublime, and vast, do not harbor doubt or fear within their hearts, nor do they feel cowardice, nor do they treat it with contempt, nor do they slander it;
rather, they give rise to a mind of certainty, a firm and steadfast mind, a mind of reverence, and a mind of affectionate respect.

You should know that such a person is a true child of the Buddha. They do not sever the lineage of the Buddha, they do not sever the lineage of the Dharma, and they do not sever the lineage of the Saṃgha.
These lineages continue in constant succession, increasing from one to another until the end of the future.
Furthermore, such a person is personally granted a prophecy by all Buddhas and is protected and remembered by all immeasurable bodhisattvas.
Suppose there were someone who could transform all sentient beings filling the three-thousandfold world system and cause them to practice the ten wholesome paths of action;

this would not equal the merit of another person who, for the duration of a single meal, correctly contemplates this Dharma. The latter’s merit surpasses the former’s beyond measure, such that no analogy can express it.
This statement demonstrates the superior gateway of the counteractive measure through analogy.

That is to say, suppose there were someone capable of gathering and transforming all sentient beings throughout a trichiliocosm, without exception, causing them all to practice the ten wholesome actions;
or suppose there were another being who, for the duration of a single meal, were to contemplate and investigate this profound [teaching]. If one were to weigh these two [acts] against one another...
Regarding the merits of these two persons: the merits of the first person are extremely slight, like a mustard seed ground into one hundred parts.
The merits of this second person are exceedingly vast, like the number of atoms produced by pulverizing the worlds of the ten directions.
(However, as for how a person could transform a trichiliocosm, this is merely a metaphor; it is used to express that [the former's merit] is utterly incomparable.)
Furthermore, if a person upholds this treatise and observes its practice, the merit they accrue in a single day and night is immeasurable and boundless, beyond description.

Even if all the Buddhas of the ten directions were each to speak of that merit for immeasurable and boundless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they could not exhaust it. Why is this? It is because of the nature of the Dharma.
Because the qualities of the nature (*dharmatā-guṇa*) are inexhaustible, the merit of this person is likewise so; it is without limit or boundary.
This refers to the gateway of praising the merit of receiving and upholding [this teaching]. "Receiving" means to directly accept and internalize it;

"upholding" means to practice and maintain it from time to time. That is to say, if there is someone who receives and upholds this treatise, examines its principles, and practices according to reality...
If one practices for even a single day or a single night, the merit attained therein will be immeasurable, boundless, ineffable, and inconceivable.
Why is this? Because all words and letters are subsumed within the observation of one’s own mind.
Therefore, the attainment does not depend on the length of years or months; rather, in a single moment of thought, one immediately enters reality.

The truth is such that its nature is luminously transparent. If one further applies diligent effort and vigor, receiving it without forgetting it in the mind, upholding it without weariness over time, and explaining it so that all may hear and know it, one will not only awaken to the nature of oneself, but will also awaken the nature of hundreds of millions of people;
the merit of this is unsurpassed. How could it be otherwise?

How could one even conceive of describing it? Suppose all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time were each to take as many tongues as there are atoms in the worlds of the ten directions,
and each were to praise all the merits of that person for as many unspeakable eons as there are atoms in the worlds of the ten directions— even then, they would not be able to [exhaust them].

It is inexhaustible. Because the merit of the Dharmakāya’s true suchness (tathatā) is equal to the realm of empty space and is without limit, the merit obtained in a single day and night is already inconceivable;
how much more so for two days, or three days, or even for countless days, if one upholds, recites, contemplates, observes, and practices according to reality—this is truly inconceivable.

Is this not something inconceivable within the deliberations [of the assembly]? Therefore, one should know that those who believe in this True Doctrine must serve it with earnest devotion and practice it;
only then can they accord with True Suchness (Tathatā) and transcend the world.

If, however, one merely travels about engaging in lofty talk and grand discourse, being able to preach and write, one will externally deceive and delude the people of the world, while internally deceiving oneself.

Regarding one's own virtue: if one studies extensively only for the sake of fame and gain, yet willingly remains self-exposed and self-abandoned without practicing, such a person who understands the principles in this way is called a thief within the Dharma-gate.

Because they oppose the nature of reality (dharmatā) and constantly take rebirth in the three evil realms, how could they possess immeasurable and boundless merit to be praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions?
Furthermore, the Buddhas of the ten directions praise his merit for upholding this treatise, investigating its principles, and practicing according to reality.
Thus, one should know that by believing in this True Doctrine (Saddharma), one accomplishes the Mahāyāna—the realization of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
How could its principles ever be exhausted? It is the vehicle upon which the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions ride; its merit is boundless.
It may be said that the nectar has entered the crown of the head and the refined essence has been poured into the heart.

It illuminates the lamp of non-dual wisdom, shattering the dark delusions of the sensory faculties; it pours forth the water of single-flavored gnosis, washing away the false dust upon the ground of the mind.
It can cause thick obstructions and deep veils to be swept away like dangerous leaves by a violent wind, and dense doubts and accumulated stagnations to be evaporated as if by the scorching sun.
Like thin ice; like the Golden-Wheel King among all kings; like the morning sun among all illuminations;
like the mani-jewel among all jewels; like the blue lotus among all flowers;
like the gateway of true emptiness among all truths; like nirvana among all dharmas.
Therefore, those who encounter this teaching should rejoice within themselves.
As for those sentient beings who, regarding this treatise, slander it and do not believe in it, the roots of sin they incur will persist for immeasurable kalpas.

They will experience great suffering and distress. Therefore, sentient beings should simply rely on faith and must not slander it, for to do so would deeply harm themselves as well as others, severing the seeds of the Triple Gem.
This is because all Tathāgatas attain nirvāṇa by relying upon this Dharma, and all Bodhisattvas enter the Buddha-wisdom by practicing according to it. You should know this.
Bodhisattvas of the past have already attained pure faith by relying on this Dharma; bodhisattvas of the present are now attaining pure faith by relying on this Dharma;
and bodhisattvas of the future shall attain pure faith by relying on this Dharma. Therefore, sentient beings—
One should diligently practice and study.

First, it was stated that one incurs sin by slandering; therefore, the following section concludes by exhorting one to have faith. The phrase "Because of the profound" [and so forth] explains the reason why one incurs sin through slander and defamation.
The phrase "One should know" [and so forth] concludes by exhorting one to practice for the sake of attaining benefit.

The profound and vast meaning of all Buddhas, I now explain in accordance with the *dhāraṇī*. May this merit be dedicated according to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) for the universal benefit of the entire realm of sentient beings.
The first phrase concludes the meaning; the second phrase concludes the text; the third and fourth phrases dedicate the merit to sentient beings.
*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra-anuṭīkā*, Scroll Lower (End).
Written by the Bhikṣu Yuán-hóng-rùn of Fúshèng Ān, Shàoyìng County, Shànghǎi Prefecture, Zhèjiāng, while residing in Hángzhōu.
Carefully excerpted at Tōjō-ji Temple in Jōkyō Castle on the twelfth day of the fourth month in the third year of the Kaei era; strictly prohibited from being recorded.
